layout_dets.text: 本社编辑部

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Introduction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: This is a ‘concise dictionary' and it is ‘of linguistics'. What should such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a book be like and what should it include?

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Linguistics is defined in general dictionaries as ‘the science of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language' or 'the scientific study of language'. In the more cautious

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: wording of The New Shorter Oxford English Dictionary, it is 'the branch of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: knowledge that deals with language'. But although it is the only

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: academic discipline that deals with language alone, and there are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aspects of language that it alone is concerned with, its practitioners

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cannot claim a monopoly of the whole of their subject matter. A range

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of other disciplines, from the study of literature to computer science,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: deal with language in one way or another, and the boundaries

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between them and linguistics are not fixed. It would indeed be a pity if

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: they were. How far into these should the entries in this dictionary go?

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: differently.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Let us start from the centre and work outwards. Everyone will agree

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that grammar, in a wider or narrower sense, is part of linguistics: in its

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: widest sense, it includes both the study of the structure of words and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of syntactic constructions, and that of sound systems. In the second

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: half of the twentieth century these fields have seen an explosive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: development of technical theory, and a great deal of this dictionary is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: taken up with it. Everyone will agree that linguistics is concerned with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the lexical and grammatical categories of individual languages, with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: differences between one type of language and another, and with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: historical relations within families of languages. These are potentially

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bottomless pits, and strict limitations are needed to avoid falling

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: into them; but I hope I have included what users will judge to be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: important. Many languages are both spoken and written, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: although the nature and history of writing systems are not always

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: covered in university courses in linguistics, it is hard to see in what

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: other dictionary one might expect to look them up. Apart from the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: details of individual systems and the technicalities of their description,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: there are also issues of general theory that belong to linguistics alone:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that of change in language is one of them. But beyond this there are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: problems, and it has to be acknowledged that in a number of cases,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: involving both single entries and classes of entry, I could have decided

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Should I, for example, have included entries for parsing strategies in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: computational linguistics? The name of this field suggests that it is a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: branch of linguistics and certainly, once upon a time, it was. But it has

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: increasingly become a part of computer science, addressing problems

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of its own that do not bear, and quite properly are no longer claimed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to bear, on the nature of language as such. I have therefore asked

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: myself whether someone whose interests are centred on the topics

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that linguists must know about is any poorer, as a linguist, for not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Introduction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: VIII

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: knowing this field as well, and, after some soul-searching, have drawn

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in my net accordingly. The same test has been applied to other aspects

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of language or speech processing, and to much of, for example, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: traditional terminology of rhetoric. It also applies to the study

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of methods in language teaching, which, as part of what is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conventionally called 'applied linguistics', again appears, at first sight,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to belong to our subject. But we are past the days when this was seen

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as literally an application of linguistics, and linguists in general do not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: still expect to gain many insights from it. A further test wás whether,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in drafting an entry, the terms on which a definition would rest are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: themselves terms in linguistics or in à field that is clearly separate.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A dictionary of linguistics cannot systematically include things that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: belong to computer science in general, or to acoustics, or to anatomy

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or physiology, or to general psychology or the social sciences, even

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: when, as terms in neighbouring subjects, they are used by linguists in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: some branches of their own. But it would frustrate the reader if other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: entries were then to take them for granted. In some cases this has

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: forced me to cut corners: something must be in and, even if its

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: explanation has to be less precise than a technical definition would be,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it may at least be possible for readers who need the relevant entry to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: get some help from it. In other cases even circumlocution has failed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and, where the term is marginal, I have judged it safer to leave it out

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The need to cut corners was most pressing in some areas of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonetics and of semantics. Acoustics is not in general part of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: linguistics; nor, at least as I conceive it, are topics such as the anatomy

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the larynx. But some specific terms in acoustics are, and the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinctions between different types of phonation, which is à hard

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: enough topic in our present state of knowledge, might be made more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: precise if anatomical detail could be assumed. Philosophy and logic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are not part of linguistics either, but the literature on semantics is full

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of terms that derive from them. Many have a long history and are not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: univocal; sometimes their use by linguists reflects this only in part;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sometimes, as linguists have borrowed them, their senses have slid yet

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: further. But since they do belong to another discipline, a dictionary of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: linguistics sometimes cannot do more than pick up a fag end. It is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: perhaps in this area that I feel least happy with the solutions I have at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: times been driven to.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In the centre of the subject it is, of course, much easier both to lay

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: down principles and to apply them. Since this is a dictionary, it does

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not include entries that are purely encyclopaedic. Since it is a concise

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dictionary, my aim has been to explain as many things as possible

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and as briefly as possible, not, as might be done in another kind of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dictionary, to cover less but cover it more expansively. But some things

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: have to be left out. There must, for example, be entries for some

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: individual languages: those that have speakers safely into the millions,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: those that are important in the history of scholarship, those that,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: quite simply, the majority of those who wili buy this book will feel

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ix

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Introduction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: they should be able to look up. But most languages meet none of these

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: criteria and, however one counts, they are well in the thousands. There

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: should, I believe, be notes on individual scholars, some of them still

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: living. But which? I have tried to limit such entries to people who are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cited for their contribution to general linguistics, as opposed to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: study of a particular language or family. But if I had relaxed that test

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the list could have gone on and on. There must also be entries for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: schools, or for the competing models of syntax, phonology, and so on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that tend to define schools. Where these are more than one-man bands

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: they are, I hope, in. But both schools and individual scholars also tend

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to develop specialized terminology, both new terms and altered senses

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of old ones. These sometimes pass into general currency and then, of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: would again have been much larger.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: course, they must be included. But where they remain peculiar to a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: specific model, and are not needed in the entry that explains the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: model itself, I have had to leave them out. If I had not, the dictionary

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: There must also be limits on what certain classes of entry contain.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Under the headings for individual languages, I have said at the least

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: where they are spoken and what family, if any, they are known to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: belong to. But I have not in general said how many people speak them,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and in most cases I do not think this information can be given without

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reference to surveys at specific dates and the specific evidence and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: criteria that they used. That is more than a concise dictionary can or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: should do. I have also refrained from saying anything about their

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure: it would, for a start, take more space than can be spared.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In the entries for grammatical categories, I have given concrete

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: illustrations where they can be drawn from languages with which a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: substantial body of readers will be familiar. These naturally tend to be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: European. Where this cannot be done the illustrations are schematic. I

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: had not at first intended that they should be and, in failing to decorate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: some entries in this way, I still feel rather as my wife would if she were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: forced to go to town without make-up. But decoration is, in reality, all

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it would be. A monograph or textbook must, of course, supply specific

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: evidence that a category exists. But a dictionary need not and cannot.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Its job is simply to make clear how the term is used, and a concrete

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: illustration will at best get in the way if it comes from a language

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which few readers know and whose general structure is unfamiliar. At

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: worst, there was a danger that I would misunderstand my source or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: use one that was itself wrong and, without references, no one might

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: know what it was. I would like to feel that, if there are mistakes, they

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are unequivocally my own.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The rest is mainly a matter of style. In line with other Oxford

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dictionaries, I have used an asterisk to point to related entries:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: although its uses in linguistics are for other purposes, I do not think

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that, in practice, this will cause confusion. Where I refer to scholars

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for whom there are also entries, I have used their surname without

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: initials, with a first name in brackets where necessary: thus 'Chomsky'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Introduction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: X

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or '(Daniel) Jones'. Where an abbreviation is common I have given an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: entry for it, unless it immediately precedes the term it abbreviates:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thus 'ABs = absolutive'. The abbreviation 'cf.' means, as usual,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: compare'; I have also used an ad hoc abbreviation ‘opp.' to indicate a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: term which is the opposite of the one defined: thus bound . . . Opp.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: free'. Where a term is used in two or more related senses I have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguished them within an entry: thus substratum. 1... . 2. . .

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: But where senses are effectively unrelated I have separated the entries:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: round brackets, they generally indicate what an adjective or the like

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thus 'head (1)' and 'head (2)'. When a definition begins with words in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is used of: thus 'consecutive. (Clause, etc.) indicating . . .'. In giving

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: examples, I have indicated stress or emphasis, where necessary, by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: putting a syllable in small capitals; thus 'I need the HAmmer' (not e.g. the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: screwdriver). These are often preceded by an accent which gives a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rough indication of the intonation: thus He's coming' (with the pitch

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: falling from ‘co' onwards), 'He's not ‘coming' (with the pitch rising).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Is he "coming?' (fall followed by a rise). Other conventions, e.g. in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: use of italics, follow what is now general practice.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Finally, I have included pronunciations (in the IPA transcription

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: used in The New Shorter Oxford English Dictionary) only when I thought

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that readers might be in doubt. For a dictionary of this kind to include

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: them throughout did seem otiose.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Acknowledgements

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A book like this can only be written by one person. If I had had to plan

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it as an editor, I would have allotted too much space to some entries

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and too little to others, and individual contributors might in any case

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: have overshot my instructions, even when I was right. But one person

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cannot be a specialist in the whole of linguistics and, in the fields one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thinks one knows, one can make strange mistakes. I am therefore

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: very grateful to all those who have helped me: in particular, at the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: beginning of the project, to Francis Nolan, Stephen Levinson, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the call of duty.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Nigel Vincent, who vetted my original list of headwords, and, at the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: very end, to Nigel Vincent once more and to Jim McCawley, who read

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: through a complete draft. McCawley especially supplied comments

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and corrections with a thoroughness and understanding quite beyond

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: I am grateful to Angus Phillips of the Oxford University Press, for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: his advice and patience. I have also been fortunate in my copy-editor,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Margaret Aherne, who has done extremely well a job that requires

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: many kinds of vigilance simultaneously. My wife, Lucienne Schleich,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: has commented from a user's viewpoint on the wording of many

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: entries, and has helped me very much to develop the right style. She

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: has also had to put up with my tantrums when, at times, the project

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: has been driving me round the bend: without her love and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: encouragement I would not have finished it.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: December 1996

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: P.H.M.

layout_dets.text: A. 1. = adjective. 2. = agent (2); cf. P, S (3). 3. = argument, as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *A-bound.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: abbreviated clause = reduced clause.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: abbreviation. See acronym; blend; clipping.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: abbreviatory convention. Any convention which allows a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *generative grammar to be shortened by collapsing two or more rules

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: into one. E.g. a phrase-structure rule A' → A + Comp (a constituent

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: within an adjective phrase can consist of an adjective plus a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complement) can be combined with a rule A' → A into the single

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: expression A' → A (Comp). By the relevant convention ‘A (Comp)' is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: understood as 'either A or A + Comp'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The abbreviated expression is technically a *rule schema.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: abduction. Process of reasoning by which, e.g. from 'All dogs bark'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dog'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and 'This animal barks', one draws the conclusion ‘This animal is a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Central, in one view, when people develop their native language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. they may learn that if a noun has the ending -s it is plural: so, as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one premiss, 'All noun forms in -s are plural'. They may then want to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: use some noun in the plural. Call the form required f: so, as a second

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: premiss, 'f is plural'. By abduction, the conclusion will be 'f is a form in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: -s': therefore, all else being equal, a form in -s is what they will use. In

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: this process of reasoning the conclusion does not necessarily follow:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thus the noun in question might have a plural that does not end in -s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: But as the result of it the language may change, with -s generalized to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nouns that did not previously have it.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Abductive change is change due, it is claimed, to abduction.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Abduction as a process of reasoning was distinguished by Peirce, who

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stressed its role in human life in general.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: abessive. *Case indicating that someone or something is absent: e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: schematically, I came money-AßEss 'I came without money'. From Latin

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: abesse ‘to be away, be absent'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Abkhaz. North West *Caucasian language, spoken between the west

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: end of the Caucasus Mountains and the coast of the Black Sea.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ablative (abL). *Case whose basic role, or one of whose basic roles, is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to indicate movement away from some location: thus Latin cedit Romā

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ('departed Rome-ABLsG') 'He left Rome'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ablative absolute. *Absolute construction in Latin in which a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: participle and its subject are in the ablative case and are subordinated,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ablaut

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with no other mark of linkage, to the rest of the sentence: e.g. in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence urbe capta '(the) city-ABLsG having-been-taken-ABLsG' Caesar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: recessit 'Caesar withdrew'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ablaut. Morphological variation, in Germanic and other *Indo-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: European languages, of a root vowel. E.g. in Ancient Greek the root of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the perfect or in the adjective loipós 'left over'; lip-, in the aorist or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grade, with neither e nor o.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the verb 'to leave' appeared in three forms: leip- in the present; loip,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as the first member of compounds. This illustrates the three original

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'grades' of ablaut: the e grade, the o grade, and the zero or reduced

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Similarly, in English, of vowel variations in *strong verbs (e.g. drive,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: drove, driven) or between verbs and nouns (sing, song), whether or not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: they derive directly from the Indo-European system.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A-bound. *Bound (2) by an element in the normal syntactic position

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of a subject or other *argument of a verb. E.g. in I saw myself, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reflexive myself is A-bound by its antecedent I.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: position they are said to be ‘À-' or 'A'-bound'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A term in *Government and Binding Theory, where it is claimed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that some elements, like reflexives, must be A-bound. Other elements

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: need not be: when they are bound by an antecedent not in such a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: continuant.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: abrupt. *Distinctive feature in the scheme proposed by *Jakobson.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Characterized acoustically by ‘a spread of energy over a wide frequency

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: region': thus, in particular, a feature of oral stops as opposed to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fricatives. Also called 'discontinuous' or 'interrupted': opp.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ABS = absolutive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: affix.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: absolute. (Syntactic element) not accompanied by an element to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which one might expect it to be linked. E.g. in This is bigger, bigger is an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: absolute comparative, not linked, as other comparatives are, to a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: standard of comparison (bigger than . . . ); in His is bigger, his is similarly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an absolute possessive, not linked, as possessives in general are, to a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: noun (his garden, his kitchen. . . . ). An absolute case, e.g. in Turkish, is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: so called because it is realized by a root alone, unaccompanied by an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: An absolute construction is one in which a subordinate element is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not linked by a conjunction or in any other specific way to the rest of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence. E.g. in We left, the wine having run out, the last five words stand

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in an absolute relation to we left: cf. We left because the wine had run out

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (with the conjunction because), or We left, having finished the wine (with a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: direct relation between having and we).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: From Latin absolutus freed from linkage'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: absolute neutralization. Term in *Generative Phonology for the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: suppression in all contexts of an underlying difference between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'abstract case'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: elements. E.g. in a language with *vowel harmony, a single open vowel

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: might relate sometimes to front vowels and sometimes to back vowels:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a distinction might therefore be established between a front ‘a' and a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: back ‘a', which undergoes absolute neutralization after the rules for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: harmony have applied.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: absolute synonymy. See synonymy.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relative universal, statistical universal.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'absolute universal'. A *linguistic universal that is genuinely

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: universal: i.e. that holds for all languages, without exception. Opp.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: absolutive (ass). *Case which identifies both the *patient in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: basic transitive construction and a single argument or valent in an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: intransitive. E.g. schematically, men bread-Aßs ate The men ate the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bread'; bread-Aßs disappeared ‘The bread disappeared'. The *agent in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transitive construction will then be *ergative: bread-ABs ate men-ERG.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The case is called ‘absolutive' because, in many languages, it is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguished by the absence of an affix.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thence in general of syntactic elements that unite the same roles,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whether or not the language has cases

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: another.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'absorption'. 1. Used variously of phonological changes or processes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in which one element is seen as incorporated in another. Thus 'tonal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: absorption' is a process in some languages of West Africa by which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the ending of a *contour tone (rising , falling ) is ‘absorbed' by a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: following syllable whose tone is at the same level: rising  plus high

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: → lowplus high ; falling  plus low→ high  plus low `. Cf.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fusion. 2. Process in which a case or case role is assigned to one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: element in a construction and can then no longer be assigned to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speech.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: abstract. (Structure, representation) which differs from that which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is most transparent. E.g. the representation of righteous as 'rixt-i-s',

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proposed at an underlying level in *Generative Phonology at the end

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the 1960s, is more abstract than one which corresponds closely to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a phonetic transcription [raitfəs]. Similarly, a representation of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: syntax of a sentence is more abstract the more the order in which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the words are arranged and the units and categories to which they

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are assigned differ from their order and potential grouping in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Since the end of the 1960s most linguists have tried to put

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: restrictions on the degree of abstractness that their models will

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: permit: e.g. to exclude representations such as rixt-i-əs'. But it has

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: been hard to propose firm limits that all will accept; hence in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonology a long-standing abstractness controversy.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'abstract case'. See case.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: abstract noun

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: abstract noun. One which denotes an abstract state, property, etc.:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. love, happiness. Opp. concrete.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Acc = accusative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on a distinction, drawn by Chomsky in the 1960s, between the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: acceptability of a sentence, taken as a datum, and its conformity to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: acrolect. Variety of a language which, of a series of varieties spoken

layout_dets.text: predominantly at different social levels, has the highest prestige or is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: active (1) (acr). (Construction, sentence) in which a verb has a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *subject which is characteristically the role filled by an *agent rather

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: than a *patient. Thus the agent my wife is the subject in the active

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence My wife cut the grass. Also (and more traditionally) of the form

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of verb in such a construction. Thus cut is an active verb and, in e.g. the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: woman cutting the grass, cutting is an active participle.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: traditionally neuter.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Opp. passive. In older usage verbs were active' only if they had a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: passive in e.g. The grass was cut. If a verb was active in form but had no

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corresponding passive it was called ‘neuter'. Thus a verb like appear is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: active (2). (Vocabulary) that a speaker uses, as opposed to passive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vocabulary, that is known but not used. Likewise active knowledge

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of a language is knowledge that enables one to speak it, as opposed to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: passive knowledge, which enables one to understand it.

layout_dets.text: 'active language'. One which has two basic *intransitive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constructions. In the first the noun is identified by its case or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is identified with the *patient in a transitive construction. Thus, in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transitive, the agent and patient might be marked as nominative vs.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Sarah'. An intransitive would then have variously the nominative or

layout_dets.text: animate in terms of an *animacy hierarchy, but The tree-Acc fell, where

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: and French by speakers of Luxembourgish or of standard German by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: adjacency. The usual term in linguistics for 'position next to'. Thus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: adjective. A word of a class whose most characteristic role is as the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: modifier of a noun: e.g. in tall men, tall is an adjective modifying men.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Hence typically understood as referring to properties (thus in this case

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that of being tall) not essential to whatever is denoted (in this case all

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: possible men) by the noun. Adjectives were seen in antiquity as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinct subclass of nouns, added or adjoined to (ad-') others; as such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: they were sometimes said to have a role parallel to that of adverbs in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: their relation to verbs. They were distinguished as a separate *part of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speech ('noun adjective' vs. noun *substantive') in the later Middle

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Ages, and are often, in the modern period, seen either as sharing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: properties with verbs or as intermediate between verbs and nouns.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: An adjectival element is one either associated with or having the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: adjunct. 1. Any element in the structure of a clause which is not part

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: range of *adverbials including those of manner, place, and time: e.g.

layout_dets.text: element is added next to another. E.g. in who have you met?, who is

layout_dets.text: the sentence: [who [have you met]]. 2. Specifically, in terms of *X-bar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: together form a unit whose category is in turn that of B. E.g. if B is a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *CP, the adjunction of A will form a larger unit, {A [B] ]. which is also a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Theory only when B is a *maximal projection (in this case of C); the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure that results is an adjunction structure.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Chomsky-adjunction and *sister-adjunction are types distinguished

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in earlier transformational grammars.

layout_dets.text: adnominal. (Word, etc.) directly depending on a noun. Thus, in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: girl singing, the participle singing depends on girl; a participle is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accordingly, in some accounts, an adnominal form of a verb.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ("pre-") or after ('post-’).
