layout_dets.text: adposition. Cover term for *prepositions and *postpositions. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sense is that of an element positioned ‘next to' (ad-'), whether before

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: superstratum.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: adstratum. A language which has influenced one spoken by a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: neighbouring population. Thus in the modern period French has been

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an adstratum in the development of English. Cf. substratum;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Adv = adverb.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Advançed RP. See Received Pronunciation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: narrowed.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Advanced Tongue Root. A distinctive feature of vowels e.g. in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: many West African languages. Abbreviated [± ATR]: in the production

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of vowels that are [+ ATR] the tongue is drawn forward so that the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: space between the tongue root and the back of the throat is widened;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in vowels that are [- ATR| the tongue is retracted so that this space is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Often described as ‘tense'vs. 'lax' before the nature of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinction was made clear.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: advancement = promotion.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'advantage'. See dative of advantage.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: adverb. A word of a class whose most characteristic role is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: traditionally that of modifying a verb or verb phrase: e.g. badly in He

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: adverbial

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: wrote it badly, where (in different accounts) it modifies either wrote or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the phrase wrote it.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: One of the *parts of speech established in antiquity. In the grammar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of English and many similar languages, an adverb is effectively a word

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that modifies anything other than a noun. Thus badly as above;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: certainly in Certainly I'll come, where it modifies I'll come; highly in highly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inflammatory, where it modifies inflammatory; nearly in nearly there,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: where it modifies another adverb there. The reasons for lumping these

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: roles together are (a) that they are often served by words of the same

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: form (e.g. words in -ly), (b) that the same words often serve two or more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of them.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: adverbial. (Syntactic element) whose role is one served by adverbs.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thus on Monday is an adverbial phrase, or an adverbial, in I'll do it on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Monday: cf. I'll do it tomorrow, with the single adverb tomorrow. Likewise

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: when I'm ready is an adverbial clause in I'll do it when I'm ready.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: adverb phrase. A *phrase (1) whose *head (1) is an adverb: e.g. very

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: badly, headed by badly, in I sing very badly.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not work.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: adversative. Usually of a form or construction marking an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *antithesis: e.g. but is an adversative conjunction in I'll try, but it may

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rate of flow.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aerometry. The measurement of air flow, e.g. in the production of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speech. The techniques used in phonetiçs involve the insertion at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: appropriate places in the vocal tract of instruments which measure a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: drop in air pressure across a resistance, which is directly related to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: affected object. The *direct object of a verb denoting an action, etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which affects individuals or things already in existence. Thus the silver

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is an affected object in I polished the silver, since silver exists before it is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: polished. Opp. effected object.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'affection'. Older term for the effect of one sound on another that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: precedes or follows: cf. assimilation; coarticulation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: affective. (Function, meaning) having to do with a speaker's feelings.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. one might say, as a neutral statement, 'I have finished it'; or one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: might say, with triumph or amazement, 'I have ‘Actually 'Finished

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it'. What is śaid is in other respects the same, but the utterances differ

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in āffeçtive meaning. Likewise intonations or words like actually have,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or have at times, an affective function.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also called ‘emotive', 'expressive'. Opposed variously to *cognitive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaning, *propositional meaning, or to the representational or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: referential *function of language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: affirmative. (Sentence, form, construction) by which one asserts

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: what is, as opposed to what is not, the case. Opp. negative; also, by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: implication, to interrogative, imperative, etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: agent

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: affix. Any element in the morphological structure of a word other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: than a *root. E.g. unkinder consists of the root kind plus the affixes un-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and -er. Hence affixation, for the process of adding an affix. Also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: affixal: thus un- in unkind is an affixal element, and the formation of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: unkind is that of an ‘affixal negative'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Affixes are traditionally divided into *prefixes, which come before

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the form to which they are joined; *suffixes, which come after; and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *infixes, which are inserted within it. Others commonly distinguished

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are *circumfixes and *superfixes.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'affix hopping'. Rule posited in *transformational grammar in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1950s by which elements realized by affixes of verbs in English are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: placed in affixal position. E.g. Jim left is assigned an underlying

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure Jim PAst leave, where PAst is syntactically an auxiliary. To

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: derive the actual or surface structure, PAst hops over' leave and is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: attached as a suffix to it: Jim leave-PAsT.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: affricate. A *stop consonant released with a *fricative at the same

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: place of articulation: e.g. [tf] (written ch) in chip.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the languages of West Africa.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: African languages. Currently classified, for convenience or as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: working hypothesis, into four main groups. *Afro-Asiatic, across North

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Africa, the Sahara, and the adjacent Near East, includes, as its largest

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: member, *Arabic. A *Khoisan group includes a minority towards the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: southern tip of the continent. The other two are much more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speculative. 'Nilo-Saharan' is an attempt to group together *Nilotic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages with others spoken between the upper Nile and the Congo.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Niger-Congo' covers all the remainder, including *Bantu and most of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The classification derives in part from an application of *mass

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: comparison by Greenberg in the early 1960s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Afrikaans. *Germanic, derivative from Dutch, spoken in South

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Africa and elsewhere in Africa by emigration. Sometimes claimed to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be a Dutch-based *creole, a claim also strongly resisted.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Afro-Asiatic. Proposed family of languages including *Semitic and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Cushitic; also *Berber, *Egyptian, and the *Chadic languages in sub-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Saharan Africa. Previously called 'Hamito-Semitic', on the assumption

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that Semitic forms one major branch and the others thought to belong

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to it form another, called 'Hamitic'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: agent. 1. Noun phrase, etc. identifying an actor or actors performing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: some action. E.g. Mary is an agent in Mary went out or Mary made it.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2. A syntactic category which is characteristically that of agents as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposed to *patients. Thus the subject of a transitive construction in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English has the role of agent (A) in opposition to an object as patient:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Mary (A) shut the door (P). 3. The element in a passive sentence which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: would correspond to a subject in the active, e.g. by Mary in The car

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was driven by Mary: cf. active Mary drove the car.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: agentive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: agentive. 1. Having the semantic role of an *agent (1): e.g. I is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: agentive in I did it. 2. (Case) = ergative. 3. (Noun) = agent noun: also of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a process or affix by which such nouns are formed.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: agentless passive. A passive without an *agent (3): e.g. She was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: promoted, as compared with She was promoted by her company, with agent

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by her company. Cf. reduced passive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: agent noun. A derived noun whose formation has the general

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaning someone who does . . .': e.g. builder, from build + er, meaning

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'someone who builds'. Cf. action noun.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and -in (genitive).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: agglutinating. (Language, formation) in which words are easily

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: divided into separate segments with separate grammatical functions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. in Turkish, dişçilerimin ‘of my dentists' is transparently made up of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a root (diş ‘tooth') and four suffixes: -i (agentive), -ler (plural), -im ‘my',

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Opp. inflecting; isolating. Agglutination is likewise the process by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which such structures or this type of structure is formed.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: AGR {agr] or ['agə]. A syntactic category in Chomsky's *Principles and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Parameters Theory. Originally an element within *INFL, comprising

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: features of person, number, and gender as opposed to those of tense.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Later an independent element, or two such elements, one relating to a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subject and the other to an object.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which it is pronounced.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Originally an abbreviation for ‘agreement': hence the first way in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and hesitant.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: agrammatism. Form of *aphasia in which grammatical elements

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are lost. The resulting speech is often described as 'telegraphic',

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consisting mainly of lexical items and fixed expressions; also slow

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one woman.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: agreement. Syntactic relation between words and phrases which are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: compatible, in à given construction, by virtue of inflections carried by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at least one of them. E.g. these and carrots are compatible, in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: construction of these carrots, because both are inflected as plural.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Likewise, in the Italian sentence Maria e Luisa sono arrivate 'Mary and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Louise have arrived', sono (lit. 'be-3RdpL') agrees in respect of plural

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: number with arrivate (arrived-FEmpl') and both, or sono arrivate as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whole, agree with a subject, Maria e Luisa, which refers to more than

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also called concord. Distinctions are drawn between *grammatical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: agreement and *notional agreement; also between agreement and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: some similar relations of compatibility, such as the *government (2) of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cases by prepositions. But the last of these is often at best imprecise.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: AGT = agent, agentive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Alexandrians

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: airstream mechanism. Any system by which a flow of air is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generated in the production of speech. Types of mechanism are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguished by two criteria: (a) as egressive or ingressive, according

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to the direction of flow; (b) as *pulmonic, *glottalic, or *velaric,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: according to the way in which the flow is initiated.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The main mechanism, and in many languages the only one that is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: normally employed, is breathing out. This is (a) egressive, in that air

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: flows outwards, and (b) pulmonic, in that air is pushed out from the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lungs as their volume is reduced by the contraction of the chest

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: click; ejective; implosive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: muscles. For other mechanisms of particular importance in speech see

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Akan. Group of dialects or closely related languages, spoken mainly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in Ghana: separately named Asante, Fante, and Akuapem (or Twi).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Akkadian. Ancient *Semitic language spoken especially in Assyria

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and Babylonia. Written in *cuneiform from about 2500 BC and by the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: middle of the next millennium an international language throughout

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the Near East. It has no modern descendant.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also spelled ‘Accadian'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Aktionsart. The lexical class to which a verb belongs by virtue of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: type of process, state, etc. that it denotes. E.g. walking is an activity;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: therefore walk is an ‘activity verb'. Knowing something is a state of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mind; therefore know is lexically *stative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The German term means ‘kind of action'; sometimes replaced in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English by ‘aspectual character', 'aspectual value'. or 'semantic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: value'. Aktionsart is linked to *aspect, from which some scholars would

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: argue that it is not separate.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Albanian. Attested from the 15th century AD, now spoken

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: throughout Albania and in the neighbouring province of Kossovo; also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in pockets in Greece and southern Italy. *Indo-European, forming a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: separate branch within the family.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alethic [ə'li:θik]. (Modality) opposing in particular what must

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: logically be true to what may be true in specific circumstances.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Distinguished by logicians from *epistemic modality; but not usually,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: if ever, a distinct category in languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: From the Greek word for 'true.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Alexandrians. School of scholars and scientists associated with the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: library of Alexandria from the early 3rd century BC. Aristarchus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (c.217-145 Bc) is especially important in the history of literary and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: textual scholarship, and it is within this tradition that earlier analyses

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of language, by the *Stoics especially, developed into the discipline of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammar as it has been understood from the 1st century BC onwards.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The details are uncertain, a particular problem being the authenticity

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the grammar attributed to Aristarchus' pupil *Dionysius Thrax.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alexia

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alexia. Loss of a previously acquired ability to read in consequence of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: disease or injury to the brain. Distinguished as such from *dyslexia.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Algonquian. Family of languages spoken or once spoken over a large

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: part of North America, in Canada and, in the USA, especially in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Great Lakes region and the eastern seaboard. Varieties of *Cree and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Ojibwa now have the greatest numbers of speakers.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also spelled 'Algonkian'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: algorithm. See heuristic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: possession.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alienable possession. Possessive construction in which the thing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: possessed is not an inherent part of the possessor: e.g. that of Bill's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: house, since a house exists independently of its owner. Opp. inalienable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the shop'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: allative (all). *Case whose basic role is to indicate movement to or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: towards some location: e.g. schematically, I-walked shop-All 'I walked to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: allegro form. A form as modified phonetically in rapid speech. E.g. I

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: can't see him has, as one possible allegro form, [əkà'sı:m]. Likewise rapid

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speech is sometimes called allegro speech.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or *allomorphs.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: allo-. Prefix used for variant forms of any linguistic unit. Thus in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: general 'X-emes', e.g. *phonemes or *morphemes, are invariants,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: abstracted from and realized by alternative ‘allo-Xes', e.g. *allophones

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: allograph. A variant form of a *grapheme: i.e. of a letter in writing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: seen as analogous to a *phoneme.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: allomorph. One of a set of forms which realize a morpheme: cf.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morpheme (3). E.g. -[ən] in taken and -{d] in removed are among the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: allomorphs of the ‘past participle' morpheme.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: allomorphy. *Alternation in the forms that realize morphological

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or lexical units. E.g. in Latin rēgis 'king-GENsG' vs. domini 'master-GEnsG'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: there is allomorphy of the genitive singular ending (-is/-i); in ferō 'I

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: carry' vs. tulī 'I carried' there is allomorphy in the root (fer-/tul-).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: allophone. An audibly distinct variant of a *phoneme. E.g. the [d]

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and [∂] of Spanish ['deðo] ‘finger' are allophones of the same phoneme,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: written d in the spelling dedo.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: allophones.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thence allophonic, as in ‘allophonic variation', i.e. variation among

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alpha (α). See Greek letter variables; move α.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alphabet. A writing system, strictly one in which consonants and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vowels are represented equally by separate letters. Hence especially the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'ambilingual'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Greek alphabet and its *Roman and other derivatives; but also of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *consonantal alphabets of the *Semitic type.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alpha-syllabic. (Writing system) in which successive characters

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sometimes represent a single consonant or vowel, as in an *alphabet,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and sometimes a syllable, as in a *syllabary. The type is characteristic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of systems in or derived from India, such as *Devanagari.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Altaic. A proposed family of languages, including *Turkic,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Mongolian, and *Tungusic in east Siberia.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: final syllable is reduced.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Alternating Stress Rule. A rule of English phonology proposed by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Chomsky and Halle, *SPE which assigns stress e.g. to the first syllable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of hurricane. By the 'Main Stress Rule', which applies first, 'primary

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stress' is assigned to the final syllable: hurricáne. By the Alternating

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Stress Rule, the second syllable before a primary stress also receives

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: primary stress: húrricáne. Then, by a rule applying later, that of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ending.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alternation. Variation in the forms that *realize linguistic units;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hence often = allomorphy. Also a specific instance of such variation:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. in taken vs. removed there is an alternation in the past participle

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Hence alternant, one of the forms that enter into an alternation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alveolar. Articulated with the *tip or *blade of the tongue against

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the ridge behind the upper teeth: e.g. [t} and [d] are normally alveolar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in English. The ridge is called the alveolar ridge from the ‘alveoli' or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sockets for the teeth contained in it.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alveolo-palatal. A consonant articulated like a *palatal consonant

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: but in a more forward position.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: said.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ambient it. The it of e.g. It is snowing, where the sentence refers to no

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: individual but simply to a state of the world in which this might be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ambiguous. (Sentence, etc.) having two or more meanings. Thus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: I filled the pen is ambiguous, since the pen might refer to a writing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: instrument or an enclosure for animals. Most accounts distinguish

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lexical ambiguity, as in this example, from grammatical or syntactic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ambiguity. Cf. e.g. I like good food and wine, where good might bear a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: syntactic relation to both food and wine ('good food and good wine') or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to food alone ('good food and any wine').

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Many linguists will talk of ambiguity only when they see it as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: property of *sentences as opposed to *utterances or as explained,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as in these examples, by the *language system. But such criteria are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: problematic as these notions are problematic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'ambilingual'. *Bilingual who has equally mastered both languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ambisyllabic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ambisyllabic. Belonging to two syllables. E.g. single intervocalic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonants form a syllable, in one view, with the following and with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the preceding vowel.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ameliorative. (Change) by which a word develops a more favourable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sense. E.g. in the meaning of nice, originally borrowed from Old French

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the 13th century with the meaning 'foolish, stupid'; or that of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: minister, as in Prime Minister, originally meaning 'servant'. Also called

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meliorative: opp. pejorative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: American Sign Language. See sign language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Post-Bloomfieldians.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'American structuralism'. The school or theory of linguistics

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dominant in the USA from the 1920s or 1930s until the end of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the 1950s: especially, therefore, that of *Bloomfield and the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: assessment of his methods.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Amerind'. Conjectural *phylum or grouping of families comprising

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: all the indigenous languages of the Americas other than *Eskimo-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Aleut and *Na-Dené. Proposed by Greenberg on the basis of *mass

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: comparison; hence valid or purely speculative, depending on one's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Amerindian. Cover term for the indigenous languages of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Americas. See Central American languages; North American languages;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: South American languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Ameslan. See sign language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Amharic. South *Semitic, the official language of Ethiopia and a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: second language, there and in Sudan, for many for whom it is not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: native. Written in a South Semitic alphabet, distinctive to it and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: neighbouring languages, such as *Tigrinya.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'amplifier'. See intensifying.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'not following'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: anacoluthon [anəkp'lu:θən]. A sentence, etc. which switches from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one construction to another. E.g. in He told me that he was desperate and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: could I please help the interrogative could I please help does not construe

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with the that of that he was desperate. From Greek, with the meaning

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: analogists vs. anomalists. Controversy regarding the basis for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: correct language, said by *Varro to have raged in the 2nd to 1st

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: centuries Bc. One side argued that irregular inflections should be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: regularized, as far as was reasonable, by a principle of *analogy: this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: view is also known from other sources. The other argued that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'anomalies', in the sense of inflectional irregularities, should be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: retained: for that sense Varro, and others following him, are our

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: only testimony.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: anaphor

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: analogy. Process by which a form a is either changed or created in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: such a way that its relation to another form b is like that of other pairs

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of forms whose relationship is similar in meaning. E.g. if a speaker says

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contácted instead of cóntacted, it is possibly by analogy with other verbs

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whose stress is on that syllable. Thus contáct (verb) is to cóntact (noun) as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: impórt is to ímport, dispúte to (for many speakers) díspute, and so on. If a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speaker were to invent a verb 'locketize' (meaning to enclose in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: locket) it might be by analogy with other formations in -ize: locketize is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to locket as palletize is to pallet, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thence generally of any changes in which similarity in meaning

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: leads to formal similarity. E.g. in the history of English cows (plural)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: may be said to have replaced kine by a process in which a form

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: analogous to that of other plurals (cow + -s) has replaced one which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was irregular. But analogy is logically distinct from processes of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *regularization. E.g. in some dialects regular dived has been replaced

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by irregular dove, by analogy especially with drove vs. drive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thence analogical change, change explained by analogy.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: century, for which the term was invented.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: analphabetic notation. *Phonetic notation in which segments are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: represented not by single letters but by arrays of symbols that refer to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: individual *articulators. E.g. one devised by Jespersen in the late 19th

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'analysis by synthesis'. Any strategy in *speech processing in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which, given a set of rules that generate a set of speech forms, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure of an input form is determined by the rules applied in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: successful attempt to synthesize it. Proposed in the 1960s in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: context of phonetics and phonology.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inflections. Opp. synthetic (1).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: analytic (1). (Form, language) in which separate words realize

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammatical distinctions that in other languages may be realized by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thus the perfect is realized analytically in English (has come) but by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an inflection in e.g. Latin (veni 'I have come'). Likewise constructions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with prepositions are analytic, as opposed to case forms.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: analytic (2). (Proposition) which by definition cannot but be true.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. spinsters are by definition unmarried: therefore 'If Jane is a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spinster, Jane is not married' is analytic or analytically true. Opp.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: synthetic (2). Analyticity is similarly the property of being analytic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: anaphor ['anəfo:]. 1. A pronoun or similar element that can only be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: understood in relation to an *antecedent. Thus themselves is an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: anaphor whose referent, e.g. in They helped themselves, is the same as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that of they, but which has no referent, and accordingly cannot be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: understood e.g. in Please help themselves. In *Government and Binding

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Theory, anaphors are classed as [+ anaphoric] and [- pronominal]

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: while pronouns such as he are [− anaphoric] and [+ pronominal].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2. Any element standing in a relation of *anaphora.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: anaphora

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: anaphora {ə'nafərə]. The relation between a pronoun and another

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: element, in the same or in an earlier sentence, that supplies its

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: referent. E.g. in Mary disguised herself, the reflexive pronoun herself is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: understood as anaphoric [anə'fprık] to Mary: that is, it refers to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whoever Mary refers to. Likewise, e.g. in conversation, across sentence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: boundaries. Thus if A asks 'Where's Mary?' and B says 'She's in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: garden', she in the sentence B utters is meant to be understood as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: anaphoric to earlier Mary.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thence of similar relations involving elements other than pronouns:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. the idiot is anaphoric to John in I asked John but the idiot wouldn't tell

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: me; do so is anaphoric to help in I wanted to help but I couldn't do so. Also to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'up': i.e. to something earlier. Hence anticipatory anaphora is often

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguished as *cataphora (referring down’).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cases of 'anticipatory anaphora': e.g. she is anaphoric to Mary in When

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: she read it Mary was delighted. But the term is the Greek for referring

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: anaptyxis [anə'ptıksis]. Process or change in which successive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonants are separated by a vowel. E.g. the word for 'milk' has

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: developed an anaptyctic vowel in Luxembourgish (mellëch) and some

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: other Germanic dialects. The Greek term means 'unfolding'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: anastrophe [ə'nastrəfi]. Term in rhetoric for a *figure of speech

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which departs from the usual order of words or other syntactic units

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Anatolian. Branch of *Indo-European, including *Hittite and other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages attested in what is now Turkey in the 2nd to 1st millennia

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: BC. Of the others Luwian is also early and is known from various sites

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the west and south of the region.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ancestor language. An earlier language from which one or more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: later languages are descended: e.g. Proto-Germanic as the posited

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ancestor of the modern Germanic languages. The converse term is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'daughter language'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: angled brackets < >. Used: 1. To distinguish orthographic units

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and forms written in them. E.g. orthographic <ph> is one way of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: writing [f]. 2. By Chomsky and Halle, *SPE in an abbreviatory

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: convention by which, e.g. A <B> C <D> conflates a sequence AC, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which neither B nor D is present, with ABCD, where both are present.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: See tailless arrow for < or > used separately.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Anglo-Frisian. Traditional division of *West Germanic which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: includes English and *Frisian.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Anglo-Saxon = Old English.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'animacy hierarchy'. A proposed hierarchical ordering of noun

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phrases, etc. ranging from personal pronouns such as I as maximally

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'animate' to forms referring to lifeless objects as minimally ‘animate'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Those at one end of the scale may differ in syntax from those at the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: anti-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: other: e.g. the construction characteristic of an *accusative language

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: may be found with those that are maximally animate, that of an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *ergative language with the remainder.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The scale reflects degrees of *empathy: thus people empathize most

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with themselves and other people, least with stones, etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: animate. 1. (Noun) denoting entities that can act, or are perceived

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as acting, of their own will: e.g. man, horse. Hence a feature involved

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in collocational or 'selectional' restrictions: e.g. a verb such as die

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: typically takes an animate subject. 2. (*Gender, *noun class)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: characterized by nouns which are animate in that sense. Thus in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: older Indo-European languages there are traces of a system in which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nouns were initially classed as animate or inanimate. The inanimates

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: divided into *masculine and *feminine.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are those described as *neuter, and the animates were secondarily

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Annamite. An older name for *Vietnamese.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'anomalist'. See analogists vs. anomalists.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: anomia. Impaired ability to name things. Sometimes the main

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: feature of *aphasia, in which case called anomic aphasia.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accordingly he in turn refers to 'Bill'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: antecedent. A phrase, etc. which supplies the interpretation of an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *anaphoric element. E.g. in Bill promised he would come, the referent

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of he is supplied, in one interpretation, by the antecedent Bill:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: would be the antecedent of who.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A *relative pronoun is described in the classical tradition as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: anaphoric to a noun preceding it. Thus, in the people who came, people

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: antepenultimate. Third from the end: thus the accent of háppily is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on the antepenultimate syllable, or antepenult.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: anterior. Articulated by obstructing the airflow in a position forward

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from that of e.g. English [S]. English [p], [t], and [s] are therefore among

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the consonants so classed. A distinctive feature in the scheme of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: antipassive (anripass). (Construction) which stands to the basic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or physical damage to the brain. The term is used generally for both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: words. Of the grammarians whose thought we can assess directly,

layout_dets.text: applicative. Construction in which an *oblique element is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *promoted to the role of an object, with the verb inflected to show

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by, say, dog instead.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of Welsh, not just in the forms but also in the way the spectrum, e.g. in

layout_dets.text: archaism. Form or use of a form which is obsolete or belongs

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that it defines.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposition between [t} and [d] after initial [s]: the unit written t in e.g.

layout_dets.text: argument. Any syntactic element seen as required by a verb: e.g. love
