layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: expression P (x. y). the variables x and y are the arguments of a two-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: place *predicate P. The argument structure of a verb or other lexical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: unit is the range of arguments that it may or must take: cf. valency.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: arhyzotonic. Having the accent elsewhere than on the root.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Aristarchus. See Alexandrians.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Aristotle (384-322 Bc). Greek philosopher, important in the early

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: history of western linguistics both for his general contributions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to logic, rhetoric, and poetics and for a specific classification of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speech units. These included minimal sounds and syllables, both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence as a unit which is meaningful and has parts that are also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: others.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguished as units that do not in themselves have meanings; the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaningful; and the beginnings, though in a form hard to interpret,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the system of *parts of speech developed later by the Stoics and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Many of the terms that are later used in grammars are in Aristotle's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: work, though not necessarily with the same sense. A specific analysis,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which recurs at intervals throughout the history of logic and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: linguistics, is that of a finite verb, such as walks, into a participle linked

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to its subject by a *copula: 'is (in a state of) walking'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Sahak.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Armenian. First known from texts of the 5th century AD, though

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: surviving in later copies; now spoken in the Armenian Republic, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Turkey, and by a diaspora in many countries. *Indo-European, forming

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a branch distinct from Greek, *Indo-Iranian, etc. Written in a distinct

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alphabet devised in the 5th century primarily by St Mesrop and St

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2. See implication.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: arrow (→). 1. Used in linguistics for a synchronic process or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: operation; e.g. s → z indicates a change of s to z. To be distinguished

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from the tailless arrow (>), used for a historical process.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The use of the arrow in the notation of phrase structure rules

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: derives from Chomsky's initial formulation in the 1950s, in which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: they were seen as *rewrite rules.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ars. The Latin word for ‘art' or 'skill'; used in the title of grammars

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (ars grammatica or 'art of grammar'); hence often alone, e.g. in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: translation into other modern languages, in that sense.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in a girl.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: article. A *determiner whose basic role is to mark noun phrases as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: either *definite or *indefinite: e.g. definite the in the girl, indefinite a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: articulation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Articles are distinguished from other determiners for two reasons.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Firstly, they cannot form phrases on their own: compare e.g. the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: demonstrative this in This is my sister. Secondly, the distinction they

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mark is obligatory. Delete, for example, the in I am looking for the girls;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the object girls is then specifically indefinite, like the singular a girl

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in I am looking for a girl, and does not merely cease to be specifically

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: definite.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: articulation. 1. The production of speech sounds: thus *manner

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of articulation, * place of articulation. 2. The property of being

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: analysable into *discrete units standing in specific relationships: thus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *double articulation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'inarticulate'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Sense 2 is the older. Thus in the classical tradition speech was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguished as 'articulate' (lit. 'jointed') from cries, etc. that were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ('dental').

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: articulator. Any vocal organ used to form specific speech sounds: e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the upper and lower lips, in the production of [p] in pít, or the blade

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the tongue and the ridge behind the teeth, in that of [t] (t). *Places

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of articulation are defined by the raising of a movable or active

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: articulator, e.g. a part of the tongue, towards a fixed or passive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: articulator, e.g. a part of the roof of the mouth. For example, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *labiodental place of articulation, which is that of fin fish, is defined

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by the placing of the lower lip ('labio-') in contact with the upper teeth

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: articulatory gesture. See gesture.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: articulatory phonetics. The study of the production of speech

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sounds. Opp. acoustic phonetics.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Articulatory Phonology. Model developed by C. P. Browman and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: L. Goldstein from the mid-1980s in which an utterance is represented

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at the phonological level by a temporally coordinated series of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: articulatory *gestures. These form a gestural score', from which the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: actual movements of articulators are derived.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Compared by its authors to *Autosegmental Phonology, in that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: gestures which are physically independent characterize different

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *tiers of representation. But the units in Autosegmental Phonology

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are features, not gestures; and tiers in Autosegmental Phonology are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: defined by structural domains, which do not flow from the nature

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the units themselves.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: articulatory setting. A medium- to long-term disposition of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vocal tract, underlying the articulation of successive units. When

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: permanent or virtually permanent, settings may identify the voice of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an individual: e.g. that of some speakers is characteristically nasalized.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: They may also be characteristic of particular languages or accents; in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the shorter term they may carry *affective meaning, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aspectual character

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: articulatory target. See target.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'artificial language'. Any invented 'language', whether an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *auxiliary language such as *Esperanto, or a formal system used e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in logic or in computer programming.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'artificial underlying form'. A *basic form of a morpheme which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is not identical to any of those by which it is realized. For ‘artificial' cf.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: abstract.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Aryan'. See Indo-Aryan. 'Aryan' was sometimes used in the late 19th

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: century in the sense of *Indo-European.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ascension = raising (2).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ascriptive. (Sentence) which ascribes a property to some entity. E.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in Zoe is beautiful, Zoe is ascribed the property of beauty, in Zoe is an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: undergraduate that of being an undergraduate. Also of the construction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of such a sentence, if distinct from others. Cf. equational.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'ash'. The digraph ‘æ', devised originally in the spelling of Old

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English, for a vowel that was phonetically [a] or [æ].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: .ASL. See sign language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aspect. General term, originally of specialists in Slavic languages, for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: verbal categories that distinguish the status of events, etc. in relation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to specific periods of time, as opposed to their simple location in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: present, past, or future. E.g. I am reading your paper means that the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reading is in progress over a period that includes the moment of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speaking: am reading is therefore present in *tense but *progressive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (or continuous) in aspect. I have read your paper means that, at the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: moment of speaking, the reading has been completed: it is therefore

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: present in tense but *perfect in aspect.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Aspectual categories are very varied, and since both tense and aspect

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are defined by reference to time, a clear distinction, where it exists,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: will usually be drawn by formal criteria. It is also hard to separate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aspects marked by inflections or auxiliaries from the *Aktionsart or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inherent lexical properties of verbs. Hence the term is commonly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: extended to include these and, effectively, any distinction that does

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not clearly fall under tense or mood.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: For other individual aspects see aorist; durative; habitual;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: imperfective; inchoative; iterative; punctual.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Aspects = Aspects of the Theory of Syntax, by Chomsky (1965). This

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: expounded what was later called the *Standard Theory of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transformational grammar, also called 'Aspects-theory'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aspectual character. See Aktionsart.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aspirated

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aspirated. (Plosive) whose release is followed audibly by a short

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: period in which the vocal cords are not vibrating. Thus the t of English

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tea is usually aspirated: in phonetic notation [thi:] or [t‘i:]. For ‘voiced

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aspirates' see murmured.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Assamese. *Indo-Aryan language of the valley of the Brahmaputra in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: north-east India; grouped with *Bengali in all attempts to subdivide

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the family. Spoken in the Indian state of Assam and in Bangladesh

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: assertive. (Mood, verb, particle) by which speakers commit

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: assertive in opposition to *subjunctives.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: themselves, to a greater or lesser degree, to what they are saying. E.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: assure is an assertive verb in I assure you he is coming; *indicatives are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English by which e.g. *fetjan > fe[tf]an 'to fetch'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: assibilation. Change into a *sibilant. Thus of a sound change in Old

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: assimilation. Sound change or process by which features of one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: element change to match those of another that precedes or follows.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. Italian scritto 'written' derives from Latin scriptu(m) by the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: assimilation of a bilabial (p) to a following dental (t); English cats is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: described synchronically as deriving from an underlying [kat] + [z] by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the assimilation of voiced [z] to voiceless [t].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. coarticulation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Divided into *progressive assimilation and *regressive assimilation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: association line. A line drawn to represent a relation between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: elements at different levels or *tiers of phonological representation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Originally from *Autosegmental Phonology: thus, in the illustration,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a low tone (L) is an autosegment associated with one syllable on a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *skeletal or ‘CV' tier; a high tone (H) with two successive syllables, of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which the first might then have a rising contour.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: autosegmental tier

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: skeletal tier

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *paradigmatic relations.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'associative relation'. Saussure's term for any relation between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: linguistic units which is not *syntagmatic; e.g. between phonemes or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: words that can be substituted one for another, between forms of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: word with different inflections, between words formed in the same

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: way or with a sequence of sounds in common. Relations of the first

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: type are those distinguished later (by Hjelmslev and Jakobson) as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Assyria(n). See Akkadian.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: augment

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: asterisk (*). Used: 1. In historical linguistics, to mark forms that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are *reconstructed, not directly attested: e.g. Germanic *kuninga-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (> English king, German könig, etc.). 2. In work on syntax since the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1950s, to mark forms judged to be ungrammatical: e.g. *I yesterday

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: did it, as opposed to I did it yesterday.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: An asterisked form (or starred form) is one marked, in historical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: linguistics especially, with an asterisk.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: asyndeton {a'sindətən). The joining together of syntactic units

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: without a conjunction: e.g. in I'm tired, I'm hungry, or I'm exhausted, I've

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: walked twenty miles. A sentence, etc. which has such a structure is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: asyndetic {asın'detık): the Greek term means 'not bound together'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: atelic. (Verb, etc.) that is not *telic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spelled Athapaskan, Athabascan.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Athabaskan. Family of languages in the American South-west and in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: western Canada and Alaska; another group were formerly spoken on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the Pacific coast, north and south of the border between California and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Oregon. *Navajo has by far the greatest number of speakers. Also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: athematic. Not having a *thematic vowel. E.g. Latin fertis 'you are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: carrying' is a relic of an athematic formation in Indo-European, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which the inflection (-tis) is added directly to the root (fer-)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Atlantic languages. See West Atlantic languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: atonic. (Word, syllable, vowel) not accented.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ATR = Advanced Tongue Root.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: attested form. One for which there is direct historical evidence, as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposed to one that is *reconstructed. In historical linguistics only

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: attested forms are cited without an *asterisk.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: attraction.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: attraction. Agreement of a word with an adjacent element to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which it does not bear a direct syntactic relation. E.g. in Nobody but

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammarians say that, the subject of say is or is headed by the singular

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nobody; but the verb agrees with the plural grammarians. See also case

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: attribution = modification (1); likewise attribute = modifier. An

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: attributive adjective is one which modifies the head of a noun

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phrase, as opposed to one which is *predicative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: auditory. Having to do with hearing. Thus auditory phonetics is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: concerned with the perception of speech sounds; *pitch is one of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: auditory properties of sound.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: augment ·A verbal prefix (reconstructed *e-) in Indo-European,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: marking finite forms with past time reference. E.g. in Greek é-graph-on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'I was writing'; compare gráph-ō 'I am writing'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: augmentative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: augmentative. (Affix, etc.) primarily indicating large or larger size.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. Italian cassone 'large case, chest, etc.' is an augmentative form of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cassa 'box, case', with the augmentative ending -one. Opp. diminutive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Austin, John Langshaw (1911-60). British philosopher, important

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in linguistics as the originator, in the 1950s, of the distinction between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *constative and *performative utterances, and the definition of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *felicity as the requirement that the latter must meet. How to Do Things

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with Words (edited posthumously, 1962) is the first attempt to develop

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a general theory of *speech acts, distinguishing in particular the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *locutionary, *illocutionary, and *perlocutionary aspects of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: utterances.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grouped as 'Non-Pama-Nyungan'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Australian languages. Estimated to have been about 200 before the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English invasion. Languages in an area covering most of the continent

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are classed on *typological grounds as ‘Pama-Nyungan'; the name

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: derives from the word for ‘man'at the north-east and south-west

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: extremes. Those not assigned to this group are or were spoken in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: north of Western Australia and the Northern Territory, and are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A handful still have over 1,000 speakers.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Austro-Asiatic. Proposed family oflanguages with *Mon-Khmer and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Munda as its main branches.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Austronesian. Family of languages distributed over a large area,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mainly islands, from Madagascar in the west to Hawaii and Easter

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Island. It includes the indigenous languages of Taiwan, of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Philippines, of Micronesia and Polynesia, and most of those in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Indonesia, Malaysia, and Melanesia.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distribution.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The name is from the words for 'south' in Latin (austro-) and ‘island'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in Greek (nes-). The major subdivisions of the family are still partly in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dispute, and with them the routes that led to much of this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: other. Cf. hyponymy.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: auto-. From the Ancient Greek form for ‘-self'. Hence, e.g. a word is an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'autohyponym' if it has two senses one of which is included in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: automatic alternation. An *alternation in morphology to which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: there are no exceptions. E.g. the regular plural suffix is always [ız} after

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sibilants (fish-es), [s] after other voiceless consonants (cat-s), and [z]

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: elsewhere (dog-s, cow-s).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'autonomous'. (Linguistics, syntax, etc.) viewed as a discipline or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: object of study independent of others. E.g. linguistics as separate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from, or as a separate part within, psychology; syntax as a level or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: component of language separate from semantics.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: autosegment. See Autosegmental Phonology.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Avestan

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Autosegmental Phonology. Model of *non-linear phonology

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: developed in the 1970s by J. Goldsmith. The basic insight is that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: certain phonological features, such as *tones or those involved in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *vowel harmony, may be realized variously in a single vowel or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonant, or in two or more such units, or, in effect, in only part of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one. Thus, in Turkish eller 'hand-PL', the vowel of the plural suffix (-ler)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is front in harmony with that of el ‘hand': it cannot be otherwise, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: we may therefore speak of just one feature, 'front' or [+ front], which is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tones might be realized sometimes on two separate syllables (CýC)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be phonetically falling (C). Features like these are described as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: realized in both syllables. In the case of tones, successive high and low

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and sometimes on a single syllable. The tone on that syllable will then

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: autosegments, and are represented at a structural level which is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: higher than that of the individual vowel or consonant segments. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ways in which they are realized in particular forms are then shown by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *association lines which relate the units at each structural level, or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *tier, to what is, in developed versions, no more than a CV skeleton

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (called the *skeletal tier or CV tier).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: AuX [:ks]. A syntactic unit proposed by Chomsky in the 1950s,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: basically comprising the inflections of a main verb with any

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *auxiliaries accompanying it. E.g. in He left, the AUX consists of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: past-tense inflection (-t); in He may be leaving, of the auxiliaries may

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and be plus the inflection of the participle (-ing). Cf. INFL.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: auxiliary (Aux). A verb belonging to a small class which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: syntactically accompanies other verbs: opp. lexical verb, full verb.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. could and have are auxiliaries in He could have done it. The first

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: belongs to a class of *modal verbs used only with other verbs or in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: elliptical sentences where a verb is understood. The second is an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: auxiliary related to the past participle (done); distinguished as such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from have as a full verb, e.g. in I have the answer.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Auxiliaries typically mark *modality, *tense, or *aspect: e.g. the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: construction of have with a past participle marks the *perfect. Hence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the same term has been used of other *grammatical words that mark

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: such categories, whether or not they are verbs.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: auxiliary language. A language such as *Esperanto, invented as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subsidiary means of communication among people with different

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: native languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aversive. (*Case) indicating someone or something feared or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: avoided. Characteristic of Australian languages: e.g. in Yidiny (nort h

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Queensland), ('He hid') bama-yida ‘from, to avoid being seen by, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: people', the aversive is marked by -yıda.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Avestan. Ancient *Iranian language known from texts of uncertain

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: date, but similar in form to those in *Vedic. These are the oldest part

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: avoidance style

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the Zoroastrian scriptures called the Avesta, compiled when the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language was no longer spoken.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: avoidance style. Style of speech that has to be used, in some

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: communities, in talking in the presence of someone with whom close

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: social contact is taboo. Widespread in Australian languages, where a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: part or almost the whole of the vocabulary must be replaced by special

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: avoidance terms in the presence of certain relatives. Often called

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'mother-in-law language', this relative being typically or specially

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: taboo.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'axis'. Bloomfield's term for an element *governed by a verb or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: preposition. E.g. me is the ‘axis' in the construction of to me or saw me.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Aymará. Spoken mainly in Bolivia, on the plateau south of Lake

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Titicaca. The main member of the Jaqí family, conjecturally but not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: securely related to *Quechuan, spoken to the north and south.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: provinces of Iran.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Azerbaijani. *Turkic language, closely related to *Turkish, spoken

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mainly in Azerbaijan and, by a greater number, in the neighbouring

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Both the speakers and the language are also called Azeri.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Aztec. See Nahuatl.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: B

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: babbling. The vocal sounds of very young children, especially

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: involving repeated syllable-like forms, before the development

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of anything recognizable as speech.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Babylonian. See Akkadian.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'baby talk' = motherese.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Bach-Peters sentence'. One in which each of two noun phrases

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: includes a pronoun anaphoric to the other: e.g. in The girl who won it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: really deserves the prize she won, the first pronoun (it) might have the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: same referent as the prize she won, the second (she) the same referent

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as the girl who won it.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: back. (Vowel) articulated with the highest point of the tongue

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: central.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: towards the back of thė mouth. E.g. [u:] in moon. Opp. front; also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In the scheme of Chomsky and Halle, *SPE [± back} is a distinctive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: feature of consonants as well as vowels. Of the consonants, *velars,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *uvulars, and *pharyngeals are {+ back]; *palatals are [− back].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with B as a 'back-channeller'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'back-channelling'. The use of any channel of communication seen

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as subsidiary to a main channel. Hence in particular, in *Conversation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Analysis, of any communication from a listener, who does not ‘have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the floor' according to the turn-taking hypothesis, to the speaker

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whose turn is in progress. E.g. while A is speaking. B may express

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: surprise, or grunt in agreement. But this does not count as a turn by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: B as, technically, a speaker. Instead it is treated as back-channelling,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: back-formation. The formation of a simple or simpler word from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one understood as derived, e.g. gruntled from disgruntled.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'backgrounded'. Treated, presented, or marked as subsidiary. E.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in a narrative, events are backgrounded if they are subsidiary to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: main story; in the structure of a sentence subordinate clauses are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: backgrounded, or tend to present backgrounded information; and so

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on. By analogy with 'foregrounded'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: background knowledge. Knowledge of the world in general, or of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the life of their specific society, that people can be assumed to share as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a framework for talking to one another. E.g. if someone says ‘His dog

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: kept me awake', tl.e person spoken to will share the knowledge that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: people own dogs, that dogs make a noise by barking, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: backshifting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: backshifting. Change of tenses e.g. in *indirect speech. Thus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: someone called Emma might say 'I am busy'; this might later be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reported by Emma said she was busy, with the verb (was) backshifted into

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the past tense. Contrast Emma said she is busy, without backshifting.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *pronominalization'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: backward anaphora = cataphora. Likewise 'backward

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bahasa-Indonesia. See Malay-Indonesian.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: called possessive or *exocentric compounds.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bahuvrihi. Sanskrit term for compounds such as whitethroat, meaning

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not 'throat which is white' but 'something having a white throat'. Also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: much-rice'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Named after a representative of the type, bahuvrihi '(having)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as e.g. Javanese.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Balinese. Spoken mainly in Bali; *Austronesian, of the same branch

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: area' or *Sprachbund.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Balkan languages'. Various languages of the Balkans, especially

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Albanian, Bulgarian, Greek, Macedonian, Rumanian, Serbo-Croat, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more peripherally Turkish, seen as a classic instance of a 'linguistic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ballistic. In the sense of 'broadly parabolic'. Thus a syllable may be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: seen as produced by a ballistic gesture of the vocal organs, whose peak

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corresponds to its vowel or nucleus.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hence *Balto-Slavic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Baltic. Branch of *Indo-European, of which *Latvian and *Lithuanian

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are the surviving representatives. Closer to *Slavic than to any other;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Balto-Slavic. Hypothetical branch of *Indo-European, subsuming

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Baltic and *Slavic. Long proposed but never universally accepted.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Baluchi. *Iranian language spoken mainly in the Baluchistan and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: neighbouring Sind provinces of Pakistan and in neighbouring parts

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of Afghanistan and south-eastern Iran.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bambara. See Mande.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: border eastwards.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bantoid. Term covering a large group of African languages which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: includes *Bantu and others broadly from the Nigeria-Cameroon

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: family.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bantu. Family of languages covering most of southern Africa, broadly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: south of a line crossing Cameroon, north Zaire, Uganda, and Kenya, a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: few degrees. north of the equator. Its members are similar in structure,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and in large areas form *dialect continua, with many local varieties.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The divisions between languages are in places conventional, and there

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is no single, universally accepted scheme of classification within the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: basic form

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The most important is *Swahili; for the location of some others with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speakers in the millions, either as a native language or as a lingua

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: franca, see Bemba, Kikuyu, Kongo, Lingala, Luba, Luganda, Makua,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Mbundu, Nyanja, Rwanda-Rundi, Shona, Sotho, Swati, Tsonga, Xhosa,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and Zulu.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bar (-). 1. As a mark of negation: thus x = 'not x'. 2. As a *macron,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indicating a long vowel. 3. See X-bar syntax.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Distinguished as such from a *solecism, which involved a combination

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of words.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: barbarism. The ancient term for an error in an individual word.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: That made him jump.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'bare infinitive'. An *infinitive in English without to: e.g. jump in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not operate.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: barrier. Used in *Government and Binding Theory for a boundary, or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the category defining a boundary, across which *government could

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accent) on the final syllable.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: barytone. A word, originally one in Ancient Greek, that is not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accented (and therefore had in ancient terms a low-pitched or ‘grave'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *root or *stem.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: base. Any form to which a process applies. Especially in morphology:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thus a singular noun in English (man, horse) is traditionally the base for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the formation of the plural (→ men, horses). Where processes apply to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: units smaller than words, 'base' is sometimes used equivalently to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: base component. A component of a *generative grammar which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: assigns an initial representation to each of a set of sentences. From

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: this other representations may be derived by other components.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The term belongs particularly to the period 1965-75, when the level

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of structure to be represented by a base component was a central issue.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: base-generated. (Element, construction) forming part of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure assigned by the *base component of a generative grammar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thus it was an issue at one stage whether pronouns should be base-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generated or derived by later rules of *pronominalization.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: French-based'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: base language. The language from which a *pidgin or *creole

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: has drawn the bulk of its vocabulary. E.g. the creole of Haiti is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Basic English. A reduced English vocabulary devised by C. K. Ogden

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the 1930s, with the intention that it should be used internationally.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: basic form. A form of an affix or other morphological unit from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which a range of alternating realizations is derived. Thus in most

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accounts the regular English plural ending has the basic form [z]. This

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: basic-level terms

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is unchanged in ties or dogs; but it changes to [ız] in words like horses or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: houses, where the preceding forms themselves end in [s] or [z], and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: changes to [s} in words like cats, where the form which precedes it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ends in a voiceless consonant.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. underlying form.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: basic-level terms. Lexical units belonging to a neutral level in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: taxonomy. E.g. if one runs over a dog one will say 'I have run over a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dog', not usually, unless perhaps one fails to recognize it as a dog, 'I

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: have run over an animal', nor, unless perhaps one is collecting the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: names of breeds that one hits, 'I have run over a labrador'. In that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sense dog belongs, with cat, horse, and others, to a neutral or basic level

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in comparison both with animal, which is more general, and with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: labrador, poodle, etc., which are more specific.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: basic vocabulary. Any set of words or concepts assumed to be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: central: e.g. that which was taken as the basis for *glottochronology.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposite (un livre rouge).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: basic word order. An order of words or phrases which is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguished as the commonest, or because it is in other respects

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *unmarked, or because others are derived from it. Thus in English

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the order adjective + noun is basic (a red book); in French it is the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mesolect.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: basilect. The variety of a language which, of a series predominantly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spoken at different social levels, has the lowest prestige or is most

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distant from a standard form. Especially in studies of *creoles, where

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the basilect is the variety with the most creole features. Opp. acrolect;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: any other family.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Basque. Language of the western Pyrenees, spoken by bilingual

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: coinmunities in Spain and France. The only language indigenous to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: western Europe that is not *Indo-European; nor related plausibly to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Baudouin de Courtenay, Jan (1845-1929). Polish linguist, whose

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contribution to phonology, originally in collaboration with his

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shorter-lived pupil Mikolai Kruszewski (1850-87), was fundamental

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to the development of structural linguistics in Europe, especially by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Saussure and in the work of the *Prague School in the 1930s. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: earliest to distinguish clearly between a *phoneme, seen as the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: psychological equivalent of a speech sound and a unit of what he

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: called ‘psychophonetics', and the speech sound itself; also remarkable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for his study of *alternations, and of the changes of status that an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alternation may undergo from one stage of a language to another,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which are the foundation for what was later called

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *mornhonbonolom

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *morphophonology.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Professor at Kazan' in Russia 1875-83; hence the leader of what is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: called the Kazan' School.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Benveniste, Émile

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: beat = ictus.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Behaghel's Law'. Name sometimes given to the general principle,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ascribed to work by O. Behaghel in the 1930s, by which syntactic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: elements that are closely related in meaning also tend to be next to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: each other in the sentence. Cf. iconicity.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: behaviourism. Movement in psychology which sought to eliminate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: all reference to subjective concepts or experience. The data were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accordingly restricted to the observable reactions of subjects to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: observable stimuli. Inaugurated by the American psychologist J. B.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Watson just before the First World War; also developed by A. P. Weiss

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and, through him, a major influence on *Bloomfield from the 1920s

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: onwards. Developed further after the Second World War, especially by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: B. F. Skinner; arguably still, through Bloomfield, an influence on the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Post-Bloomfieldians, but rapidly abandoned, in both psychology and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: linguistics, in the early 1960s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Associated with the heyday of *positivism in philosophy over the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: same period.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: has diverged only since the late Middle Ages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Belorussian. East *Slavic, closely related to Russian, from which it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Copperbelt region of Zambia.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bemba. *Bantu language spoken mainly in the north and in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: benefactive. *Case or *case role of units that refer to individuals

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with an interest in an action, etc. who are not directly part of it. E.g. for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the Red Cross is benefactive in They were collecting money for the Red Cross.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The case role is also described as that of a beneficiary.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Indo-Aryan.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bengali. *Indo-Aryan, the national language of Bangladesh, with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: half as many speakers in the Indian state of West Bengal. Also spoken

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: widely, through emigration, in Britain and elsewhere. Attested by texts

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from the early Middle Ages onwards; written in an *Indian script that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it shares with *Assamese, to which it is also closely related within

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in eastern West Africa.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Benue-Congo. Term currently applied to a vast group of African

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages, including *Bantu and most of those to the south of *Chadic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Benveniste, Émile (1902-76). Indo-Europeanist and general linguist

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whose works on Indo-European include an elegant theory ofthe

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure of thę root (1935), a subsequent account of agentive nouns

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and action nouns (1948), and two brilliant volumes (1969) on the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nature of Indo-European society as revealed by inherited vocabulary,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: together with a long series of monographs and articles on Iranian

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages especially. His contributions to general linguistics are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reprinted in two collections (1966, 1974), and include important essays

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Berber

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on the nature of communication and the act of utterance, on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subjectivity in language, on *deixis and the system of persons and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tenses. Many of his ideas, especially on the centrality of the speaker

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ('sujet parlant'), have been as influential outside linguistics as within.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Berber. Generic name for a group of languages in North Africa and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: across the Saharan region, generally where Arabic is also spoken. Most

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speakers are in the north-west, in Morocco especially. Grouped with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Semitic and others within *Afro-Asiatic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: BEV. See Black English (Vernacular).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bhojpuri. *Indo-Aryan language spoken in the east of Uttar Pradesh

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and in west Bihar, including Varanasi (Benares). Largely unwritten.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in both directions. Cf. di-.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bi-. From a Latin prefix related to the word for ‘two'. Thus a sentence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is 'biclausal' if it contains two clauses; a syllable is bimoraic if it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: counts as two *morae; processes, etc. are bidirectional if they operate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bidialectal. (Person, community) using two distinct dialects. Thence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bidialectalism: cf. bilingual.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: others.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bihari. Proposed branch of *Indo-Aryan, including *Maithili and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Magahi (in Bihar to the south of the Ganges); also *Bhojpuri and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pit [p] is a bilabial stop.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bilabial. Articulated with the lower lip against the upper lip. E.g. p in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bilateral. 1. (Opposition) between terms distinguished by a single

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: feature. Especially in phonology: e.g. [i:] in feel and [u:] in fool are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguished by a single feature ( {± front| or front vs. back). Opp.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: multilateral opposition. 2. Two-sided: e.g. a dependency is bilateral

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: if a depends on b and b also depends on a. Opp. unilateral.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bilingual. Having an effectively equal control of two native

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages. Thus a minority of people in Wales are bilingual in Welsh

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and English; many in England are bilingual in English and e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Punjabi. A bilingual community, as in Welsh-speaking parts of Wales,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is one in which bilingualism is normal.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Loosely or more generally, in some accounts, of people or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: communities that have two or more different languages, whether or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not control is effectively equal and whether or not more than one is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: native. Bilinguals in the ordinary sense are then variously called

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'ambilingual' or 'equilingual', or are qualified as 'full', 'true', 'ideal',

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or 'balanced' bilinguals.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: binarism. Tendency in many schools of structural linguistics to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reduce relations to binary distinctions. Thus the relations between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: three levels of vowel height (close, mid, open) are commonly analysed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Black English'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: into *binary features: [+ close, - open], {- close, – open], {– close,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: + open]. Similarly, the relations between three elements that make

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: up a syllable (onset, nucleus, coda) is reduced to a pattern of *binary

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: branching: [onset [nucleus coda] ].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Jakobson was the earliest and most doctrinaire exponent; through

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: his influence, directly or indirectly, such analyses were established in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the 1960s at all levels of *generative grammar, in *Generative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Phonology especially.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and [− animate] (inanimate). Opp. multivalued.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: binary. (Feature, etc.) with two values. Usually of one whose values

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are positive and negative: e.g. [± voice] has the values [+ voice] (voiced)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and [− voice] (voiceless), [± animate] the values [+ animate} (animate)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: feature [± voice], in English.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Elements distinguished only by a binary feature are in a binary

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposition (or binary contrast): e.g. [t} and [d], distinguished by the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: excluded.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: binary branching. Any configuration in a *phrase structure tree in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which a node is connected directly to two lower nodes. Opp. multiple

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: branching, which in some accounts is explicitly or effectively

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: binding. Relation in which an element is *bound (2) by an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *antecedent. E.g. in They helped each other, the subject they binds each

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: other. 'Binding Theory' is the part of *Government and Binding Theory

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: concerned with this relation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not white and black.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: binomial. A pair of words linked by a conjunction such as and. Called

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'irreversible' when their order is fixed: e.g. (I'll put it in) black and white,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: binyan. Term in Hebrew grammar for a pattern of stem formation,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: characteristically involving the addition of vowels to a consonantal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: root, of the kind general in Semitic languages. Cf. pattern.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'bioprogram'. A set of genetically inherited rules of language for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which, according to a hypothesis advanced by D. Bickerton in 1981,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: there is evidence e.g. when *creoles develop from *pidgins without

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: influence from other languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: biuniqueness. Constraint in phonology by which the phonetic and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonological representations of a form should each uniquely

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: determine the other. Identified by critics as a restriction implicit in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: theory of the *phoneme current in the USA in the 1940s and 1950s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: object.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bivalent. (Verb) having two *valents. Thus, in particular, a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *transitive verb such as love or drink, whose valents are a subject and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Black English'. Any distinct variety of English native to black,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: especially urban, populations in the USA and, by extension, in other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: blade

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: societies whose members are predominantly white. Also referred to by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the abbreviation BEV, for 'Black English Vernacular'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: blade. The upper surface of the tongue immediately behind the tip:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. in the articulation of [l] in leaf the blade is against the teeth ridge.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Distinguished as an *articulator from the tip and the *dorsum: hence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: laminal or lamino- (‘with the blade') vs. apical or apico- ('with the tip')

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or dorsal (with the dorsum').

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'bleaching'. Change by which the meaning of a word becomes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: increasingly unspecific. Typically, therefore, in instances of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *grammaticalization (2): e.g. the meaning of French pas (from Latin

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: passus ‘step, pace') was ‘bleached' as it developed into a mark of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: negation: (ne ...) pas 'not'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bleeding. Relation between rules which are *ordered in such a way

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that the application of the earlier rule restricts the set of forms that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the later will apply to. Especially in *Generative Phonology: e.g. a rule

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by which vowels are deleted in unstressed syllables bleeds a later rule

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by which medial consonants are voiced when a vowel follows.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Opp. feeding; cf. counter-bleeding, counter-feeding.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: blend. Word formed by joining the beginning of one form to the end

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of another. E.g. smog, formed in 1905 from smoke and fog.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: blocking. The barring of a process. E.g. one of word-formation: thus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the formation of a noun kingess, on the lines of princess, countess, etc. is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: seen as blocked by the existing word queen.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: block language. The form oflanguage used in newspaper headlines,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in cables, in notices, on labels of products, and so on. Distinguished by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: specific rules or patterns, which have developed in part independently

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of those in ordinary language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bloomfield, Leonard(1887-1949). American linguist and one of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the most influential of the 20th century. Originally a Germanist, but

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: famous for his general theory and for comparative and descriptive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: studies of *Algonquian languages, especially Menomini. His first

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: general work, An Introduction to the Study of Language (1914). was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: influenced by the psychology of W. Wundt; from the 1920s, however.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: he was committed to a ‘physicalist' philosophy of science in which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: all scientific statements are reducible to accounts of observable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phenomena, and in his great work Language (1933) he sought to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: establish the foundations of linguistjcs, as an autonomous science, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a way that would be compatible with this view and specifically with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *behaviourism in psychology. This led, in particular, to an account of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaning in terms of the practical events' accompanying a speech

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: signal, in which the meaning of a word, for example, is constituted

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by features of such ‘events', including events within a speaker's body,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: common to all the occasions on which it is uttered. Bloomfield's work

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: boundary marker

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was continued, partly in a new direction, by the *Post-Bloomfieldians

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and still, in part, by their successors. Many ideas now current,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: especially in the theory of grammar, are therefore his in origin.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Boas, Franz (1858-1942). American anthropologist, the teacher of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Sapir and other eminent scholars in both linguistics and anthropology

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and, more than any other before or since, the founder and organizer

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of linguistic field-work in the USA. His most important general

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contribution is his introduction to the Handbook of American Indian

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Languages (1911), which emphasizes, in particular, the structural

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diversity of languages and the need to describe them in terms

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inherited in the European tradition.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: independent, where necessary, of the grammatical categories

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'body language'. Popular term which lumps together some

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conventional forms of *non-verbal communication with other states

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or dispositions of a human body, voluntary or involuntary, identifiable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as some kind of 'sign' to other people.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bokmål. See Norwegian.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: borrowing. Conventional term for the introduction into language

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a of specific words, constructions, or morphological elements of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language b. Thus table and marble are among the many *loan words

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: borrowed into English from Old French in the period after the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Norman conquest. 'Dialect borrowing' is a similar transference of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: features from one dialect to another, often posited to explain the lack

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of consistent divisions between them.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bottom-up. (Procedure) which determines the structure of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence, etc. by working from smaller units to larger. Opp. top-down,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. as alternative strategies in *parsing (2).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bound (1). (*Morpheme) which cannot stand as a word on its own.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thus un- in unkind is a bound form, since there is no word 'un'. Opp.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: free (1): cf. minimal free form.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bound (2). (Pronoun, etc.) linked syntactically to an *antecedent. E.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in He saw himself, the reflexive himself would (according to most views of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the scope of syntax) be 'bound by' he. The syntactic relation between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: such an element and its antecedent is one of bound *anaphora.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Opp. free (2). The sense is derived from use in logic, where a variable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: catachresis [katə'kri:sis]. Ancient term for the incorrect use of words:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. the use of the term ‘universal' is catachrestic when it refers to

layout_dets.text: cataphora [kə'tafərə]. The relation between an *anaphoric

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: expression and an 'antecedent' that comes later. E.g. in When he had

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: finished, Jones was exhausted, the referent of he might be Jones; if so, it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is a cataphoric element, whose ‘antecedent' is the later phrase Jones.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also called ‘anticipatory anaphora' or 'backward anaphora'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: categorial component. The *base component of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *transformational grammar: i.e. one whose rules, called 'categorial

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rules', deal with relations among syntactic categories.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: categorial grammar. A type of formal grammar, originally devised

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by the logician K. Ajdukiewicz in the 1930s. Its basis is a lexicon, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which words are assigned to categories of greater or lesser complexity:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: if a string of words is well-formed, these will combine, by a repeated

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: operation of cancellation, to a designated simple category. E.g. run is a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: word with which a preceding noun (N) can form a sentence (S): men

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: run. So, assign run to a complex category N\S, indicating precisely that.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: By the operation of cancellation, X followed by X\Y reduces to Y; hence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: N (men) plus N\S (run) reduces to, and is thus assigned as a whole to, a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence category S. An adjective such as young can combine similarly,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: but in the opposite order, with a following noun. So, assign young to a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complex category N/N. By the operation of cancellation, Y/X followed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by X also reduces to Y. So, for the string young men run, the reduction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: will be in two stages. First, N/N (young) plus N (men) reduces to N: i.e.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the form as a whole is also of this category. Then N (young men) plus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: N\S (run) will again reduce to S.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Categorial grammars have the same *weak generative capacity as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *context-free phrase structure grammars. For the operation of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cancellation compare later concepts of *unification.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'categorical rule'. See rule (2).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: category. Any class or system of grammatical or lexical units

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguished at some level in the structure of a language. 'Noun

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: c-command

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phrase', for example, is a *syntactic category. 'Case' and 'tense' are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inflectional or *morphosyntactic categories. Colour terms or terms for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: kinship might be said to form a 'lexical category', and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: category-neutral. (Rule, principle, etc.) which applies regardless of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the category to which a unit is assigned: thus regardless, especially,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of any of the syntactic categories noun, verb, etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: catenative. A verb such as need in I need to stop, seen as a link between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the subject (I) and the following infinitive (to stop). Named from the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Latin word for chain' (catena): e.g. like and promise form part of a chain

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in I would like to promise to do it tomorrow.

layout_dets.text: Caucasian. Cover term for languages whose families are indigenous

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to the Caucasus. South Caucasian ('Kartvelian') includes *Georgian,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and is for many though not all scholars a family with no plausible

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relationship to the others. North West Caucasian includes *Abkhaz,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: West Circassian (Adyghe), and East Circassian (Kabardian), and is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: separated by Ossetic, which is *Iranian, from North Central Caucasian

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (*Chechen, Ingush) and North East Caucasian (in terms of geography,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: east), of which Avar (north-east Dagestan) and Lezgi (south Dagestan

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and north Azerbaijan) are the largest. The North Central and North

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cAus = causative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: causal conjunction.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: causal. (Clause, etc.) indicating a cause or reason; e.g. because I am busy

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in I can't see you because I am busy. The subordinator because is in turn a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: causative (caus). (Construction, verb, affix) used in saying who or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: what causes something to happen. E.g., schematically, I eat-Caus-PAsT

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the baby 'I fed the baby': i.e. 'I caused the baby to eat'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A verb derived in this way will take a further argument, referring to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the causer'; thus, schematically, non-causative Y (Z) verb (transitive or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: intransitive) → causative X Y (Z) verb. Similarly when the causative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: element is itself a verb: English he ate (the apple) → I made him eat (the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: apple). Hence extensions of the term, common in the 1970s, to e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English feed (with two arguments) vs. eat (with one argument), where

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: there is no ‘explicit' causative element.

layout_dets.text: c-command. A relation of *command (2), variously defined in detail

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which obtains e.g. between the subject of a sentence and an anaphoric

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: element in its predicate. For example, in John's father hurt himself, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: is not c-commanded by John, and it is for that reason, it has been

layout_dets.text: Cebuano. A language of the Philippines, spoken in Negros and other
