layout_dets.text: Celtiberian. See Celtic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Celtic. Branch of *Indo-European, conventionally divided into

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Continental Celtic', extinct by or soon after AD 500, and 'Insular

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Celtic', spoken in (or in the case of *Breton originating in) the British

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Isles. Continental Celtic is attested only by inscriptions and place-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: names, and by references in Latin authors, but forms of it were spoken

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: widely in the area of north Italy (Lepontic), France (Gaulish), and parts

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of Spain (Celtiberian) before the Roman expansion; also in ancient

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Galatia (now part of Turkey). Insular Celtic is divided into Brythonic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or Brittonic (Welsh, Breton, Cornish) and Goidelic (Gaelic).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Within Indo-European, Celtic shares features with *Italic especially:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hence an old conjecture, never generally accepted, that they might at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a higher level form a single 'Italo-Celtic' branch.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ceneme. Hjelmslev's term for a unit of *expression. A'cenemic'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: system of writing is one which represents phonological units as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposed to units of the lexicon or grammar: i.e. an *alphabet or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *alpha-syllabic system or a *syllabary.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: From the Greek word for 'empty': opp. plereme, 'pleremic'.

layout_dets.text: central. (Vowel) intermediate between *front and *back. For

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: example, [ə] in [batə] (butter) is a mid central vowel; u in Welsh du

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Central American languages. The indigenous languages of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: geographical area, now dominated in most parts by Spanish. Those

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: described as Meso-American form a linguistic area or *Sprachbund,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: broadly between a line across the centre of Mexico (from the state of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Nayarit to northern Veracruz) and another east of Guatemala: they

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: include, in particular, the *Mayan family to the east, with the *Oto-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Manguean and languages of the Nahuan or Aztecan branch of *Uto-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Aztecan to the west; also smaller families (Mixe-Zoquean, centred on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the Tehuantepec Isthmus, and Totonacan, in the north-east of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: area), and individual languages, especially Tarascan (in the state of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Michoacán), Huave, and Tequistlatec (both in Oaxaca), not belonging

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to any of these. Oaxaca and adjacent parts of neighbouring states form

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the region of greatest linguistic diversity.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Outside the Meso-American area, languages of the Sonoran branch

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of Uto-Aztecan are spoken in north-west Mexico; to the east of the area,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mostly ones of families also represented in South America.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: than cardinal [a]. 2. (Vowel) resulting from a sound-change or other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: process by which its quality becomes central or more central.

layout_dets.text: centre-embedding. The inclusion of a syntactic unit within another

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which is of the same category. E.g. in the girl [who the man [who you met]

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: larger (a).

layout_dets.text: which a velar stop, as in Latin centum ‘hundred', did not change to a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: chain shift. A series of two or more sound changes, by which sound

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a > sound b, sound b > sound c, and so on. E.g. in the Greek dialect of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ancient Athens, by which [u:| > [y:| and {o:| in turn > [u:}. Divided in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: principle into drag chains and push chains. E.g. in the example cited

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the fronting of [u:] might be seen as having 'dragged' [o:] after it into

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the phonetic space so vacated; alternatively, the raising of {o:} to {u:}

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: might have pushed' the existing (u:] out of it.

layout_dets.text: change is change in *phonology, morphological change change in

layout_dets.text: Chinese. Branch of *Sino-Tibetan. The most important member

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (conventionally 'dialect') is Mandarin, native in most of China roughly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: 'Old Chinese' is the form spoken from the 5th century BC to the end

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Classical Chinese, as a written language, derives. The *Chinese

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: millennium Bc. *Pinyin is now the standard Roman spelling.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: evidence, in at the latest the first half of the 2nd millennium Bc. First

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (oracle bones') dating from the 14th century. The characters now used

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Each character represents a minimal grammatical element or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *morpheme, realized phonetically by a single syllable. Some

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: characters are simple, often pictographic in origin: e.g. the precursor

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the one which represents the morpheme meaning water' was made

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: up of wavy lines. But the vast majority are 'compound' characters,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in which, in particular, a character taken to represent a syllable as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a phonetic unit has been combined with one which represents a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morpheme with a related meaning. E.g. the compound character for a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morpheme meaning ‘sea' has as its ‘semantic' element the radical of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the character for the 'water' morpheme, and, as its phonetic' element,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one which also represents a homonymous form for ‘sheep' (yáng).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Characters of Chinese origin are used for *Japanese, partly in a very

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: in a *structure.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the terminology of Halliday especially, there is 'choice' among the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: chômeur. An element in *Relational Grammar that has been

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'demoted', by a syntactic operation, from the *nucleus of a clause to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: its *periphery. Thus in the passive construction an *agent (3) would

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be a chômeur demoted from the nuclear role of subject: nucteusla wall

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: blocked my path] → mucteus[my path was blockd] by a wall.

layout_dets.text: From the French word for ‘unemployed'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Chomsky, Avram Noam (1928- ). American linguist whose theories

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: have revolutionized much of the subject in the second half of the 20th

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: century. In Syntactic Structures (1957), his first book and for many still

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: his most important single work, he overturned the strategy of analysis

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: developed by the *Post-Bloomfieldians and replaced it with a formal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: theory of *generative grammars and the concept of an *evaluation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: procedure as a means of justifying them. In his next major book,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Aspects of the Theory of Syntax (1965), he proposed a theory of *levels

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which included, in particular, the distinction between *deep structure

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and *surface structure; he also introduced the notion, in the long

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: run far more important, that much of the structure oflanguage in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: general is innate' or genetically inherited. From the end of the 1960s

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Chomsky's work has been directed above all to the development of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: theory of *universal grammar (2), conceived as an account of what is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: so inherited, and, by implication, to confirming that such a universal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammar does exist. A succession of works in the 1970s led by the end

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the decade to a *Principles and Parameters Theory, embodied and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: developed further in the 1980s in what is called by his followers

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Government and Binding Theory: see in particular Reflections on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Chomsky-adjunction'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Language (1975), Lectures on Government and Binding (1981), Knowledge of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Language (1986), and, at a more popular level, Language and Problems

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of Knowledge (1988). The latest versions are those developed in his

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: programme of *minimalism from the early 1990s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Chomsky-adjunction'. Any operation on a *phrase structure tree

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in which an element is added to a constituent of class A in such a way

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that both become part of a larger constituent, also of class A. E.g. if

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: horse has the structure [horse], the addition of -s by Chomsky-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: adjunction would yield the structure I [horse] s]. Cf. sister-adjunction.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the mid-1950s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Chomsky-hierarchy'. A ranking of *finite state grammars,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *context-free and *context-sensitive phrase structure grammars,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and *unrestricted rewrite systems, in respect of increasing *power

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or *weak generative capacity. The term refers to work by Chomsky

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: duration.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'chroneme'. (Daniel) Jones's term for a phonological unit of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: duration: e.g. long and short as chronemes distinguishing vowels in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: some forms of English. Likewise 'chrone', for any phonetic degree of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Chrysippus. See Stoics.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Chukotko-Kamchatkan. Small family of languages, of which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Chukchi is the most important, spoken on the Chukotka and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Kamchatka Peninsulas in Siberia.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Circassian. Alternative name oftwo North West *Caucasian

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages, Adyghe (West Circassian) and Kabardian or Kabardo-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cherkess (East Circassian).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: frag-. Cf. parasynthetic (2).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: circumfix. A combined *prefix and *suffix, treated as a single unit.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. in German gefragt ‘asked', the forms which mark the participle,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ge- and -t, might be seen as a circumfix (ge . . . t) enclosing the root

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fall in intonation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: circumflex (^). In origin a sign invented for Ancient Greek to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: represent an *accent (1) realized by a falling pitch. Used in linguistics

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: either for a falling *tone in tone languages or for a rise followed by a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: circumstantial. (Adverb, adverbial) which indicates the external

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: setting, in space and time especially, of an event, etc. E.g. both in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Chicago and yesterday are circumstantial elements in We met her in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Chicago yesterday. From French, where circonstant' or 'complément

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: circonstanciel' would be variously applied to these and other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *adjuncts forming the *periphery (1) of a clause.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: citation form. The form used to refer to a lexical unit. The choice is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a matter of convenience and is often arbitrary. E.g. in French a verb is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'clear l'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: referred to by the infinitive: manger'to eat'. But in Latin it is referred

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to by the first-person singular of the present indicative: edo 'I eat'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: classeme. A semantic feature characterizing a class of lexical units

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: similar in grammar as well as meaning, which cuts across the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: organization of the lexicon into semantic fields: e.g. animate vs.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inanimate. More usual in French or German accounts of word

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaning ('classème', 'Klassem') than in English-speaking countries

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'that-ge man').

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: classifier. Used, in accounts of Chinese especially, of a form which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: marks a noun of a specific semantic class and which has to accompany

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. a numeral. Thus in Chinese yí-ge rén 'one man' ge is a classifier,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: originally from a word for ‘bamboo stalk', which has to follow the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: numeral (yí ‘one') when it modifies any of a large class of nouns,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: including rén ‘man'. Often called a 'numeral classifier', though e.g. a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: classifier is also required in Chinese by a demonstrative (schematically

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clause. Any syntactic unit whose structure is, or is seen as reduced

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from, that of a sentence. Thus, in particular, one which includes a verb

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and the elements that accompany it.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The smaller unit who you introduced me to is accordingly a clause in I

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: liked the girl who you introduced me to. So, in many accounts, is meeting her

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in I liked meeting her or to meet her in I want to meet her, or even, in some,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a single word or phrase like in his cups in He sang hymns (sc. when he was)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in his cups. So, in current usage, is each of these sentences as a whole.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clause chaining. Used of a variety of constructions in which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clauses or elements seen as clauses are linked in ways unlike those

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: characteristic of European languages. Hence, in particular, of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constructions with *switch-reference; also, in some accounts, of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *serial verb constructions; also of ones in which only one verb in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sequence has a full set of inflections; also of ones in which relations

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between clauses are marked by verb endings and not by conjunctions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clausemate. The relation between two syntactic elements that are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: part of a single clause. E.g. in Jane promised [she would visit her], she and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: her are clausemates; therefore, by a rule which distinguishes them as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: such, they must be understood to refer to different people.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clause union. Syntactic process, distinguished by this term in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Relational Grammar, by which a main clause and a subordinate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clause become one. Applied especially to constructions with an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: infinitive in Romance languages: e.g. in Italian, La farò venire (lit. 'her

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: I-will-make to-come') is treated as a single clause derived from a main

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clause with a causative verb ('I will make') with, at an underlying

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: level, a second clause as its complement (‘she to come’).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'clear l'. See dark 1.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cleft

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cleft. (Construction) of e.g. It was my sister (who/that) he married. In cleft

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentences the copula (was) is preceded by it and followed by a noun

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phrase (my sister) and a relative clause: distinguished as such from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *pseudo-clefts (e.g. what he did was marry my sister).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cliché. In the ordinary sense: hence some *idioms and set

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *expressions are clichés; also some other expressions involving

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: habitual *collocations.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: click. Sound produced by suction of the tongue against the roof of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mouth. A body of air is trapped between the back of the tongue, which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is in contact with the velum, and a second closure further forward.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The space enclosed is then enlarged, the air within it is rarefied, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: second closure is released, and air flows inwards.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in sounds outside the system of phonemes, e.g. the one written 'tut!

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tut!' in English. Defined by phoneticians as a sound produced by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by the velum.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Clicks are an important part of the consonant system in *Khoisan

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and neighbouring *Bantu languages in South Africa; elsewhere mainly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an ingressive velaric *airstream mechanism. But this is perhaps

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: misleading, since the movement of air is not in reality initiated

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cline = gradience.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shortening high fidelity.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clipping. Process of word-formation in which an existing form is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: abbreviated. E.g. fan 'devotee, enthusiast' was formed in the late

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 19th century by shortening fanatic, hi-fi in the mid-20th century by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that precedes it.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ditic. A grammatical element treated as an independent word in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: syntax but forming a phonological unit with the word that precedes or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: follows it. E.g. Ancient Greek tis is a clitic in nêsós tis ‘a (certain) island':

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it is inflected independently (in this case as nominative singular) but

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accentually it forms a unit with the word for island' (basically nêsos)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to [haftə] go.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: From the Greek word for 'leaning': thus unaccented tis leans on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nêsos. ‘Enclitics' are clitics linked phonologically, as here, to the word

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: preceding, *proclitics those linked to the word following. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinction between clitics and *affixes is naturally fluid: e.g. English

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: -n't in haven't or aren't is a clitic by some criteria but has been claimed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as an affix by others. So too is the boundary between clitics and full

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: words: e.g. unstressed to is a clitic, by some relevant criteria, in I have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clitic climbing. Syntactic process, e.g. in Italian, in which a *clitic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pronoun or another similar element forms a unit not with the verb to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which it bears a direct syntactic relation but with one to which that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: verb is subordinate. E.g. in lo faccio venire 'I make him come', lo 'him' is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the subject of the infinitive venire 'to come', but 'climbs' to form a unit

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with faccio 'make'. Cf. raising (2); also described in terms of *clause union.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cluster

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'clitic doubling'. The use of a *clitic pronoun with the same

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: referent and in the same syntactic function as another element in its

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clause. E.g. in Spanish le vi a Juan 'I saw John', le ‘him' is a clitic parallel

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to a Juan '(to) John'. One case of what Bloomfield called *cross-reference.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: becomes a *clitic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cliticization. Syntactic process or historical change by which a word

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: movement'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clitic pronoun. A pronoun which is a *clitic: e.g. in Modern Greek

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ton simpathí (lit. 'him likes') the verb has as its object a clitic (hence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: unaccented) pronoun ton. Such pronouns are often seen as moved from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a basic position of an object or other element; hence clitic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are 'high'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: close. (Vowel) produced with the body of the tongue close to the roof

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the mouth: e.g. those of heat or hoot. 'Close' is opposed to ‘open' in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the classification of *cardinal vowels; in other schemes close vowels

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: close approximation. Narrowing of the space between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *articulators sufficient to cause turbulence in a flow of air: e.g. of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lower lip and upper teeth in the articulation of [f] or [v]. Distinguished

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as a degree of stricture from *open approximation and *closure.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: closed class. A class of words or morphemes whose membership is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fixed and can be listed. E.g. there is a closed class of determiners (the,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: this, etc.). Opp. open class.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: closed syllable. One which ends in a consonant: e.g. the first

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: syllable, [as], of aster. Opp. open syllable.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: close juncture. The normal linkage between successive sounds

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: within a word. Cf. juncture.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: close-mid (vowel) = half-close.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: close transition. Linkage between sounds characterized by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *coarticulation. Opp. open transition: cf. close vs. open juncture

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: closing diphthong. One which changes from relatively open to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relatively close: e.g. [au] in how.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: closure. Contact between *articulators by which a flow of air is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: completely blocked: e.g. between the lips in the articulation of [p} or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [m]. Distinguished as a degree of stricture from *close approximation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and *open approximation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cloze test. A test in which pupils or subjects are instructed to supply

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: words, etc., that are missing from text presented to them.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cluster. A sequence of consonants before, after, or between vowels.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. |str] is a medial consonant cluster in words like astray.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: coalescence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: coalescence = fusion.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: coarticulation. The simultaneous or overlapping articulation of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: two successive phonological units. E.g. in a normal pronunciation of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sweet [swi:t} the lips are rounded in the articulation of [s]; i.e. there

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is coarticulation of [s] and the [w] which follows. In one normal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pronunciation of [kp} in duckpond {dakppnd], the contact of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: back of the tongue with the soft palate (for [k]) does not end before

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the closure of the lips (for [p]): i.e. there is a period of coarticulation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of both consonants.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (= perseverative) assimilation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: To be distinguished from *double articulation (2) in that the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sounds are separate phonological units. Coarticulation is classed as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: anticipatory, where the articulation of a following unit is anticipated,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vs. perseverative, where that of a preceding unit continues. Compare

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the distinction between *regressive (= anticipatory) and *progressive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [st] in [best] (best).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: coda. The part of a *syllable, if any, that comes after the nucleus; e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'code mixing'. See code switching. Also used by some sociolinguists

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for what is generally called *borrowing.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: intervals.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: code switching. Switching from one language, dialect, etc. to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: another. E.g. two business associates meet and chat in one language;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the meeting becomes formal and they switch to another. Sometimes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguished, and then by no means consistently, from 'code mixing'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. in 'code switching' the switch is made, as in this example, because

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the nature or the subject of the conversation changes; in ‘code mixing'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speakers switch to and fro, for no specific external reason, at frequent

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Code' itself is used by some sociolinguists effectively of any

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinct variety of a language. Also by others of varieties and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages generally, whether or not they are believed to be 'codes'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (like the morse code or a code of morals) in any illuminating sense.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cognate. (Languages, words, etc.) that have developed from a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: common ancestor. E.g. English is cognate with German; likewise

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English beam is cognate with German Baum 'tree'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cognate object. An object in syntax whose head noun parallels and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: repeats the meaning of the verb. E.g. life parallels lived in She lived her life

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in Berlin, or She lived a full life.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cognitive Linguistics. Movement in linguistics, nascent from the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: late 1980s, emphasizing the continuity of language with the workings

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the mind in general and seeking to ground a theory of language in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accounts of cognition. Thus opposed especially to structuralist schools,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: including that of Chomsky, which stress the autonomy of linguistics.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: collective noun

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Leading proponents include R. W. Langacker and G. P. Lakoff, both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: advocates, in their early cáreers, of *Generative Semantics.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'cognitive meaning'. The meaning of a sentence considered in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: abstraction from *affective or emotive meaning, stylistic nuances,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the meaning of word order in specific contexts, and whatever else is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: deemed or assumed to be irrelevant to it. E.g. Harry kissed her (in an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: amazed whisper) might be said to have the same cognitive meaning as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Harry kissEd her (shouted at the top of one's voice), or HARry kissed her,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is said to be preserved in paraphrase.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or She was kissed by Harry, and so on. Often therefore, in practice, what

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to answer. Cf. cohesion.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: coherence. Used semi-technically of the way in which the content of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: connected speech or text hangs together, or is interpreted as hanging

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: together, as distinct from that of random assemblages of sentences.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Especially in studies of conversation: e.g. it is by a principle of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: coherence that, if one speaker asks a question, the other is expected

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: belong to other words.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cohesion. 1. The connection between successive sentences in texts,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conversations, etc., in so far as it can be described in terms of specific

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: syntactic units. E.g. A says 'Peter came' and B replies ‘But he was very

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: late': in this interchange the role of but as a conjunction and the link

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: betwen the pronoun he and its antecedent Peter are both aspects of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cohesion. 2. The property of syntactic units which are not interrupted

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by elements that do not belong to them. Thus words are generally

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cohesive: i.e. they are not interrupted by other words or elements that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cohort model. Model for the perception of spoken words proposed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by W. Marslen-Wilson in the mid-1980s. It assumes a 'recognition

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lexicon' in which each word is represented by a full and independent

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'recognition element'. When the system receives the beginning of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relevant acoustic signal, all elements matching it are fully activated,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and, as more of the signal is received, the system tries to match it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: independently with each of them. Wherever it fails the element is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: deactivated; this process continues until only one remains active.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: co-hyponym. See hyponymy.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: co-indexing. The linking, by subscript *indices, of elements which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: have the same referent.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: convention.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: collapsing (of rules). Their conflation by means of an *abbreviatory

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: collective noun. One used to refer to individuals as a group: e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clergy, meaning 'clergymen in general'. Also of a noun or form of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: noun which distinguishes a kind from individuals of that kind: e.g. in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Egyptian Arabic, [xo:x| ‘peaches as a kind' in opposition to [xo:xa] (an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: colligation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: individual peach) or the plural [xo:xat] (three or more individual

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: peaches).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: colligation. Firth's term for the general relation between elements

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in a construction, as opposed to a *collocation or relation between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: individual words. Thus the collocation e.g. of heavy and smoker in She's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a heavy smoker instances the colligation of an adjective with an agent

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: noun, or with a noun generally.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: collocation. A relation within a syntactic unit between individual

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lexical elements; e.g. computer collocates with hate in My computer hates

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: me. Used especially where words specifically or habitually go together:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. blond collocates with hair in blond hair or Their hair is blond; drunk

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with lord in as drunk as a lord; run with riot in run riot. Hence of *idioms:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. blow and top are part of a ‘special collocation' in She blew her top.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A collocational restriction is any restriction on the collocability of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one individual word with another. Cf. selectional restriction (1).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phoneme, which are in *complementary distribution.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: combinatory variants. Variant realizations, especially of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: combining forms.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: combining form. A form of a word, or a form related to or in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaning like a word, used only as an element in compounds: e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Anglo- in Anglo-American or socio- in socioeconomic; also retro- in retrovirus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or bio- in biotechnology. Common in English, where in some putative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: compounds, such as autocrat or technocrat, both members would be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: comitative. *Case or *case role with the meaning 'together with,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accompanied by': e.g. with my husband, or the preposition with, is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: comitative in He went to town with my husband.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: command (1). An utterance which constitutes an order: e.g. 'Get

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: out!' as an order to someone to leave the room. An indirect command

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is a clause representing a command in *indirect speech: e.g. in I ordered

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [it to be sold] or We directed [that they should be rewarded]. Cf. imperative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: command (2). Cover term for various relations defined over nodes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in a *phrase structure tree. In the most general case, a *node A on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one branch commands' a node B on another branch if (a) both are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *dominated by the same node C and (b) C is the lowest *branching

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: node that dominates A.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The relation most widely invoked is *c-command, where C, as above,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: may be any branching node. In other relations it is one of a specific

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: type: e.g. it must represent a *maximal projection of some category

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ('m-command'), or it must be a cyclic node as defined by a principle

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of *subjacency ('k-command’).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: comment. A syntactic element which forms a basic sentence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: construction with a *topic (3). Hence the equivalent, in such a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: commutation test

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'topic-comment' construction, of the *predicate (1) in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subject-predicate construction.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also, more generally, of the parts of a sentence other than a topic,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whether or not they are seen as forming a single syntactic unit. E.g. in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The beer you can, of course, drink, the comment is everything after the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: topic the beer.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: seen as expressing a comment, etc. which is in meaning, at least,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parenthetical. E.g. ones like I think in Nothing, I think, happened or as you

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: know in As you know, nothing happened; also, e.g. one like what is odd in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: What is odd, she had her husband with her.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: comment clause. Used by Quirk et al., *CGE to cover various clauses

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: commissive. A type of *speech act by which speakers e.g. commit

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: themselves to doing something: thus especially a promise.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'common core'. The core of a language as defined by units,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constructions, etc. that distinguish all its dialects. Thus the order

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of subject and verb might belong to a common core of English;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the inflection e.g. of the verb 'to be' does not.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: common gender. 1. Traditionally of the gender of nouns with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which either masculine or feminine forms can agree: e.g. in French

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: le ministre 'the-MAsc minister', la ministre 'the-FEM minister'. Cf. epicene.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2. Also of the use of a masculine, as a neutral gender, when reference

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is indifferently to male and female.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: common noun. One whose application is not restricted to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: arbitrarily distinguished members of a class. E.g. girl is a common

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: noun that may be used in reference to any individual characterizable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in general as a girl. Opp. proper noun.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: communicative competence. A speaker's knowledge of the total

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: set of rules, conventions, etc. governing the skilled use of language in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: society. Distinguished by D. Hymes in the late 1960s from Chomsky's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: concept of *competence, in the restricted sense of knowledge of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: communicative dynamism. See Functional Sentence Perspective.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: communicative language teaching. Method of teaching a foreign

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language which aims to develop *communicative competence, as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposed to simple knowledge of grammatical and similar structures.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: commutation test. *Hjelmslev's term for the basic test which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguishes one unit of a language from another. Strictly, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: replacement of one unit by another on the level of *expression

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (crudely a change in form) must entail a replacement at the level of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *content (crudely a change in meaning) and vice versa. But often,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: especially in practice or in later usage, of a test involving the exchange

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of expression units only.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Comp

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Comp. See X-bar syntax. For complement', but not always a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *complement in any other sense.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CoMP (C). Category posited in Chomsky's *Principles and Parameters

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Theory whose realizations include *complementizers. E.g. in He asked

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: if I made them, the subordinate clause is a ‘COMP phrase' (CP) headed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by if.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: compact. *Distinctive feature in the scheme proposed by *Jakobson

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Characterized acoustically by a concentration of energy in a narrow

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: part of the spectrum: thus with reference to, in particular, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *formants (1) of *open vowels. Opp. diffuse.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The opposition of compact and diffuse is one of two that were taken

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by Jakobson to define both a triangle of vowels and a triangle of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: maximally *grave and [t] is maximally *acute. This scheme was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: important achievement of Jakobson's binary method.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonants parallel to it. In the illustration. [a] is maximally compact,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [p] and [t} are maximally diffuse; on the horizontal axis, {p] is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: abandoned by Chomsky and Halle in *SPE, but remains the most

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: comparative. (Construction, inflection, etc.) by which individuals,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: etc. are compared, in respect of some property, with others. Originally

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of inflected forms with the meaning 'more (than)': e.g. taller, with a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: comparative suffix er, in He is taller than me. As such a term in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: category of degree or grade. Thence of constructions. whether or not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: they are marked by inflections: e.g. in He is more fortunate than me; also;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with less . . . than, in He is less fortunate than me.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. equative; superlative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: classification.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: comparative linguistics. 1. The comparison of languages by the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *comparative method. 2. The comparison of languages for whatever

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: purpose, whether e.g. for *genetic classification or for *typological

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: comparative method. The method of comparing languages to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: determine whether and how they have developed from a common

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complementarity

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ancestor. The items compared are lexical and grammatical units, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the aim is to discover correspondences relating sounds in two or more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: different languages, which are so numerous and so regular, across sets

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of units with similar meanings, that no other explanation is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reasonable.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Three points are worth underlining. (a) The argument does not rest

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on mere similarities. Since sounds change over time, the older the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ancestor the more likely it is that correspondences will be between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sounds that are not similar: e.g. initial k- in one language might

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: correspond to v- in another and to s- in a third. Likewise the greater the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: danger that similarities as such will be misleading. (b) The argument

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cannot safely rest on two or more correspondences. E.g. an s in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language A might correspond quite frequently to an s in language

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: B, not because the words in question have been inherited from a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a conjecture.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: common ancestor but because they have been *borrowed, e.g. from B

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: into A, in the not too distant past. (c) It is a matter of judgement how

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: far other explanations, such as borrowing or chance, can be excluded.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: But the more remote the postulated ancestor the more likely it is that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: judgement will have to be suspended, and the hypothesis will remain

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: comparative philology. The study of a *family of languages,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: especially the *Indo-European family, by the *comparative method.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: compensatory lengthening. Any change or process by which a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vowel is lengthened as an element is lost: e.g. that in morphology by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which Ancient Greek melan- 'black' + -s (NoM sG) → melās.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: competence. Chomsky's term in the 1960s for a 'speaker-hearer's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: knowledge of his language', as represented by a *generative grammar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Opp. performance: cf. I-language; also communicative competence.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complement. A syntactic element seen as 'completing' the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: construction of another element. Thus, in particular: 1. Of elements

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: other than a subject which are within the *valency of a verb or other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lexical unit. E.g. in He put it on the floor, both it and on the floor are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complements of put and, within on the floor, the floor is the complement

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of on. 2. Specifically of such elements when they are clauses: thus that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: he came is a complement clause in They said that he came or the news that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: he came. 3. Specifically of *subject complements and *object

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complements: e.g. happy in He seems happy or That will make him hannv

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The term is originally from French ('complément'). But French and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English usage no longer match: in particular, the 'compléments' of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: verb include all other elements of the predicate, whether or not they

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are complements in any of the senses above.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complementarity. Relation between lexical units whose meanings

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are mutually exclusive. E.g. between male and female: what is male is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complementary distribution

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thereby not female, and vice versa. Words which stand in such a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relation are complementary terms (or complementaries).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Distinguished in typologies of *sense relations from other relations

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: broadly between opposites: cf. gradable antonymy especially.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complementary distribution. Relation between sounds or forms

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whose *distributions do not overlap. Thus in southern British English

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (*RP), an unaspirated {p] appears after an initial [s], e.g. in [spın] (spin);

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an aspirated [p] e.g. initially in [phın]; but there is no context in which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: both would be normal. Therefore they are in complementary

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distribution, and therefore, in part, they are described as *allophones

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the same *phoneme.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. contrast for contrastive distribution: also free variation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complementation. 1. A set or series of *complements that a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: verb, etc. may or must take. E.g. verbs such as read have as their

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complementation a direct object (I read a newspaper); that of put

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: includes both a direct object and a locative (I put it on the floor); that of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be, if described in a similar way, might be a predicative adjective (I am

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cold), noun phrase (I am a nervous wreck), or locative (I am in the kitchen).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Equivalent, therefore, to *valency (or *argument structure) minus the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subject. 2. The general relation in which complements stand: thus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguished, in particular, from that of *modification (1).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. that in She said [that she would]. Cf. COMP.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complementizer. A word, etc. which marks a *complement clause:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complementizer phrase = CP.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complete reduplication. See reduplication.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: I can't.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complete sentence. One in which no element in its construction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: requires another element that is missing. Cf. ellipsis: thus I can't help is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one of many complete sentences that would correspond to an elliptical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Traditionally one which, in particular, lacks neither a subject nor a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predicate: hence one said to express a complete thought'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: completive. See perfective.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complex. 1. (Sentence, clause, noun phrase) which includes one or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more *subordinate clauses: e.g. I know [he is there] or the fact [that he is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: there]. 2. (Preposition, subordinator, etc.) which consists of more than

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one word: e.g. on top of or provided that, seen as having the same syntax

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as above or if. Distinguished from *compounds (e.g. throughout or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whenever) in that the words remain separate. 3. (Word) whose form is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: derived by the addition of a *derivational affix: e.g. maker, derived by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the addition of -er to make. 4. (Coordination) in which the forms that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are joined are not single syntactic units, e.g. in {I was] and [she wasn't]

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: coming]: cf. I [was coming], She [wasn't coming].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: composition

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complex NP constraint. Proposed principle by which an element

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in a clause which is in turn an element in a noun phrase cannot be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: related to one in any larger construction. Designed to exclude e.g. What

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: did you appreciate the fact that he had done?, with what construed as the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: object of a verb (had done) whose clause is within the noun phrase the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fact that he had done.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. island. Formulated in the late 1960s as a constraint on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: movement: thus what could not be extracted by *wh-movement from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: its position in you appreciated [the fact [that he had done what]]. Subsumed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the 1970s under a principle of *subjacency.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complex nucleus. A nucleus of a *syllable which includes more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: than one unit: e.g. [baun] in bounty has a complex nucleus [au]

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'complex symbol'. Chomsky's term in the mid-1960s for the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: syntactic class of a word as represented by a set of component features.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fall-rise (") in southern British English: When will he be coming?

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complex tone. An intonational contour in which the pitch changes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in two or more successive directions on a single *tonic syllable. E.g. the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: monotransitive; ditransitive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complex transitive. Used by Quirk et al., *CGE of both the verb and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: its *complementation in constructions with both an object and some

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: complement other than an object: e.g. those of That drove him mad,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: They made me their leader, He threw it on the fire, I heard him singing. Opp.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: surface structures.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: component. 1. A semantic feature: see componential analysis. 2. A

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subset of rules within a *generative grammar, which is distinguished

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: either by assigning a specific kind of representation to sentences, or by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relating one such representation to another. E.g. the *base component

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of a transformational grammar, which in the model of Chomsky's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Aspects assigned the representations called deep structures, or the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transformational component, which related deep structures to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: componential analysis. A treatment of lexical meaning in which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the sense of each unit is distinguished from those of others by a set of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantic features or components. E.g. the basic sense of bull might be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: analysed into three components: 'bovine', distinguishing it from those

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of stallion, ram, etc.; 'fully adult', distinguishing it from that of calf or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bullock; and 'specifically male', distinguishing it from that of cow.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Several versions of componential analysis were developed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: independently from the 1930s onwards. In English-speaking countries

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the best known was that of J. J. Katz and J. A. Fodor, proposed in 1963

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: within the framework of a generative grammar. This assumed, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: addition, that components such as ‘bovine' (or [+ bovine]), ‘adult'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ( + adult]), or 'male' (|+ male)) were *substantive universals.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: composition. The process of forming *compounds.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: compositional meaning

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: compositional meaning. The meaning of a syntactic unit seen as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: derivable from those of the smaller units of which it is composed and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the constructions in which they stand: e.g. that of tall girls as derived

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from the meanings of tall as one lexical unit, of girls as the plural of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: another lexical unit, and of a syntactic construction in which girls is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: head and tall a modifier.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: According to the principle of compositionality the meanings

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of sentences are compositional if considered in abstraction from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: particular occasions on which they are uttered. Often adopted as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hypothesis, or implicitly by definition, in theories that insist on a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: division between semantics and *pragmatics.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: compound. A word formed from two or more units that are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: themselves words: e.g. blackboard from black and board, or German

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Schreibmaschine 'typewriter' from schreiben 'write' and Maschine

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'machine'. Compounding and composition are alternative terms

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for the process of forming compounds.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: compound bilingualism. Bilingualism in which the speaker's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: knowledge of the structure of one language is hypothetically

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: integrated with that of the other. Opp. coordinate bilingualism.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: compound letter. Two or more successive letters which represent

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a single phonological unit: e.g. sh in English or sch in German, both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: representing [S]. Cf. digraph. Likewise a compound logogram (or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'ideogram') is a *logogram which represents a single lexical or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammatical unit but can be analysed into parts that correspond to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: other separate logograms.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: compound sentence. One formed by the *coordination of two or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more smaller sentences: e.g. He sat down and she moved over.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'compound stress'. Stress in English on the first member of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: compound: e.g. in bláckbird as opposed to (a) black bírd. Common

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and taken by some as a defining feature. The compound rule', or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Compound Stress Rule', is the one in Chomsky and Halle, *SPE, which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: places stress in that position.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: composé’), as (j’)ai tué 'I killed'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: compound tense. A form with an *auxiliary seen as forming part

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the system of tenses. From French: e.g. the compound past ('passé

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: compound tone. A unit of *intonation in which two successive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *tones are associated with a single *tone group: e.g. a fall-plus-rise'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (falling tone followed by rising tone) in I `THiNk it may snow.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conative. (*Function of language) in trying to get an addressee to do,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: think, etc. what the speaker wishes. From the Latin word for 'to try'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (infinitive conari); defined by Jakobson in 1960 in terms of orientation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: towards an addressee, as opposed to orientation towards the world

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conditioned variation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (the *referential function) or orientation towards the speaker (the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *emotive function).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also of verb inflections with the meaning 'try to'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: concatenation. The mathematical operation of juxtaposing units to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: form *strings.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conceptual field. See semantic field.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: concessive. (Clause, etc.) indicating something conceded but not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: detracting from what is said: e.g. the clause introduced by although,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and although as the subordinator, in Although I am old, I am not stupid.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: concord = agreement.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: kitchen'. Opp. grammatical case.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: concrete case. A *case whose main role is to distinguish different

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meanings of adverbials. E.g. an *instrumental or a *locative:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: schematically, cut knife-insTR kitchen-Loc 'cut with a knife in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: concrete noun. One denoting a range of concrete objects or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: individuals: e.g. cat, table. Opp. abstract.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: condition. 1, = constraint. 2. The circumstances, or a statement of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the circumstances, under which a *rule (2) or a subrule applies. Thus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a rule for German might introduce a glottal stop under the 'condition'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: # - V: i.e. at the beginning of a word (# -) before a vowel (− V).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by one.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conditional. (*Mood) characteristically marking either a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *conditional clause or, as implied by the use of the term in accounts

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of French and other Romance languages, a main clause accompanied

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conditional clause. One which expresses a condition: e.g. provided he

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is sober, if he can stay sober, unless he is drunk. For types see remote.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conditional sentence. One which consists of a main clause and a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *conditional clause. The conditional clause is traditionally the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *protasis, the main clause the *apodosis: e.g. If you can come (protasis)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: I would be delighted (apodosis).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conditioned. (Sound change) explained by the phonetic context or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the position in a word in which it takes place: e.g. the voicing of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonants between vowels, or a reduction of vowels in unstressed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: syllables. Opp. spontaneous; unconditioned.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [m], e.g. in bumper.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conditioned variation. Variation in the realization of a unit under

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: specific conditions. Especially of units in phonology: thus the [m] of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: comfort can be described as a conditioned variant, in the position

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: before a labiodentaľ fricative, of the unit realized by another variant,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'configurational language'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'configurational language'. One in which syntactic units stand in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a *fixed (2) order. Effectively one, like English, for which it is easy to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: draw *phrase structure trees, in which configurations' of categories

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: form configurational structures'. Opp. non-configurational.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: confirmative. (Particle, etc.) indicating that a statement is about

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: something directly witnessed.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: congruence. The property by which words come together in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: construction. E.g. these is a demonstrative and can combine with a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: following noun; people is a noun; in addition, both are plural. As such,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: they are congruent in the sense required to form a larger unit these

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: people.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: An ancient concept, going back at least to *Apollonius Dyscolus, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: central, whatever the term used for it, in any theory in which the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: combinability of units is primary: see especially unification; Word

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Grammar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conjoin. Used by Quirk et al., *CGE, for a phrase, etc. linked to another

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by *coordination: i.e. what other grammarians call a *conjunct.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conjugation. The inflection of verbs; also a class of verbs which share

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ‘second conjugation'. They had an -a- in most forms where those of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a pattern of inflection. Thus verbs of the first conjugation' in Latin

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: followed a pattern which differed in various ways from those of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: second conjugation had an -e-: e.g. am-a-re to love' (first) but mone-re 'to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: advise' (second). They also had e.g. a present subjunctive in -e- (third

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: singular am-e-t) where the second and other conjugations had -a-.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A conjugation marker is a form which simply distinguishes one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conjugation from another: thus the -a- and -e- of amare vs. monere are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conjugation vowels, with no specific grammatical meaning.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conjunct. 1. Any phrase, etc. linked to another by *coordination:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cf conjunction (2). 2. Used by Quirk et al., *CGE, of an adverbial

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indicating a connection between its clause or sentence and what

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: precedes: e.g. however in We, however, could not, or then in If not, then burn

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it. Cf. adjunct; disjunct; subjunct.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (= coordinators).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conjunction (1). A word, etc. which joins two syntactic units.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Especially in *coordination: e.g. and and but are conjunctions in {He

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: did] and [he didn't] or He [[came] but [didn't stay]]. But also, especially in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: older uses, of words like when in He arrived when I left, or that in He said

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that he did, seen as linking the *subordinate clause to the unit it is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subordinate to. Hence a distinction between subordinating

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conjunctions (= subordinators) and coordinating conjunctions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Distinguished as a *part of speech since antiquity.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conjunction (2). Logicians' term for a proposition of the form p & q

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which is true if and only if both p is true and q is true. Hence of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonant

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *coordination with e.g. English and; thence, in some usage, other cases

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of coordination.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Conjunction reduction' is or was a rule of transformational

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammar by which 'conjoined' phrases, such as you and your sister in I

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: saw you and your sister, are reduced from conjoined sentences: in this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: case, from I saw you and I saw your sister.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conjunctive. The ancient term for *subjunctive, as German

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Konjunktiv'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conjunctive order. Relation between *ordered rules each of which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: can apply, in sequence, to the same form. Opp. disjunctive order.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conjunctive pronoun. Term for unstressed or *clitic pronouns in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: eating it'. Opp. disjunctive pronoun.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
