layout_dets.text: the Romance languages: e.g. Italian lo in lo mangio (it eat-1sG') 'I am

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: connectionism. Model of mental processing inspired by the physical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: connections among brain cells, in which operations of different kinds

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are carried out in parallel by a network of different processing units,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: linked in such a way that each can either excite or inhibit others. Also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: described as a model of Parallel Distributed Processing (or PDP), and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contrasted with that of serial processing, in which operations of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: different kinds are carried out in sequence, each having access only to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the results of those that have gone before.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: connotation. Used variously to refer to differences in meaning that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cannot be reduced to differences in *denotation. E.g. queer, when

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: applied to male homosexuals, has a connotation different from those

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of gay or homosexual. The usual implication is that denotations are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: primary and connotations secondary.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consecutive. (Clause, etc.) indicating a consequence or result:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. the that-clause in I was so tired {that I slept for ten hours].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: verb-object order.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consistent. (Language) seen as conforming in every respect to a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proposed structural *type. Thus a consistent' *VO language would

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: have all the properties associated, in a specific theory of types, with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonant. Originally a sound or *letter that had to be accompanied

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by a vowel: hence the term (Latin consonans sounding with'). Now

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generally of phonological units which form parts of a syllable other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: than its *nucleus (2), or whose primary role, at least, is to do so. E.g. [n)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is a consonant in English, whose primary roles are as the onset of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *syllable (e.g. in no) or as its coda (e.g. in on): its role as a nucleus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (e.g. in ridden ('rıdn]) can be seen as secondary.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In phonetic terms, most consonants are sounds in whose production

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the flow of air is obstructed at some point in the mouth, throat, or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: larynx, at least sufficiently to cause audible friction: i.e. they are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonantal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: produced with a degree of *stricture greater than *open

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: approximation. But no phonetic definition will quite match the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonology of all languages; hence a distinction, in many accounts,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between consonants as units in phonology, and *contoids.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonantal. *Distinctive feature in the schemes of *Jakobson and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of Chomsky and Halle, *SPE. That of all consonants except *glides,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which are defined as both non-consonantal and non-*vocalic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: optional.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonantal alphabet. One in which the characters represent

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonants, with vowels either not indicated or indicated by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subsidiary marks. The original North *Semitic alphabet was purely

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonantal; in later derivatives marks for vowels may remain

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonant cluster. See cluster.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonant harmony. Agreement in respect of one or more features

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between consonants that are not adjacent to one another: cf. vowel

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: harmony, which is more varied and more widespread.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'conspiracy'. Used in *Generative Phonology in the early 1970s, to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: refer to rules which the model required one to formulate separately,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: but which in effect contributed to a single pattern. E.g. a pattern in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which all syllables were open (CV) might be achieved by rules which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conspired' variously to delete consonants (CVCCV → CVCV) or insert

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vowels (CVCCV → CVCVCV).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constant opposition. An opposition between phonemes that is not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subject to *neutralization.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constative. An utterance by which a speaker expresses a proposition

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which may be true or false. Opp. performative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constituency. Relation, especially in syntax, between a unit which is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: part of a larger unit and the whole of which it is part. E.g. the adjective

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phrase very friendly is a constituent of the noun phrase very friendly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: people. The immediate constituents of a unit are the largest such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parts. E.g. the immediate constituents of meeting very friendly people are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meeting and very friendly people; those of this second constituent are in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: turn very friendly and people. Constituency is usually shown by a *tree

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diagram or by square brackets: thus [meeting {[very friendly] peoplel l.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The analysis of sentences into constituents is ‘immediate constituent

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: analysis' (or IC analysis): developed especially by the *Post-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bloomfieldians, whose underlying aim was to establish divisions that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: would allow the simplest account of the *distributions of units.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constituent sentence. See embedding.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constituent structure. A representation of relations of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *constituency: thus a *phrase structure tree is, alternatively, a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'constituent structure tree'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: construe

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constraint. Any restriction either on the application of a rule or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: process or on the well-formedness of a *representation. Thus, if Which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: have you seen? is derived from You have seen which? (see wh-movement),

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: this process might be constrained, by a general principle, from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: deriving e.g. *Which were you always asleep when you have seen? from You

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: were always asleep when you have seen which?, where which is within an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *island formed by an adverbial clause. Alternatively, the constraint

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: might be interpreted as a *filter by which, at a specific level of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: representation, the structure of such a sentence is ill-formed.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A model of grammar is *declarative (2) to the extent that specific

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constraints on the well-formedness of representations replace rules

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which specify a process by which representations are derived.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *notional agreement, if seen in this way.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constructio ad sensum. Process by which word a is taken to be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: syntactically related to word b supposedly 'by meaning' (Latin ad

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sensum) although they do not conform to some proposed rule. E.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: construction. 1. The grammatical structure of a sentence or any

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: smaller unit, represented by a set of elements and relations between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: elements. Thus His family hunts has a construction with two elements:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a noun or noun phrase, (his) family, as subject and a verb, hunts, as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predicate. The relation between them is one of sequence, or specifically

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one in which, e.g. one element depends on the other. 2. Also,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: informally, of the individual units within a sentence that are described

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as having constructions. E.g. his family is a smaller construction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (= phrase) within His family hunts.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Constructions as units are central to some models of syntax. Thus, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: particular, that of Bloomfield, who included them in his concept of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *tagmeme: see also Construction Grammar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constructional homonymy = grammatical ambiguity.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Construction Grammar. Concept of syntax developed in the 1990s

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by C. J. Fillmore, G. P. Lakoff, and others, in which, in contrast to those

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dominant in the USA and elsewhere since the 1940s, constructions and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: their meanings, sentence types, etc. are basic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: man cOat-CONSTR.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: construct state. Used in accounts of *Semitic languages for the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: form taken by a noun that is modified by another noun. Thus, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a phrase which means '(a) man's coat', the relation between the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nouns for 'man' and ‘coat' is marked on the latter: schematically,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (it, next week) adjacent to it.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: construe. To determine what word, etc. is syntactically related to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: what. Hence of the relation between such units: e.g. in I'll try it on next

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: week, on 'construes with' try and not directly with either of the units

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consuetudinal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: No longer usual in technical accounts of syntax. But in Chomsky's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: terminology rules e.g. for *control or *binding were called 'rules of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: construal' at one stage in the 1970s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consuetudinal = habitual.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contact language. Any language used systematically in contacts

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between speakers whose native languages are different. This could be a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language native to one participant: e.g. French might be described as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contact language' for speakers of English after the Norman conquest;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: also for a linguist in the 20th century, either French-speaking or not,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: beginning an investigation e.g. of an African language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Likewise 'contact dialect'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by contamination from male.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contamination. The influence of one form on the historical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: development of another form to which it is related in meaning. E.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Old French femelle, borrowed into English in the 14th century, > female

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *expression.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: content. Level in *Hjelmslev's model of language whose *substance

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is that of meaning. Defined formally by its opposition to the level of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: content word. A word with *lexical meaning: hence = lexical word.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also called '(a) contentive'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: context. Any relevant features of the setting in which a form appears

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or might appear. Suppose, e.g. that one person shouts to another 'Let's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: get out of here!' Within the sentence uttered, get is in a 'context'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formed by the surrounding words Let's – out of here! The surroundings

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in which it was uttered might, e.g. have been in a room full of noisy

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: machinery: that is an aspect of the context' that explains why it was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shouted. Of its elements, let's is appropriate tò a 'context' in which one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: person proposes joint action to another; the place referred to by here

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is identified in the context' of where they are situated; and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The term *co-text is sometimes used of linguistic context as distinct

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from thè wider setting. To contextualize' is to put a form into a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: context in which it might be said: e.g. My sister will be a dormouse can

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be contextualized in a conversation about a dramatic performance of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Alice in Wonderland.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: context-free grammar. A form of *phrase structure grammar in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which each rule holds for a specific category regardless of context:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hence, more fully, context-free phrase structure grammar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: As originally formulated in the 1950s, a phrase structure rule was a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *rewrite rule by which a single element in a string (A) is replaced by a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: string of one or more elements (Z). Each rule had in general the form

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: XAY → XZY, where X and Y are further strings of elements, and the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: form of grammar was context-free if it met the restriction that, in any

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contour tone

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: such rule, both X and Y are null: i.e. the replacement of A with Z

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: applies regardless of context. A form of grammar not subject to this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: restriction was defined as context-sensitive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A 'context-free language' is a *formal language that can be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generated by a context-free grammar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: context of situation. Used by Firth to cover all the relevant

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: circumstances in which a specific act of speech takes place. E.g. when

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a specific person says on a specific occasion 'Well played!', it might be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: part of the context of situation that the speaker is sitting. with others,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In the analysis of a language, features recurring in individual

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: watching a cricket match, that a batsman has driven for four through

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: covers, that the speaker is from a certain social background, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: utterances (considered again as specific acts of speech) will be related

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to specific types of situation and to specific features in them.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The term was originally that of the anthropologist B. Malinowski.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: context-sensitive grammar. A form of *phrase structure grammar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which is not subject to the restriction that defines a *context-free

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammar: hence, more fully, context-sensitive phrase structure

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammar. A context-sensitive language is a *formal language that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: can be generated by a context-sensitive grammar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: continuant. (Consonant) that can be articulated continuously:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thus the r in many forms of English is described as a frictionless

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: continuant. Also a *distinctive feature in the scheme proposed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by *Jakobson, characterized negatively as not *abrupt.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: continuous (1). See discrete.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: continuous (2) (cont) = progressive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contoid. A consonant defined phonetically, by the way it is produced,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as distinguished from a consonant in a phonological sense, defined by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: its role in the structure of words and syllables. Thus a syllabic nasal,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as in the second syllable of button ['batņ], is a contoid even if, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonology, it were treated as vocalic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. vocoid: both terms were introduced by Pike in the 1940s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contour. A pattern of successive levels of pitch. E.g. in intonation:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thus the question What is it? will often be marked by a contour in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which the pitch falls from the second word onwards (What `is it?).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and so on).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contour tone. A tone in some *tone languages, such as Chinese,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which is characterized by a movement or potential movement in pitch

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as opposed to a specific pitch level. Distinguished as such from a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *register tone: note, however, that in many tone languages a phonetic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contour may be characterized in phonology as a sequence of two

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or more specific levels (falling = high + low, rising = low + high,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: which are relevant to the analysis of a language will necessarily lead

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to the same result. E.g. that a set of morphemes identified solely by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: their *distributions will be the same as one identified by reference to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaning; that, if this is not so, only one of these criteria must be truly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relevant; and so on. Identified, named, and attacked by C. E. Bazell in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'correspondence hypothesis'. The assumption, rife among

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: psycholinguists from the 1960s onwards, that structures to be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: investigated in the minds of speakers will correspond, in some more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or less precise way, with the rules of a language as established

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: independently in grammars.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: correspondence theory. Concept of truth by which a proposition

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is true if there is a correspondence between it and a state of the world

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that it describes. Thus, in a stock example derived from work by the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: philosopher A. Tarski, the proposition 'Snow is white' is true if and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: only if snow is in fact white.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corrigible. Capable of being corrected: e.g. a form I today have done it,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which is contrary to a rule for the position of adverbs, can be corrected

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to I have done it today. A test for a *rule (1), or rule in the strict sense, is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thus the corrigibility of forms that would break it.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: restored.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Coseriu, Eugenio (1921- ). Rumanian linguist, finally based in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Germany, whose early work, written in Montevideo in the 1950s,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: brought an important clarification to the structuralist concept of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *language system and the explanation of change in language. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: system is an abstraction from the usual patterns of speech in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: community, and it is the *norm which is constituted by these

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: patterns, not the system, which directly constrains a speaker. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: norm is in turn an abstraction from individual acts of speech on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: individual occasions; but, on the basis of these, may over time shift

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: gradually in such a way that the system itself becomes in part

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: unstable. If so, it will change to a new system, in which stability is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cost

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In later work, Coseriu distinguishes the overall character of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language (German 'Sprachtypus') as a still more abstract construct. At

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the lowest level of abstraction, the norm can change easily; the system

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is more resistant, but can undergo saltatory changes in consequence;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the overall character, as an inflecting language, or one with a certain

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tendency in word order, is the most resistant but may in the end

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: change also.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as measured, or measurable, by an *evaluation procedure.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cost. The contribution of a *rule (2) to the complexity of a grammar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: co-text. The relevant text or discourse of which a sentence, etc. is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: part: e.g. the co-text of Why wouldst thou be a breeder of sinners? (Hamlet,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: I11. 1) is that speech of Hamlet's (Get thee to a nunnery . . . ), or the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dialogue in that scene between Ophelia and Hamlet, or whatever

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: longer text is relevant to some specific inquiry. Sometimes defined as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: part of *context in a wider sense; sometimes as opposed to it.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: countable. (Noun) whose syntax is that of ones denoting individuals

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that can be counted; thus, in English, one such as sparrow that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguishes singular and plural (the sparrow, the sparrows), that can

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: take a numeral (three sparrows) or the indefinite article (a sparrow), etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Opp. uncountable; alternatively ‘count nouns' (such as sparrow) are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposed to 'non-count' or 'mass nouns' (such as poultry). But the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinction is not absolute. Many nouns, such as chicken, are variously

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: countable and uncountable: three chickens but also, e.g. the price of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: chicken. Some are intermediate: e.g. a hundred cattle, but not a cattle.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Many basically of one class may have the syntax of the other on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: occasion: e.g. I'm not going to eat sparrow.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: counter-bleeding. Relation between *ordered rules whose order is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: designed to avoid an effect of *bleeding; i.e. if one does not want rule a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to remove the whole or part of the input to rule b, one orders a after b.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: counter-example. Any example which is taken to show that a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proposed rule, etc. is wrong or must be qualified. E.g. examples like

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'She was sure that he would never fall in love with herself' (Trollope)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are potentially or arguably counter-examples to a proposed universal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: principle by which a reflexive in a finite clause (he would never fall in love

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with herself) cannot have an antecedent (she) outside that clause.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: counterfactual. (*Conditional clause) expressing a condition not in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fact met: e.g. if she had been there . . . (but she wasn't). Cf. remote.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: after b.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: counter-feeding. Relation between *ordered rules whose order is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: designed to avoid an effect of *feeding; i.e. if onedoes not want the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: output of rule a to become part of the input to rule b, one orders a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'counter-intuitive'. (Analysis, etc.) variously contrary to a native

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speaker's feel for their language, or to an experienced linguist's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: judgement of what is right.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: creole

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: count noun = countable.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: covert. (Category) relevant to the grammar of a language but not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: overtly marked. Thus gender is coyert in English but overt e.g. in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Spanish.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'covert prestige'. The value implicitly attached by members of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speech community to forms or variants which they use quite normally

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: but claim to avoid. Thus, in particular, that of local or non-standard

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: forms which are overtly proscribed but which reflect the solidarity of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: each member with the others.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: standard forms.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Sometimes contrasted with 'overt prestige', e.g. of the corresponding

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'covert pronoun'. One realized only by a verbal ending, seen as in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: agreement with it: e.g. in Spanish Vamos 'Let's go', the form of the verb

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ('go-1PL') would be related to a zero pronoun whose properties are in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: other respects the same as those of the 'overt' nosotros ‘we'. Cf. pro in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Government and Binding Theory.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (= INFL).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CP. A phrase (P) headed by a C (= COMP). Thus, in accounts which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: follow versions of *X-bar syntax developed in the 1980s, when I saw him

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: would represent a CP which has within it an ‘IP' (I saw him) headed by I

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in one combination only.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'cranberry morpheme'. One like cran- in cranberry, which is found

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: crasis. Term in Greek grammar for the *fusion of vowels across a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: word boundary: from the word for 'mixing'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vs. normal voice.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: creak. Slow vibration of the vocal cords, typically at least at the front

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: end. Creaky voice is *voice (1) accompanied by creak: often a distinct

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *voice quality, and also exploited in the phonology of some languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. a creaky tone is a tone distinguished, in part or wholly, by creaky

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'creativity'. In its usual sense. Also used by Chomsky in his early

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: days, specifically of the ability of speakers to produce and understand

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentences they have not heard before. A *generative grammar was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: presented as explaining this ability.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cree. *Algonquian language spoken widely across northern Canada,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from the Gulf of St Lawrence to the Rocky Mountains. The different

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: varieties form a *dialect continuum.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: creole. Defined by specialists as, in a strict sense, a language that has

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: developed historically from a *pidgin. In the beginning the pidgin

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: develops from trade or other contacts; it has no native speakers, its

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: range of use is limited, and its structure is simplified. Later it becomes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the only form of speech that is common to a community; it is learned

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: increasingly as a native language, it is used for all purposes, and its

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure and vocabulary are enlarged.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'creole continuum'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thence to languages seen as being like creoles, but where there is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: no evidence that a pidgin existed. E.g. Middle English was a creole,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: according to one theory.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'creole continuum'. A continuous range of variation, found in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: particular in many creole-speaking communities, between the forms

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: used at the lowest social levels, predominantly those of the variety

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: called the *basilect, and those used at the highest, predominantly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: those of the *acrolect. The phenomenon was first described in these

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: terms by D. Bickerton in the 1970s, for the English creole in Guyana.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also called a 'post-creole continuum', since it reflects a process of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'decreolization', or progressive assimilation of a creole to a standard

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: creolization. The historical process by which a *creole, in the strict

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sense, develops from a *pidgin.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'creoloid'. (Language) which is not a *creole but which has

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structural features deemed to be significantly like those ascribed, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: general, to creoles.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Croce, Benedetto (1866-1952). Italian philosopher, whose treatise

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on Estetica (1902) develops aesthetics as a science of expression with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which, in a final chapter, general linguistic theory is identified.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Language is perpetual creation', like other forms of aesthetic activity:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the mechanisms of grammar, the parts of speech, divisions into words

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and syllables, and so on belong in contrast to a discipline concerned

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with nothing more than practical classification.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cross-categorization. Assignment of words, etc. to classes that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: intersect. E.g. the noun despair is on one dimension uncountable as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposed to countable, and on another abstract as opposed to concrete:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by contrast, butter is uncountable and concrete, theory countable and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: abstract, tree countable and concrete.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: crossed dependency. Any case in which a dependent a is separated

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from its head b by an element c whose own relationship, either as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dependent or head, is to an element separated from it, in turn, by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: either a or b. Dependencies not 'crossed' in that way are 'nested'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cross-linguistic. (Investigation, etc.) across languages. Thus any

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: attempt to identify a category in different languages is cross-linguistic;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: likewise any attempt to establish it as a *linguistic universal, or to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: develop a typology of categories which involves it.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cross-over principle. Principle proposed by P. M. Postal in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1970s, by which a syntactic process could not move a pronoun, etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: across a phrase which has the same reference. E.g. in I do admire myself

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the reflexive (myself) has the same referent as I: i.e. both refer to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speaker. Hence, if the cross-over principle were to apply, myself could

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not be moved over I by a process of topicalization: Myself I do admire.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cuneiform

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cross-reference. Bloomfield's term for the agreement of a pronoun

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or verb form with an optional noun phrase that supplies its referent.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. in Spanish Los muchachos cantarán (lit. 'the boys they-will-sing') the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: third plural ending of the verb (-n) ‘cross-refers' to the subject los

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: muchachos. Likewise in French Marie est-elle venue? (lit. 'Mary is-she

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: come?’), elle ‘she' cross-refers to Marie. For a similar case see ‘clitic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: doubling'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cryptotype. Term used by B. L. Whorf in the 1930s for a *covert

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: category revealed only when forms are combined with some specific

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: overt form. One of his examples is a group of verbs with similar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meanings (close, fasten, wrap, . . . ) that combine productively with un-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (unclose, unfasten, unwrap, . .. ).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sensitive (phrase structure) grammar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CS. For 'context-sensitive'. Thus CS-grammar or CS-PSG = context-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ‘categorial selection': opp. s-selection.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: c-selection. Chomsky's term in the mid-1980s for *valency or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *argument structure seen as determined by a syntactic category, such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as transitive or intransitive, that a verb or other word belongs to. For

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Grammar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: c-structure. One of two levels of syntax in *Lexical-Functional

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cue. Psychologists' term for a specific feature seen as an aid to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: perception e.g. of some larger structure. Thus intonation is thought of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as a cue for the construction of a sentence; a *boundary marker is a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cue for e.g. the beginning of a word; *Conversation Analysis seeks

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: among other things to discover cues for the ends of 'turns'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'culminative'. (Accent) seen as no more than a phonetic peak of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prominence on the syllable that carries it. E.g. of the accent in French

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that falls on the last syllable of a phrase: la plume de ma tánte.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the 1950s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cultural transmission. Transmission from one generation to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the next through membership of a society as opposed to genetic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inheritance. One of the set of *design features of language proposed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cumulation. The joint realization of two or more distinct inflectional

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: categories. E.g. case and number are realized cumulatively, or have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cumulative exponents, in languages like Russian or Latin: Latin

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: puella-m 'girl-AcCsG', puellae ‘girl-GENsG', and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cuneiform. Form of writing first developed for *Sumerian from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the beginning of the 3rd millennium BC; later adapted to *Akkadian

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (from the second half of the 3rd millennium) and later still to other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages of the ancient Near East, including *Elamite, *Hittite, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Old *Persian. Last used in the 1st century AD. The name means 'wedge-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shaped', the signs being formed by patterns of triangular marks

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: normally impressed in clay.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: curly brackets { }

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The signs were used in various ways, often representing words as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: wholes and often syllables; they could also serve as *determinatives,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indicating either the semantic class or the phonetic form of a word

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: otherwise represented ambiguously. These functions are found in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: differing degrees in different systems, that of Akkadian being

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: particularly complex, while that devised for Old Persian in the 6th

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: century Bc comes nearest to a pure syllabary. Cuneiform signs were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: also used in the *Ugaritic alphabet.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: curly brackets { }. See braces.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cursive. (Script) in which, in writing a word or other sequence of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: characters, the writing instrument is not in principle raised from the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: medium. Hence the characters are linked, not separate.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cushitic. Group of genetically related languages, including *Somali

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and Oromo, spoken in parts of East Africa from the coastal area of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Sudan to northern Tanzania. Traditionally and by most still seen as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: smaller family within what is now called *Afro-Asiatic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CV tier = skeletal tier.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cyclic(al) principle. Principle in generative grammar by which a se

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of rules applies first to the smallest constituents which are of a given

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: type or types, then to the next largest such constituents, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'post-cyclic(al)'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Introduced in transformational grammars in the 1960s, when a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: specific set of *transformations were said to apply to successively

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: larger units of the clause or sentence category 'S'. Transformations

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not part of this set were accordingly either ‘pre-cyclic(al)' or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Generative Phonology.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The same principle was applied to successively larger units in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: Cyrillic. Alphabet devised for Slavic, according to tradition by St

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cyril, a missionary from Thessalonica, in the 9th century AD. Used

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for Russian and other Slavic languages where the Orthodox Church

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predominates: also for others, including many that are not Slavic,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the former Soviet Union.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Based on contemporary forms of the Greek alphabet. Its relation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to *Glagolitic, also used for Slavic from the early Middle Ages and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: possibly the alphabet in fact devised by St Cyril, is not wholly clear

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Czech. West *Slavic, attested in writing from the 13th century,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spoken mainly in the Czech Republic. Closely related to *Slovak, with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which there is for the most part mutual intelligibility.

layout_dets.text: Daco-Romance. Branch of *Romance of which *Rumanian is the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: main representative. From the name of the Roman province of Dacia.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dangling participle. A participle which does not depend on any

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: other individual element of a clause: e.g. walking in Walking back, it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: snowed. The term is the one by which the construction is traditionally

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proscribed; alternatively, it is *absolute.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Danish. North *Germanic, spoken mainly in Denmark and with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: official status there and in The Faeroes and Greenland; there are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: also some speakers across the border with Germany and, through

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: emigration, in North America. A distinct language from the late

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Middle Ages; a standard form developed from the translation of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bible in the 16th century.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Dari. See Persian.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. again in many forms of English, that of leave [li:v].

layout_dets.text: dark I. One which is accompanied by *velarization: e.g. that of tell

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [tεł in many forms of English. A clear l' is one that is not velarized:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dash (—). Used to mark the position in a context or environment in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which a form appears or a process takes place. E.g. the appears before

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: words such as house: i.e. in such environments as ‘- house'. Consonants

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: might be voiced between vowels: i.e. in the context 'V-V'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dative (par). *Case whose basic role, or one of whose basic roles, is to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguish the recipient of something given, transferred, etc.: e.g. in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Latin librum ('book') dedit ('he-gave') Mariae ('Mary-DAT') ‘He gave a book

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to Mary'. Also extended to phrases in which this semantic role is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: marked differently: e.g. to Mary would often be described as ‘dative' in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English, or as marked by to in the role of a ‘dative' preposition.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dative movement. Syntactic process relating e.g. I lent my copy to Jim,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: where to is traditionally said to mark the *dative, to I lent Jim my copy.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also called 'dative shift'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In the first construction to Jim is an *indirect object; also, in most

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accounts, Jim in the second. In an alternative view, the effect of 'dative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: movement' is to *promote an indirect object to the status of a *direct

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: object: I lent my copy to Jim (IO) → I lent Jim (DO) my copy. It is for that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reason, it is claimed, that e.g. it can correspond to the subject of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: passive (Jim was lent my copy).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dative of advantage

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dative of advantage. Use of the *dative, e.g. in Latin, as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *benefactive. Also of equivalents in other languages: e.g. for you in I did

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it for you. A dative ‘of disadvantage' is a similar element referring e.g. to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: someone who suffers rather than benefits.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dative subject. A noun, etc. which is morphologically in the *dative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: case, but which syntactically has some of the characteristics of, and is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: therefore described as being, a subject. E.g., schematically, cats-DAr love

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: milk-nom, where the word for 'cats', though dative, is subject e.g. on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the grounds that the verb agrees with it (love-3PL) and not with the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nominative 'milk'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: daughter. 1. Any of the later languages that develop separately from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a single earlier language. E.g. French and Spanish are 'daughter

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages' in relation to Latin. Opp. ancestor language. 2. Also of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of node Y if Y immediately dominates (is the ‘mother' of) X.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *nodes in a *phrase structure tree. Thus a node X is the 'daughter'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: what was to become *Word Grammar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Daughter-Dependency Grammar. A precursor in the 1970s of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a deadjectival noun.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: deadjectival. (Process) by which words of other classes are derived

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from adjectives. Also of the words so derived: e.g. happiness (← happy) is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dead language. One that is no longer the native language of any

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: community. Such languages may remain in use, like *Latin or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Sanskrit, as *second or *learned (e.g. as liturgical) languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: decidable. Capable of demonstration by some formal procedure.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Mathematicians' term used in the study of *formal languages: e.g. it is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: undecidable (i.e. there is no guaranteed way of determining) whether

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a language which is *context-sensitive is also *context-free.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an *evaluation procedure.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'decision procedure'. Used by Chomsky in the 1950s of a procedure

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which would determine that a given *generative grammar g is the best

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for a given language l. Distinguished from a *discovery procedure and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: declaration. Defined by J. R. Searle as a *speech act which formally

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: changes some state of affairs. E.g. 'You are fired', said by an employer

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in appropriate circumstances, makes someone unemployed.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: declarative (1). (Sentence, construction) whose primary role is in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: making statements. Thus David has come is a declarative sentence, or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'a declarative', in opposition to the *interrogative Has David come?

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Declaratives can in principle be distinguished from statements

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: made by them. E.g. You must stop at once has the construction of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: declarative; but when uttered it will often constitute an order rather

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: than a statement.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: deduction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: declarative (2). (Model of grammar, etc.) in which the well-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formedness of an expression is determined by a set of constraints on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *representations at a given level, as opposed to a set of rules by which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. a representation at one level is derived from that at another.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Hence, in particular, of 'constraint-based' models of phonology, as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposed to *Generative Phonology and its immediate successors.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: declension. The inflection of nouns and other words whose

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: categories are similar. Also of a class of nouns, etc. which share a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: characteristic formal pattern of inflection. E.g. a 'third declension'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and ablative plural in -íbus, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: noun in Latin is one of a class whose genitive singular is in -is, dative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to *downdrift.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: declination. Progressive lowering of pitch, or of successive high

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pitches in particular, over the course of an utterance. Often equivalent

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in others.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: decline. To inflect, said of nouns and other words traditionally

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: assigned to *declensions. E.g. a noun like Latin puella ‘girl' declines

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or is declined in one way, ones like dominus ‘master' or civis 'citizen'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: encoding.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'decoding'. Used sometimes of the process of understanding a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence. The assumption is that this is like recovering a message

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (the thought expressed by the speaker) from its coded' form. Cf.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: decontextualized. (Sentence, etc.) abstracted from any context

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in which it might be uttered. E.g. it is an issue whether a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: decontextualized form can properly, or safely, be judged either

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammatical or ungrammatical.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'decreolization'. Historical process by which a *creole is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: progressively assimilated to a standard language: e.g. the assimilation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of English creoles in the West Indies to standard English. Not evidently

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: different, in reality, from processes often affecting regional dialects.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: de dicto vs. de re. Philosophers' distinction between belief in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: truth of a proposition (de dicto or ‘about what is said') and belief about

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an individual (de re ‘about a thing'). Thus I believe his wife is rich can be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: seen as expressing either a belief (de dicto) in the proposition that he is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: married to a rich woman or a belief (de re) concerning an individual,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: his wife, that she is rich.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Uses in linguistics reflect or extend this sometimes more and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sometimes less faithfully.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: deduction. Process of reasoning which moves from the general to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the particular. E.g. from the general proposition that all trees have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: leaves and the further proposition that oaks are trees one may draw

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the deductive inference that oaks have leaves. Opp. induction; see also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hypothetico-deductive method.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: deep case

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In deductive reasoning the conclusion follows logically: contrasted

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in this respect with *induction; also with *abduction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: deep case = case role. Such roles were at one time represented by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: case-like elements in *deep structure, with *cases proper, in languages

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that have them, seen as belonging to *surface structure.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: deep structure. A representation of the syntax of a sentence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguished by varying criteria from its *surface structure. E.g. in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the surface structure of Children are hard to please, the subject is children

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and the infinitive to please is the complement of hard. But in its deep

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure, as it was understood especially in the early 1970s, is hard

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: would have as its subject a subordinate sentence in which children is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the object of please: thus, in outline, [please children} is hard.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Initially defined in *Aspects and in other work by Chomsky in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mid-1960s, as the part of the syntactic description of a sentence that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'determines its semantic interpretation'; as such a *phrase marker

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: specified by the *base component of a generative grammar. Later said

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to determine the semantic representation only in part, and later still,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by the mid-1970s, to have no role in determining it. Renamed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *D-structure in the late 1970s and as such the second of three levels

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of syntax in *Government and Binding Theory, until undermined

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by Chomsky's programme of *minimalism in the early 1990s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: DEF = definite.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'default category'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: default. (Rule, class, etc.) taken to be operative if no other is specified.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thus a lexicon of English must specify that certain plurals are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: irregular: man → men, child → children. But any other will be assumed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to follow the regular pattern: singular → singular + (e)s. That rule is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: therefore the 'default rule' and the class of regular plurals the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sense of *unmarked.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Likewise at other levels. E.g. it might be assumed in syntax that all

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: verbs have a passive unless, in their lexical entries, it is made clear that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: they do not; [+ passivizable] would then be the default value' of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: feature [± passivizable]. Hence default' is often the equivalent of one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: defeasible. Capable of being cancelled or overridden. E.g. if someone

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: says 'I have got two eggs', one might infer, all else being equal, that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: they have no more than two eggs. In the theory of *maxims of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conversation, this is represented by an *implicature that follows from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the maxim of quantity. But the inference might be rendered invalid by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: specific contexts. E.g. the speaker is checking ingredients for a recipe;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it calls for two eggs; so, what matters is that there should be at least

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: two eggs, not two only. Alternatively, the speaker might go on to say

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Indeed I may have got a dozen'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A term in law originally. It is a property of such implicatures that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: they are defeasible; of *entailments that they are not.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: deixis

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: defective. (Lexical unit) whose paradigm is incomplete in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: comparison with others of the major class that it belongs to.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. Latin aio was a defective verb for ‘to say' found only in some .

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tenses and for only some persons.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: deferential form = polite form.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'deficit theory'. The view once held by some educationalists that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'working-class' children are 'linguistically deprived' or handicapped by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a 'language deficit'; hence, it was claimed, they are at a disadvantage

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in lessons designed for ‘middleclass' children who are not so

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: handicapped.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In the theory of B. Bernstein such children have mastered only a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'elaborated code' of others.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'restricted code', whose structure is limited in comparison with the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: defining (relative clause) = restrictive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: so on. Opp. indefinite: cf. also indefinite reference.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: definite. Referring to, or characteristically indicating reference to, an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: identifiable individual or set of individuals. Thus Mary or the woman is a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: definite noun phrase, referring to a specific person or set of persons

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that can be identified in context by someone spoken to. Likewise she is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a definite pronoun, the in the woman or the girls a *definite article, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: definite article. A *determiner which characteristically marks

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a *definite noun phrase: e.g. the in the boy, French le in le garcon.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Distinguished from a *demonstrative in that it does not, in addition,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indicate a referent or referents through *deixis.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: noun as its *head.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: definite description. Philosophers' term used in effect of any

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *definite noun phrase, such as the man over there, which has a common

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to a single consonant.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: degemination. Change or process by which a *geminate is reduced

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: degree = grade (1): thus the category of degree in English

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguishes *positive (2), *comparative, and *superlative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: degree of grammaticalness. Chomsky's term in the 1950s for the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: degree to which a form which contravenes a rule of grammar comes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: close to being grammatical. E.g. Sincerity admires John, which was seen

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as contravening a *selectional restriction, came closer than Admires

layout_dets.text: *definite article the (limiting reference to individuals, etc. that an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: addressee can identify), *demonstratives such as this (limiting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reference to individuals standing in a relation to the speaker), with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: etc., used in opposition to these. Divided by Quirk et al., *CGE into

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (e.g. those), and 'postdeterminers' (e.g. three).
