layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: determiner phrase. A noun phrase according to an analysis

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: popular from the mid-1980s, in which it is seen as having a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *determiner as its *head. Thus the old man would be a determiner

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phrase headed by the, with old man, headed in turn by man, as its

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Devanagari. Script used for many modern and older languages of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: India, including *Hindi and *Sanskrit. Developed in an evolved form

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by the 7th-8th century AD.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Of its 48 characters, 34 represent a consonant followed, unless

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shown otherwise, by a: thus ka, ta, and so on. Where the same

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonant is followed by a vowel other than a, a character

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: representing that vowel is added: thus ki, for instance, is represented

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by the character for ka plus a character for i. Where no vowel follows,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a stroke is added instead: thus the character for ka plus the stroke

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: represents k. The system is typical of *Indian scripts in general. In

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: typologies of writing systems it is described as ‘alpha-syllabic': i.e. its

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: characters sometimes represent a single consonant or vowel, as in an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *alphabet, and sometimes a syliable, as in a *syllabary.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'developmental dysphasia'. See dysphasia.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'developmental psycholinguistics'. See psycholinguistics.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: deverbal. (Process) by which words of other classes are derived from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: verbs. Also of the words so formed: e.g. action and actor (← act) are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: deverbal nouns.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'deviant'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'deviant'. Not conforming to a rule, or what is conceived as being a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rule, of grammar. A sentence judged to be deviant in that sense will

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: often be perfectly acceptable: e.g. much poetic usage, whether or not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: traditionally covered by poetic licence', was described in the 1960s

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and 1970s as ‘deviant'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: devoicing. Process or change by which *voice (1) is lost or restricted.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ipœp!].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Common e.g. at the ends of sentences in French: thus [1] is regularly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: devoiced in that position in words such as peuple ‘people', phonetically

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: matrix.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: DF = distinctive feature; likewise DF-matrix = distinctive feature

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: so on. Opp. mono-, tri-: cf. bi- in e.g. 'bivalent'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: di-. From the Greek word for twice'. Thus a disyllabic word, or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: disyllable, has two syllables, a *ditransitive verb has two objects, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: synchronic; also panchronic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diachronic. Having to do with changes over time. Thus a diachronic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: account of a language deals with its history, a diachronic theory deals

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with the nature of historical change in general, and so on. Opp.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diacritic. Any mark in writing additional to a letter or other basic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: element: e.g. the tilde () distinguishing ñ from n in Spanish; the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: umlaut (") distinguishing å ö ü from a o u in German, or, in phonetic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transcription, to indicate that a vowel is *centralized.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: assigned.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diacritic feature. A feature in *Generative Phonology which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguishes units that are exceptions to a rule or follow a rule that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is itself exceptional. E.g., in the account of Chomsky and Halle, *SPE,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a form such as sang or rang was derived from sing or ring by a rule

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: applying only to words to which a specific diacritic feature had been

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: features'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Features such as this are, in effect, instructions to apply the rule in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: question. In that sense they 'trigger' the rule, and are also called 'rule

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diaeresis [dar'iərəsis] [dar'εrəsis]. Mark in writing ( ) used to show

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that successive vowels belong to different syllables: thus Zoë ['zəui].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also to show that a letter is not ‘silent': e.g. the ü [w] of Spanish

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lingüística 'linguistics'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diagrammatic. Having the property of *iconicity.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dialect. Any distinct variety of a language, especially one spoken in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: specific part of a country or other geographical area.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The criterion for distinguishing 'dialects' from 'languages' is taken,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in principle, to be that of mutual intelligibility. E.g. speakers of Dutch

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cannot understand English unless they have learned it, and vice versa;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: therefore Dutch and English are different languages. But a speaker

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diaphone

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from Amsterdam can understand one from Antwerp: therefore they

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speak different dialects of the same language. But (a) this is a matter of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: degree. and (b) ordinary usage often contradicts it. E.g. Italian ‘dialects'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (dialetti') are so called though many from the north and south are not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mutually intelligible. By contrast Danish and Norwegian are called

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'languages'though speakers understand each other reasonably well.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: There are also conventions among linguists themselves: e.g. the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dialects' of *Indo-European are the original branches of the family:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Germanic, *Italic, etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. accent (2).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: recordings have been made, by drawing *isoglosses, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dialect atlas. An atlas of a geographical region showing the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distribution of forms, etc. which vary from one dialect of a language

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to another. This may be shown by points on a map at which e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dialect continuum. A progressive shift from one form of speech to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: another across a territory, such that adjacent varieties are mutually

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: intelligible, but those at the extremes are not. Thus it is likely that, a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: century ago, someone who spoke a dialect of rural Devon would not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: have understood a speaker from Glasgow; but, between these, each

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: individual shift from dialect to dialect would have been minor.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dialect geography. The study of differences in speech from one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: place to another within the area in which a language is spoken. Thus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: including, in particular, the preparation of *dialect atlases.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'dialect mixture'. The presence in some form of speech of features

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: linking it to two or more different neighbouring dialects.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Usually invoked as a factor which obscures the *Neogrammarian

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: principle of regularity in sound change. E.g. in the Tuscan dialect

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which forms the basis of standard Italian, intervocalic stops which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: were voiceless in Latin are voiced in some words (as more generally

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in dialects to the north) but voiceless in others. If the change had

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proceeded mechanically they should all be voiced or all be voiceless:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that they are not is accordingly attributed to the influence on this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dialect of others adjacent to it.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dialectology. The study of geographical dialects: e.g., in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: preparation of a *dialect atlas, or of dialect grammars or dialect

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dictionaries of specific varieties.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dialectometry. The quantitative comparison of forms from different

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dialects, to determine how close one is to another. Developed by the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: French dialectologist J. Séguy in the 1950s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vowel in that of others.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diaphone. A phonological unit established across accents or dialects:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. one which subsumes both the rounded vowel of [putļ in the dialect

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of some British speakers with the unrounded, lower, and more central

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diastratic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diastratic. (Variation, study of variation) across different classes, or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: strata, in a society. Opp. diatopic; cf. social dialect.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diasystem. A phonological or other system established as an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: abstraction covering dialects whose individual systems differ. Thus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the vowels of Scottish and Southern British English differ in that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinctions of quality in one correspond to differences of length,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: etc. in the other. But both might be covered by a diasystem in which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: series of vowels are distinguished neutrally. Cf. diaphone.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: passive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diathesis {dar'aθəsis]. From the term in Ancient Greek for *voice (2):

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the sense is that of the role or 'placing' of a subject, e.g. as agent in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relation to an active verb, or as patient or 'undergoer' in relation to a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in general.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Not usual in English, but available as a term for voice-like categories

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diatopic. (Variation, study of variation) from one part to another of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the area covered by a speech community. Opp. diastratic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dictionary. In the ordinary sense: e.g. a 'dictionary word' is a word

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that would be entered in a dictionary. For related terms and concepts

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: see citation form; lexeme; lexicology; lexicon.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *distinctive features.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diffuse. The feature opposed to *compact in *Jakobson's system of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diffusion. The gradual spread of words, sound changes, etc. from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one person or community to another. Central to the *wave model in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: historical linguistics: see also lexical diffusion.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diglossia. The case in which a community uses two distinct forms of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the same language, one acquired through education and appropriate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to one range of contexts, the other acquired before formal education

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and appropriate to another. Thus German-speaking Switzerland is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: described as a diglossic community where the distinct varieties are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Standard German and the local forms of Swiss German.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thence extended to communities in which two different languages

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are in a similar relationship: e.g. in Paraguay, where the diglossia is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between Spanish and *Guaraní. In accounts of diglossia a variety

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: learned formally and used in a range of more formal contexts is the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: High form (often abbreviated H), one learned naturally and used in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: range of less formal contexts is the Low form (L). E.g. in Paraguay,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Spanish is H and Guaraní is L.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: digraph. A sequence of two letters corresponding, in application to a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: given language, to one phoneme: e.g. sh in shin, representing the single

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phoneme [S]. Cf. compound letter

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: augmentative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diminutive. (Word, etc.) basically indicating small size; e.g. piglet

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is a diminutive of pig, formed with the diminutive suffix -let. Opp.

layout_dets.text: direct method

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Diogenes of Babylon. See Stoics.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Dionysius Thrax (c.170-c.90 BC). Scholar in the *Alexandrian

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tradition, taught by Aristarchus and later established in Rhodes. A

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: short grammar of Greek has come down in his name, and from late

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: antiquity had the same influence in the eastern Roman empire and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: beyond as those of *Donatus in the west. But it is not clear how much

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: especially with the *parts of speech and their *accidents, differ in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: places from what Dionysius is known from other sources to have said,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of it he actually wrote. An initial definition of the parts of grammar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is known from other testimony to be his. But later sections, dealing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and are more consistent with a date some four centuries later.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diphthong. A vowel whose quality changes perceptibly in one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: direction within a single syllable: e.g. [au] in house, whose articulation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: changes from relatively open to relatively close and back. Diphthongs

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are *falling or *rising according to which phase is more prominent.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A distinction might be drawn in principle between a phonetic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diphthong and a diphthong in phonology, which would consist of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sequence of two vowel phonemes. Thus the [au) of house is phonetically

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diphthongal, but different phonologists have described it variously as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a single phoneme, as a vowel plus another vowel, or as a vowel plus a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semivowel. Cf. monophthong; triphthong.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diphthongization. Change or process by which a *monophthong

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: becomes a *diphthong.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to the *oblique cases.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'direct case'. Traditionally of the nominative in e.g. Latin as opposed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: directional. (Phrase, preposition, case) indicating movement to a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: location. Thus to New York is a directional phrase in We flew to New York.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: directionality. Issue regarding the direction of derivation among

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parts of a *generative grammar. Specifically as part of a controversy

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between *Generative Semantics and *Interpretive Semantics in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: early 1970s: i.e. should syntactic representations of sentences be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: derived from their semantic representations, or vice versa?

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: directive. 1. Bloomfieldian term for constructions in which a verb or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: preposition (the director) governs what Bloomfield called an *axis: e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: those of visits me, from her, and while I was there, where the directors are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: visits, from, and while and the axes me, her, and I was there. 2. *Speech act

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by which speakers direct or elicit action by others. Thus an order; also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. a question, since it invites an answer. 3. = directional.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: direct method. Method of teaching a language in which learners are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: exposed to it without translation into or any formal explanation in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: any language they already know. A reaction to conventional teaching

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of grammar, once very fashionable.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: direct object (DO)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: direct object (Do). An *object traditionally seen as identifying

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: someone or something directly involved in an action or process: e.g. my

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: books in I might leave my books to the library, where it is distinguished

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from the *indirect object to the library. Hence, in particular, the object

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: typically next to the verb in English, one marked by the accusative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: case in German, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: director. See directive (1).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: direct speech. The direct quotation of something said, thought, etc.:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. Where am I? is an example of (or is ‘in’) direct speech in He asked

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Where am I?' Opp. indirect speech.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ambiguous, since woods might refer to stands of trees or a type of golf

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'disambiguates' it.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: disambiguate. To resolve an ambiguity. Thus Woods are expensive is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: club. But its meaning will usually be clear in context: i.e. the context

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in which the symptoms hypothetically result from damage to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: auditory analysis vs. production of speech.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: disconnection model. Model proposed for some forms of *aphasia,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: connections between different parts of the brain, concerned e.g. with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: discontinuous. Not realized in an unbroken sequence. E.g. the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constituents of blow it up are, in most accounts, a *phrasal verb (blow

layout_dets.text: .. . up) and its object (it): blow . . . up is accordingly a discontinuous

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Discourse Analysis. The attempt by various linguists to extend

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the methods of analysiș developed for the description of words and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentences to the study of larger structures in, or involved in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: production of, connected *discourse. Term first used in the 1950s by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (Zellig) Harris: *textlinguistics is a similar extension many years later.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'discourse deixis'. All forms of *anaphora and *exophora in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: discourse: i.e. of relations in fact distinguished from *deixis proper.

layout_dets.text: discourse marker. Any of a variety of units whose function is within

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a larger *discourse rather than an individual sentence or clause: e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: but then in But then he might be late or well in Well what if he is?

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Discourse Representation Theory. A formal account of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaning of a discourse, developed by H. Kamp and others, in which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a semantic representation, called a Discourse Representation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Structure, is derived cumulatively, sentence by sentence, by rules

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: operating on representations of their syntax. Conceived as an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: idealized model of the way in which people in practice understand

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: passages of connected speech.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'discourse topic'. See topic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (Zellig) Harris and other *Post-Bloomfieldians. Cf. evaluation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: discovery procedure. A mechanical procedure for deriving a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammar of a language from a corpus, or sample, of sentences. Term

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: introduced by Chomsky in the 1950s, with reference to the aims of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: discrete. (Unit, etc.) which has an identity sharply distinguished

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from that of others. E.g. I love cider is analysed into the discrete units I,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: love, and cider; [lav] (love) is in turn analysed into the discrete units [1],

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [a], and [v]. Opp. continuous: e.g. it may be disputed whether

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: differences in *intonation reflect distinctions between discrete

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: units, or variation along continuous parameters.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. also non-discrete; fuzzy.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conjunct (2); subjunct.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: disjunct. Used by Quirk et al., *CGE, of an adverbial such as perhaps in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Perhaps he is there or honestly in Honestly, I can't do it, seen as an element

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: belonging to the *periphery of its clause and e.g. qualifying.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: commenting on, or giving authority for the remainder. For the second

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: example compare honestly as an *adjunct in I can't do it honestly; see also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: disjunction. *Coordination that distinguishes alternatives: e.g. in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: She will come by bike or she will take a bus. A coordinator such as or is a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: disjunctive conjunction, a question such as Will you go or will you stay?

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is a disjunctive question, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A term from logic, where a disjunctive operator (v) is defined as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: connecting propositions at least one of which is thereby represented as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: true. Thus p ∨ q = Either p is true or q is true or both'. Opp.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: disjunctive order. Relation between *ordered rules of which only

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one will apply to a given form. Opp. conjunctive order.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: disjunctive pronoun. A full as opposed to a reduced or *clitic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'I, me', Italian io 'I'. Opp. conjunctive pronoun.

layout_dets.text: dislocation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dislocation. See left dislocation; right dislocation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: displaced speech. Speech referring to objects, etc. which are not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: part of its immediate setting in space and time. A normal property of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: communication in man, but not demonstrated in any other species;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hence displacement is often included in accounts of *design features.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: displacement. 1. See displaced speech. 2. Otherwise of any

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: movement of a tone, accent, word, etc. from its basic or usual position.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constant over a period of time. E.g. if someone walks for three hours

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dissective. (Verb, form of verb) referring to a state or activity

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: then at any moment within that time span they are walking: therefore

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: walk, as a lexical unit, is dissective, as is walked in I walked for three hours.

layout_dets.text: dissimilation. Change or process by which two sounds in a sequence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: become less like each other. E.g. French pèlerin ‘pilgrim' is from Latin

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: peregrin(us) 'foreigner' by, among other things, dissimilation to l of the

layout_dets.text: distal. (Demonstrative, etc.) which basically identifies someone or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in that side of the road is distal as opposed to ‘proximal' this in this side of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinctive. Making a distinction or distinctions between units.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Especially in phonology: thus the phonetic difference between [d] and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [ð] is distinctive in English, since e.g. den [dεn] and then [aεn] are two

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: different words. Similar sounds are found in Spanish: e.g. in dedo

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'finger', phonetically [deəo]. But there the difference is not distinctive,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: since no words differ in just that way.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Contrastive' is used with the same sense: see also opposition.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinctive feature. 1. A phonetic *feature which distinguishes one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonological unit, especially one *phoneme, from another. Thus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *voice (1) is a distinctive feature in English since e.g. voiced [b] (as in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bit) is a phoneme distinct from voiceless [p] (as in pit). 2. One of a set

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of features which hypothetically characterize all such phonological

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinctions in all languages: e.g. voice considered as a *linguistic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: universal, instanced in English by voice as a feature of [b] in bit, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: German by voice as a feature of [b] in Bitte, and so on. According to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hypothesis, not every distinctive feature in this sense is distinctive in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: every individual language: thus there are many languages, e.g. in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Australia, in which voice is not. But no language will have distinctions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that no member of the set covers.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinctive feature matrix. Strictly, a *feature matrix which shows

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: only *distinctive features. Also loosely of any feature matrix.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. *laminals as [+ distributed} from *apicals as - distributed]

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English is the set of contexts I combed my —, Give me the — spray, My — is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: too long, etc., in any of which the blank (-) can be filled by it.

layout_dets.text: developed especially by leading *Post-Bloomfieldians, that the formal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one goes on to study, their meanings.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of They taught us arithmetic or They taught arithmetic to us; also the verb

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: teach, in taking such a construction. Opp. monotransitive; cf. also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: divalent = bivalent.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: applies. E.g. in many languages the word is the domain of *vowel

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: words. A class of verbs like sing, sink, or drink might also be described

layout_dets.text: domal. An old term for *retroflex.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dominance. 1. Relation defined by a *phrase structure tree between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a *node X and any lower node Y that is on a branch originating from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: X. 2. Relation, again defined by a *phrase structure tree, between a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: node X and a constituent assigned to that category.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Recently in sense 1, but ‘'dominate' was once common in sense 2.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Donatus (4th century Ad). Roman grammarian, author in particular

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of a compendium of Latin grammar (the Ars maior or 'larger *ars') and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Dong

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a catechism on the *parts of speech and their *accidents (the Ars minor

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or ‘smaller ars'), which were to have an immense influence, directly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and through their role as a model for other grammars, throughout the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: medieval and into the modern period.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Dong. See Kam-Sui.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'donkey sentence'. A sentence of the type Every farmer who owns a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: donkey beats it, or If a farmer owns a donkey he beats it, seen as problematic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in their logical structure through the relation of anaphora between it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and a donkey. Named after work by P. T. Geach which used these

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: examples.

layout_dets.text: a *velar such as [k] in cap, produced with closure of this part of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: such as [u:] in coop, in which the dorsum is again raised.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dorsal. Articulated with the convex upper surface of the tongue: e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tongue (the dorsum) against the soft palate. Also of a *back vowel

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Likewise dorso-; cf. apical, laminal, radical (3).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'do-support'. Rule in transformational grammar by which do is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: used as a *dummy auxiliary. Thus do would be added by do-support in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the negative I don't know or the interrogative Don't they know?

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: double accusative. Construction, e.g. in Latin, with two nouns both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the *accusative case. Compare what are sometimes described as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'double object' constructions in English: e.g. both him and my coat

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: have the form they would have as a direct object in I lent him my coat.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [g), etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: double articulation (1). The property of being composed of discrete

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: units at two levels. Thus, at one level, the sentence You go to sleep is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: composed of the words you, go, to, and sleep, and, at another level, it or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the successive words are composed of the phonological units [j]. [u:],

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. articulation. Also called 'duality', and claimed as one of the most

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: important of the *design features that distinguish language from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: systems of communication in other species. In a leading formulation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by Martinet, the articulation of words or other meaningful units is the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: primary articulation, that of phonological units within words the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: secondary articulation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: double articulation (2). Production of a sound at two equal *places

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of articulation. E.g. [kp], in many African languages, is a single

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonant produced with partly simultaneous closures ofthe tongue

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: against the soft palate and of the lower lip against the uppet lip.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: double bar (, X"). See X-bar syntax.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: double-base transformation = generalized transformation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'double case' See case stacking.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: downstep (')

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: double cross (#). Used as a *boundary symbol. In the conventions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: established in *Generative Phonology, a double ## marks a boundary

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between words in syntax; a single # a boundary between words that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are parts of a larger word; a plus sign (+) a boundary between smaller

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: units, such as stems and affixes. Thus e.g. large ## wood # pigeon + s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: double negative. Construction in which a single negation is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: marked by two elements each of which, in the same or another

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: construction, can indicate it independently. E.g. in Spanish: No he visto

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nada (lit. 'not I-have seen nothing') 'I haven't seen anything'. Proscribed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in English, on the grounds that sentences like I haven't seen nothing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ought to mean 'It is not the case (first negative) that I have not seen

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (second negative) anything'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: double object. See double accusative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: doublet. Two words in a language which are historically from the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: same source, but with different intervening stages. E.g. frail and fragile

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are both from Latin fragilis; but frail was borrowed into English in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Middle Ages from the form that had developed from it in Old French,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: while fragile was borrowed in the 17th century, directly from Latin as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: learned language or via a similar borrowing in contemporary French.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: downdrift. Gradual lowering of pitch over a sentence or some other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: unit. Especially in some *tone languages, where successive high tones

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are progressively lowered, often to a level phonetically below that of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: low tones earlier in the unit.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. declination. 'Downdrift' is usual when the lowering of pitch is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: governed by the phonology of a particular language; declination' can

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be used of a purely phonetic effect, due to the progressive lowering of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: air pressure from the lungs. Cf. also downstep.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: downgrading. Process by which a larger syntactic unit, such as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence, has a function like that of a smaller unit, such as a word or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phrase. Hence of regular processes of *embedding: e.g. he was alive is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: downgraded to an element of a phrase in the news that he was alive. Also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of sporadic processes: e.g. the phrasal verb cut up is downgraded to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: downstep ('). A phonological unit in some *tone languages which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is realized by a lowering of the second of two successive high or mid

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tones. Thus, in a language with a high and a low tone, this will

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguish three possibilities: (a) H L (high followed by low); (b) H H

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (high followed by high without downstep); (c) H'H (high followed by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: high with downstep). The pitch of the tone following the downstep

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in case (c) is intermediate between that of the low tone in case (a)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and that of the second high tone in case (b).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that would otherwise be unfilled. Thus, to form an interrogative, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: order of a subject and an auxiliary is inverted: They can ski → Can they

layout_dets.text: ski? But in They ski there is no auxiliary: so, in Do they ski?, do is a dummy

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: (compare They CAN ski). Another dummy in English is the it of It is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dynamic. (Verb) denoting an action, process, etc. as opposed to a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: state. E.g. buy is dynamic; own, which denotes the resulting state, is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *stative. Also of *aspects: e.g. a verb meaning 'sit' might, in a dynamic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: form, be used of the action of sitting down.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dynamic passive. One referring to an action or process, as opposed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to a ‘statal passive'. E.g. (is) opened is dynamic in It is easily opened with a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: penknife (what is easy is the action of opening), but statal in It is already

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: dys-. Greek prefix used in medical terms for malfunctions of one

layout_dets.text: (stammering), 'dyssyntaxia' (errors in syntax), etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dyslexic, of someone in that condition.

layout_dets.text: dysphasia. lmpaired or less than normal ability to speak. Sometimes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of milder cases of *aphasia; also of 'developmental dysphasia', in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which the development of language in a child is delayed or otherwise "

layout_dets.text: disorder.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with an initial consonant or syllable altered. Widespread in languages

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: upward movement of the larynx. Distinguished in phonetic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transcription by the diacritic [']; the *airstream mechanism is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: elative. 1. *Case which basically indicates movement 'out of': e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: form of an adjective or adverb. E.g. a *superlative with that sense:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: electromyography. A technique for investigating muscular

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: production of speech, by inserting electrodes which register the firing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of individual fibres.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: electropalatography. A technique for recording points of contact

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between the tongue and the hard palate; hence, in particular, for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: investigating *coarticulation in this area. The subject is fitted with a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thin artificial palate which has an array of electrical contacts. A weak

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: current is passed through the body, so that when the tongue touches

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: any of these contacts a circuit is completed and a signal can be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: registered. The technique has tended to replace earlier methods of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *palatography since the late 1970s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: element. 1. A basic or indivisible unit at some level of analysis or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: of an open syllable, (C)V, has as its elements an optional consonantal

layout_dets.text: onset, '(C)', followed by an obligatory vocalic nucleus, 'V'.

layout_dets.text: to elicit from speakers of English, either by asking or by some indirect

layout_dets.text: whose status was uncertain: e.g. in a study of auxiliary verbs, ones like

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
