layout_dets.text: -eme

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: -eme. Used in terms for basic linguistic units. Thus *phoneme, for a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: basic unit of phonology; *morpheme, for a basic unit of morphology;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *lexeme, for the basic unit of the lexicon. For others see e.g. moneme;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphophoneme; sememe.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thence, by analogy with the phoneme, to units other than those of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speech: e.g. 'chereme' (from the Greek word for hand') for the basic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: unit of sign language; 'proxeme' (see proxemics) for a distinctive unit

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of distance, etc. between speakers; 'narreme', for a unit in the literary

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: analysis of narrations.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: emergence. Process by which a structure, change, etc. is created by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the separate behaviour of many individuals. Hence, in one view, in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the repeated articulatory movements of many individual speakers; the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaning of a word arises by a process of emergence from its repeated

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as a whole is a structure generated by innumerable individual acts of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speech in a community.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: case of language: e.g. a sound change is a phenomenon emerging from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: use by individual speakers in individual contexts; a *language system

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: EMG = electromyography.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: emic. Involving, or having the status of, a unit in *-eme. A term of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Pike's in particular: thus an analysis of sounds which aims to establish

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonemes is an emic, as opposed to an *etic, analysis.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: feelings of the speaker. Cf. affective.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: emotive. (Meaning, *function of language) having to do with the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: empathy. Identification with another. Hence empathetic deixis is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *deixis, e.g. in *free indirect style, that reflects the viewpoint of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: someone other than the speaker or writer. Scales of empathy, ranging

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from a speaker at one end to objects with which speakers can

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: empathize least, play a role e.g. in direct vs. *inverse constructions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: I frankly detest him.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: emphasizer. Used by Quirk et al., *CGE, of adverbs or adverbials with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a broadly emphasizing role: e.g. actually in It actually worked; frankly in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *pharyngealization.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: emphatic (1). Term for dental consonants, especially in Arabic, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which the body of the tongue is broad and flat in the mouth and with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the front part lowered. Thus † in Egyptian Arabic țiin 'mud' as opposed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to non-emphatic t, with the front part of the tongue more narrow

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and pointed. Usually explained by phonologists as an effect of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: emphatic (2). Marking, or marking among other things, emphasis:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thus ‘emphatic stress' (But I 'CAn'T do it), emphatic word order, and so

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on. An ‘emphatic pronoun' is a full form (e.g. moi 'I, me' in French) as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposed to a reduced or *clitic form (e.g. je).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: encapsulation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Emphasis' and 'contrast' can in principle be distinguished but,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: since their realizations tend to be the same, *contrastive especially is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: often used for both.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: empirical principle. Hjelmslev's term for a principle by which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accounts of a language system should (a) be free of internal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contradictions; (b) cover the relevant data exhaustively; (c) be as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: simple as possible. The subprinciples have priority in that order:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: i.e. self-consistency should not be sacrificed to exhaustiveness, nor

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: either self-consistency or exhaustiveness to simplicity.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: empiricism. Any of a range of doctrines in philosophy which hold

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposed to *nativism.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that knowledge is derived from sense experience. Traditionally

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: category as posited by Chomsky and others.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: empty. 1. Having or described as having no meaning: e.g. a *dummy.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2. Having no phonetic or other realization: thus especially an *empty

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Confusion might be avoided if ‘empty' were reserved for sense 1 and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ‘null' or ‘zero' used consistently for sense 2.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'empty category'. An element in Chomsky's *Principles and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Parameters Theory which occupies a syntactic position but has no

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonetic realization: see pro, PRO, trace. Seen as subject to a universal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: principle (the Empty Category Principle or ECP) which rests on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Chomsky's definition, in the early 1980s, of *government.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Strictly an element rather than a category.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: empty morph. A *morph which does not directly realize a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *morpheme (3). E.g. in children [tfıldrən], a morph {tfild] realizes the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morpheme child' and a morph [ən], as also in oxen, may be said to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: realize the morpheme plural'; the intervening [r] is then an empty

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morph which is not assigned specifically to either. Cf. empty (1).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammatical word.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'empty word'. A word seen as 'empty' in that its meaning is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *grammatical rather than *lexical. Hence = form word, function word

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: enantiosemy. A case of *polysemy in which one sense is in some

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: respect the opposite of another. E.g. that of dust in I dusted the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mantelpiece, meaning that something is removed, vs. I dusted the cake

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with sugar, meaning that something is added.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Gegensinn'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: From Greek enantio-'opposite': modelled by G. C. Lepschy on German

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: encapsulation. The inclusion in the sense of word a of that of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: another word b with which a could potentially collocate. Usually of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cases where the collocation would be pleonastic: e.g. female wife,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: where the sense of wife includes that of female.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: For 'informationally encapsulated' see modular.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: enclitic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: enclitic. A *clitic attached phonologically to the word which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: precedes: e.g. Latin -que in arma virumque (lit. 'arms man-and’) 'arms

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and the man'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'encoding'. Used of a supposed mental process by which pre-existing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thoughts are encoded as sentences; also of any relation of *realization,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whether or not in the belief that it is part of such a mental process.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Opp. decoding.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'encyclopaedic knowledge'. Knowledge of the world as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguished from knowledge of the *language system. Thus in many

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accounts a word like cat might have a semantic *feature [+ mammal]

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or [+ viviparous]: to know that it has this feature and others that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguish it from other units in the lexicon is to know its meaning

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the language. But it would then be a matter of ‘encyclopaedic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: knowledge' that the young of cats are born blind, that the period of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: gestation in the domestic cat is about 65 days, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ending. lnformal term for any *suffix or combination of suffixes at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the end of a word. Cf. termination.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: endocentric. Bloomfield's term for a construction in which at least

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one element is of the same syntactic class as the whole. E.g. that of raw

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meat, whose role in larger constructions is like that of its second

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: element meat; also that of meat and fish, whose role could be filled by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: either meat or fish. Opp. exocentric. Also used of compounds: e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: blackbird is endocentric since, to put it in later terminology, it is a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *hyponym of bird, while blackcap (another species of songbird) is not,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: since it is not a hyponym of cap.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as opposed to *exophora.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: endophora [εn'dpfərə]. Sometimes used to subsume *anaphora and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *cataphora, seen as relations within (endo’) what is said or written,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: -en form. See past participle (2).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Ages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English. West *Germanic. Old English ('Anglo-Saxon') is attested from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the 7th century AD, with an extensive literature before the Norman

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conquest in the 11th century. After the conquest, Middle English was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: heavily influenced by French, most noticeably in large and central

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: areas of vocabulary. A standard form, based mainly on eastern dialects

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spoken in London, developed increasingly from the end of the Middle

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The expansion of English to other continents began in earnest in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 17th century, with the successful colonization of the eastern seaboard

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of North America. Subsequently spread by colonization both directly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from Britain and from the USA and existing colonies, across North

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: America, in Australia and New Zealand, in southern Africa, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: elsewhere. Also promoted as a *second language throughout most of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the British Empire and in countries similarly occupied by the USA;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: epistemic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hence an official language in, e.g. India or Nigeria. As a second

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language it has several regional varieties (Indian English, West African

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English, etc.); also dominant as an international language, increasingly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in forms based on American English, since the mid-20th century.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English for Special Purposes. Programme of teaching English for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: use in specific applications, e.g. in air traffic control.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: entailment. Relation between propositions one of which necessarily

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: follows from the other: e.g. 'Mary is running' entails, among other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: things, 'Mary is not standing still'. Cf. implication.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thence of propositions entailed by sentences: thus ‘Mary is not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: standing still' is entailed by Mary is running. Distinguished from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: overridden in a specific context.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *implicatures, often similarly described as propositions implicated by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentences, in that entailments are not *defeasible: i.e. they cannot be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: environment. A context within a word or sentence in which a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: change or process takes place. E.g. [n] → [m] 'in the environment'—

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [+ bilabial]: i.e. when a bilabial consonant, such as [b] or [p], follows.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: epenthesis [ə'penθəsis}. Process or change in which successive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sounds are separated by an intervening segment. E.g. the [b] of thimble

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: developed between an adjacent [m] and [l]: cf. Old English þýmel.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Likewise of processes in morphology or morphophonology: e.g. [ı] in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: horses can be described as an epenthetic vowel inserted between [s}

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and [z] in underlying [hə:s] + [z].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: From the Greek for insertion'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: EPG = electropalatography, electropalatographic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: gender.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: epicene ['εpisi:n]. (Noun) used to refer to individuals of either sex.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Traditionally of one whose grammatical gender is the same in either

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: case: e.g. French (la) grive '(the-FEm) male or female thrush'. Cf. common

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: epiglottal. Articulated with or, more loosely, in the region of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: epiglottis. The epiglottis is a flap of cartilage at the base of the throat

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whose function is to cover the larynx while swallowing.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: epigraphy. The study of inscriptions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: epiphenomenon. A by-product or secondary phenomenon. Thus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in accounts of syntax that became standard in the 1960s it is the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: individual rules that are primary; constructions, as they have usually

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: been conceived, were by implication secondary or epiphenomenal.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: episememe. Bloomfield's term for the meaning of a construction or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: other grammatical pattern (in his terms a *tagmeme)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: epistemic. Indicating factual necessity, probability, possibility, etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. the modal must is epistemic, or is used epistemically, in He must

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: epistrophe

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: surely be there by now; likewise may in It may have been lost, or might in The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: train might be late.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: From a Greek word for ‘knowledge, understanding'. Opp. deontic as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one of two major categories of *modality: see also alethic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: epistrophe. Term in rhetoric for the repetition of a word at the end

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of successive clauses or sentences: e.g. 'This house is mine; this car is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mine; you are mine'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: epithet. Usually of an adjective, etc. conventionally associated with a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: noun or with whatever or whoever it denotes: in origin the term in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Greek for *adjective or ‘adjective noun' in general.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: eponym. An individual name from which a common noun is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: derived: e.g. that of 'the eponymous' Lord Sandwich as the source for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sandwich. Eponymy is the relation between them.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: EPP = extended projection principle.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constructions that are formally similar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: equational. (Sentence, construction) by which one asserts that two

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: referents are identical: e.g. Jim's daughter is Harry's wife, by which one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: asserts that the daughter of someone called Jim is the same person as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the wife of someone called Harry. Thence of other sentences and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also called ‘equative'; cf. ascriptive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: equative. 1. (Construction) by which two individuals, etc. are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: equated with respect to some property: e.g. the as . . . as construction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in John is as clever as me. 2. (Case) marking a *predicative noun or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: noun phrase: e.g., schematically, He is father-EQUAT ‘He is the father'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. equational; also essive. 3. = equational.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: equi NP deletion. A syntactic operation in early *transformational

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammars which deleted one of two identical noun phrases. Thus in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: most accounts in the 1960s and 1970s a sentence like I asked Mary to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: come was derived from an underlying l asked Mary [Mary come] with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: deletion of the second Mary.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Often abbreviated 'Equi': a verb such as ask was similarly an ‘Equi

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: verb' as opposed to a *raising verb. Cf. control; control verb.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: privative (1).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: equipollent. Opposition between phonemes neither of which is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *marked in relation to the other: e.g. between English [p] and [t]. Opp.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *generative capacity.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: equivalent. Technically, e.g. of grammars having the same

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: equi verb. See equi NP deletion.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: equivocal = ambiguous: opp. univocal.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ERG = ergative (1).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Esperanto

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ergative. 1. *Case which identifies the *agent in a basic transitive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: construction when the *patient is *absolutive. The latter identifies

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the patient with the single argument or valent in an intransitive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: construction: e.g., schematically, intransitive collapsed wall-Aßs ‘The wall

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: collapsed'; transitive Bill built wall-Aßs 'Bill built the wall'. The ergative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: then distinguishes the agent: thus, more fully, Bill-ERG built wall-ABs.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The same terms are extended to other constructions in which an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: agent is similarly distinguished, but by e.g. word order instead of case.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2. Also used sporadically, from the early 1960s, of the relation between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. We sank the ship, where the ship is object, and The ship sank, where,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: though now the subject, its semantic relation to sank is similar. Hence,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in some accounts, sink is an 'ergative verb', as distinct from both a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: straightforward transitive and a straightforward intransitive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Sense 2 seems to have arisen, partly at least, from a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: misunderstanding of sense 1. It could perhaps with benefit be avoided.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'ergative language'. One which has an *ergative (1) vs. *absolutive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: case, or which distinguishes semantic roles, e.g. by word order, in an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: equivalent way. Languages either partly or wholly of this type are said

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: active language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to illustrate a phenomenon of 'ergativity'. Cf. accusative language;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diminutive apí-culu-s) or by others.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'erosion'. The progressive reduction of the phonetic forms of words

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by sound change. 'Eroded' words are often replaced: thus a classic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: study by Gilliéron showed how the forms derived from Latin apis ‘bee',

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: when reduced by sound changes in French to a monosyllable, were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: widely replaced by longer forms derived by suffixation (French abeille <

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: erotetic [εra'ti:tık]. From the Greek word for 'to question'; e.g. an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: erotetic logic is a logic of questioning.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: error analysis. The analysis, for practical but also potentially for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: scientific ends, of errors made by students learning another language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Erse = Irish *Gaelic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Eskimo-Aleut. Family of languages whose branches are Aleut,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spoken by a minority in the Aleutian and neighbouring islands, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Eskimo, spoken over a large area from Greenland to Siberia. The main

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: branches of Eskimo are Yupik, in south and south-west Alaska and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: across the Bering Strait, and *Inuit.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: esophagus = oesophagus.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and regular.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Esperanto. Artificial language first promoted by L. L. Zamenhof in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1887, as a neutral *auxiliary language for people whose native

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages were different. It combines elements of various European

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages, but with a morphological structure designed to be clear

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: essive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: essive. *Case indicating a state or mode of existence: e.g.,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: schematically, He cook-Ess 'He is a cook'; Cook-Ess he good 'As a cook

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: he is good'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: EST = Extended Standard Theory.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: established. (Form, etc.) accepted as normal in a community. E.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: courage is an established word in English; couragiousness, though it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: follows the rules of word-formation and might well be used on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: occasion, is not.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Finno-Ugric, closely related to *Finnish.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Estonian. Official language of, and spoken mainly in, Estonia.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: état de langue. A stage in the history of a language, considered

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in abstraction from anything earlier or later. From Saussure: also,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in translation, 'language state' or ‘state of a language'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: advantage.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ethic. (*Dative) used in referring to someone with an interest in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or indirectly affected by an action, etc. Also ‘ethical': cf. dative of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ethno-. From the Greek word for a people or nation. Thus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ethnolinguistics can have the sense of *anthropological linguistics;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ethnobotany is concerned with the ways in which specific societies

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: name and classify plants, ethnopoetics with their literature, and so

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ethnography of speaking. Term introduced by D. H. Hymes in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the early 1960s for the study of the uses and patterns of speaking in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a society, as distinct from an account of the *language system.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thus in some communities ritual utterances are a central feature of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ceremonial; in others they are not. In some, close friends will tend to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: greet each other with formal insults; in some, verbosity in speech is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: appreciated; in some, requests will tend to be made directly rather

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: than indirectly; and so on. The domain of the ethnography of speaking

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: covered features such as these which were seen as falling between the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: usual scope of linguistics, and that of ethnography in general.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. communicative competence.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ethnomethodology. Movement in sociology that sought to study

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: social interaction in terms of categories, etc. empirically valid for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: members of a society, not assumed a priori. Relevant to linguistics as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the source, in the early 1970s, of *Conversation Analysis.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ethology. Branch of science concerned with animal behaviour:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hence with, among other things, modes of communication in species

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: other than man.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: etic. Not *emic. Thus for Pike an etic account of the sounds of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language would describe them impressionistically as sounds (i.e. as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: European structuralism

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'phon-etic' units) in advance of an analysis assigning them to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonemic (i.e. ‘-emic') units.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Etruscan. Ancient language of Tuscany in Italy, with no

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: demonstrated genetic relation to any other. Written in an alphabet

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: derived from that of Greek and itself one source of the Roman.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'etymological fallacy'. The notion that the 'true' meaning of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: word is the one to be expected from its *etymology. E.g. literature is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from the word in Latin for a letter of the alphabet (litera): therefore,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a pedant might argue, it is incorrect to apply it to compositions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transmitted orally and not written.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: etymology. The study of the historical relation between a word and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Latin (via) strata ‘paved road'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the earlier form or forms from which it has, or has hypothetically,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: developed. Thus the etymology of sheep relates it, with German Schaf

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and others, to a reconstructed Common Germanic *skāpa; that of street

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relates it, through Old English strāt, to a borrowing into Germanic of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Loosely described as a study of the ‘origins of words'; but if this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: expression is taken too literally it can be misleading.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: etymon. A form at an earlier stage of history or prehistory from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which one or more later forms are derived. E.g. a root *g"o- is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reconstructed as the Indo-European etymon of English cow, French

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: boeuf'ox', etc. These are in turn its *reflexes.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: euphemism. Word, etc. used in place of one avoided as e.g. offensive,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indecent, or alarming. E.g. a word for ‘girl' used of prostitutes in place

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the specific word for 'prostitute'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: euphony. Literally the property of 'sounding well'. But commonly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at one time of a principle equivalent to that of ‘ease of articulation':

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thus it was for reasons of ‘euphony' that one consonant undergoes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *assimilation to another, or that successive syllables are matched in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *vowel harmony.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'eurhythmy'. Maximal conformity to the rhythmical pattern normal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in a given language: defined in *Metrical Phonology in terms of an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ideal 'metrical grid' to be approximated as far as possible.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tradition.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: European structuralism. *Structural linguistics as developed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: especially in continental Europe. *Baudouin de Courtenay was an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: important pioneer, followed in the early 20th century by *Saussure. In

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the 1920s and 1930s their ideas were developed especially by members

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the *Prague School, notably *Trubetzkoy and *Jakobson; from the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: late 1930s by *Hjelmslev and *Martinet among others; also, though

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: his basic assumptions were in part different, by *Firth. Among later

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: scholars, *Coseriu and, from the 1960s, *Lyons are among those whose

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ideas, despite many differences, stand clearly in the structuralist

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: evaluation procedure

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Structuralism' in literary studies developed especially in France in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the 1960s, inspired largely by readings or misreadings of Saussure.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: evaluation procedure. A mechanical procedure for comparing two

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *generative grammars, of the same format and generating the same

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language, to determine, e.g. by a measure of simplicity, which is the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: better. Proposed by Chomsky in the 1950s, as a goal for linguistic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: theory weaker than that of a *discovery procedure.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: An evaluation measure is a metric employed in such a procedure.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: evaluative. Indicating a speaker's attitude to some real or potential

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: event, etc. Thus an evaluative particle might indicate e.g. surprise:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: schematically, He suRPRisE didn't 'Amazingly he didn't'. Likewise the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence Why on earth put it in the dustbin? is likely to be said not as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: question which invites an answer, but as an evaluative utterance

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: commenting on what someone has done or proposes to do.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (cf. inferential), or on what someone else has told the speaker

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (cf. quotative), or e.g. on guesswork.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: evidential. (Particle, inflection) which is one of a set that make clear

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the source or reliability of the evidence on which a statement is based.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thus in a given language they might formally distinguish statements

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: based on direct observation from ones based e.g. on inference

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: evolution. Used both in the biologist's sense and of the development

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: over time of individual languages. Thus 'the evolution of language'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: refers in one sense to the issue of, as it is traditionally called, 'the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: origin of language'. In another it refers to the history of languages

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: without any implication that the principles of evolution, as biologists

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: understand them, will apply.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: exaptation. Introduced by R. Lass in the early 1990s for the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: development, in the history of a language, of a new semantic role for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: differences of form that have lost whatever role they may have had

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: earlier. Suppose, e.g. that the distinction of gender is lost in French:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: le mur 'the wall': also ‘le' (now la) maison 'the house'. Accompanying

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: variations in the forms of adjectives (grand/grande ‘big') would then

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: have no rationale; but, by a process of exaptation, they might develop

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a new one, e.g. in distinguishing attributive adjectives ('le maison grand

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: instead of present la maison grande) from predicative ('le maison est

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grande' instead of present la maison est grande).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: exception. A form, etc. that does not follow a rule applying generally

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to those of its class: e.g. past tense forms in English generally end in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: -ed: wait-ed, talked, etc. Forms such as ran or broke, or run and break as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lexical units, are therefore exceptions to this.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. regular. As there are degrees of regularity so, conversely, a form

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: may be an exception to a more general rule which covers forms that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are themselves exceptions to one still more general.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: exocentric

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'exceptional case marking'. That of e.g. her in I believe her to be right.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Its form is that of the object in e.g. I believe her; therefore, in many

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accounts, it too is an object. But in that of e.g. *Government and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Binding Theory it is not. Instead it is the subject of a subordinate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clause (I believe {her to be right]); therefore its case marking (realized by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: her instead of she) is ‘exceptional'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: exclamation. Sentence whose construction is characteristically used

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: etc.: e.g. How wonderful that would be! or What a filthy mess!

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in emotional reactions, as opposed to questions, statements, requests,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A distinction could in principle be drawn between ‘exclamations'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as a type of speech act and constructions that are specifically

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not exclamative but *interrogative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'exclamative'. The examples given would then be both exclamative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and exclamations; but a sentence such as How the hell do I know?

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: might be uttered as an exclamation, although its construction is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: exclamation mark (!). Used, in citing an example, to indicate that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: although it is grammatical, it is not so in the sense that is relevant. E.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in a discussion of idioms one might write !The fat was being chewed by the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: committee for three hours, meaning that, although a passive is possible in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the literal sense, in the sense of the idiom chew the fat' it is not.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: addressee. See inclusive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: exclusive. (First person) specifically excluding reference to an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: excrescent. Older term used of a consonant, etc. historically added

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to a word. E.g. -d is excrescent in sound 'noise', which had no -d (cf.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: French son) before the 15th century.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: exhaustiveness. Property of a description, grammar, etc. that covers

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: all the relevant data: cf. empirical principle. The crux, of course, lies in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the criteria for relevance.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: exhortative. (Particle, etc.) used in enjoining or encouraging an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: action by a group that includes the speaker: e.g. let or let's in Let's go.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: existential. (Sentence, construction) indicating what does or does

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not exist: e.g. the construction with there in There's a wasp in your hair,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: There are no white crocodiles.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one boy dances'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: existential quantifier (3). Operator in logic used in expressions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: interpreted as asserting existence. E.g. (∃ x)((boy (x)) & (dance (x)))

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ‘There exists some x such that x is a boy and x dances': i.e. 'At least

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: exocentric. Bloomfield's term for a construction in which no

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: element is of the same syntactic class as the whole: e.g. those of in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Washington or wrote books.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: exophora

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Opp. endocentric. Also used of compounds: e.g. pickpocket and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hardback are exocentric compounds since, to put it in later terms, they

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are not *hyponyms of either pick or pocket, or either hard or back.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: exophora [εk'sofərə]. The interpretation of a pronoun, etc. when it is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: supplied from 'outside' ('exo-’) what is immediately said or written: e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of she in shE's coming, uttered by a speaker who points to the 'she' in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: question, or for a hearer who can guess who is meant. Opp. anaphora;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: also endophora.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Pisin is one case sometimes so described.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'expanded pidgin'. A *pidgin whose form has in time become less

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: simplified but which is still not judged to meet, or to meet sufficiently,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the definition of a *creole. Also called an 'extended pidgin'; *Tok

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: expansion. In its ordinary sense: e.g. the ‘expansion of English' in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: last few centuries. Also specifically, in American structural linguistics,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of an operation designed to establish that shorter and longer

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sequences of words belong to the same class. E.g., in She came, she can

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be replaced by the ‘expanded' forms a man, the people next door, the book

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which I ordered, and so on. Accordingly all these are classed as, in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: usual term, noun phrases.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Grammar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: experiencer. The semantic role of e.g. I in I felt cold or Jane in Jane saw

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it. Seen as one of a set of universal cases' or case roles in e.g. *Case

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: experimental psycholinguistics. See psycholinguistics.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: expiratory. In or for breathing out. E.g. 'expiratory pressure' is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pressure of air being breathed out.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: explanatory adequacy. See levels of adequacy.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: expletive. From a Latin verb meaning 'to fill out'. Hence e.g. of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *dummies or ‘prop-words': thus it is expletive in It's obvious that he wil

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 5. VI

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. imprecative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *dummies or ‘prop-words': thus it is expletive in It's obvious that he will.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also, as in ordinary use, of swear words seen as padding which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: add nothing to the sense. Thence of swear words generally, and of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *minor sentences (Damn and blast!, Bugger it!) that contain them.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: explicature. A proposition explicitly expressed, as opposed to an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *implicature. E.g. Mary is ill will, when uttered, communicate the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: explicature 'Mary is ill'. It might also in a specific context implicate,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: say, 'Mary won't be in today'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: explicit performative. See performative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: exponence. Any relation between a linguistic unit, structure, etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and its realization in speech. E.g. the exponents of *stress, as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonological unit, might be variously the lengthening of a syllable, a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: difference in vowel quality, a significant pitch movement, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: external

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Hence of any relation of *realization by which this is mediated; e.g. in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphology, an affix such as -en in taken is an exponent of a feature or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: unit 'past participle'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: expression. 1. Any form of words which constitutes a unit of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaning. Rarely an explicit technical term, but cf. referring

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: expression; also e.g. fixed expression. 2. Level in *Hjelmslev's theory

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whose *substance is that of sounds or their equivalent as opposed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to that of meaning. Defined formally by its opposition to that of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *content.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: emotive; interjection.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: expressive. Type of *speech act seen as giving expression to a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: psychological state of the speaker: e.g. an apology, or an expression

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of thanks or congratulation. 2. (Meaning, *function of language)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: having to do with the state of mind of the speaker. Cf. affective;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: swoll-.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: extended exponence. The realization of a single morphological

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: category in two or more different parts of a word. E.g. in swollen the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: past participle is realized by both a suffix (-en) and the vowel [əu] in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'extended projection principle'. A principle in *Government and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Binding Theory, whose substance is that all sentences must have a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subject, seen as supplementing the *projection principle.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Extended Standard Theory'. Version of Chomsky's model of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *transformational grammar current in the mid-1970s, distinguished

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from the so-called *Standard Theory mainly in that *semantic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: representations of sentences, in so far as they belonged to an account

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of grammar, were said to be determined either wholly or in part by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *surface structures rather than by *deep structures.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: extension. 1. In the ordinary sense. Thus analogical extension is an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: extension in the range of words formed in a particular way, seen as by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *analogy with those already so formed. 'Extension of meaning' is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: used for the development of a new sense of a lexical unit: thus, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: particular, a figurative extension which involves a *metaphor or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: other *figure of speech. It is also used of the widening of an existing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sense: cf. widening of meaning. 2. Philosophers' term for the range

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of individuals, etc. to which e.g. a term applies: e.g. the extension of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: computer is the set of all computers. Hence, in particular, an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: extensional definition of a class or set is a specification one by one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of its members. Opp., in this sense, intension, intensional.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'extensive'. (Verb, complementation) that is not *intensive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: external. Not belonging to, or not conceived as directly relevant to,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a *language system. Hence *external history deals with everything

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: except the way such a system changes; 'external causes' of change

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'external argument'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are factors, such as the influence of another language, seen as lying

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: outside the system of a language whose changes are the object of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: study; 'external evidence', e.g. of *psychological reality, is evidence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: other than that on which an account of a language system is explicitly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: based.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'external argument'. An *argument of a verb external to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *predicate (1) or *verb phrase: i.e. in particular, a subject.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: external history. The history of a language as the means of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: communication in a community, as opposed to the *internal history

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of a language system. E.g. it is part of the external history of English

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: people spoke both English and French in the Middle Ages, that it was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that it was brought to Britain by immigration in the Dark Ages, that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it came to be written in a version of the Roman alphabet, that many

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spread to North America in the 17th century, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'externalized language' = E-language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: external sandhi. Processes of phonological modification (*sandhi)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that take place at or across word boundaries. Thus, by one common

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: process of external sandhi in English, an initial [s} in words like steak is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: assimilated to an [S] in e.g. fish steak.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: extraction. Any syntactic process by which something is moved from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: within a clause or other unit to a position outside it. E.g. in You said

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [who was there], who is an element within the subordinate clause; in Who

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: did you say |was there]?, it is seen as extracted from that position to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: become an element in the main clause.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: extrametrical. (Syllable, etc.) seen, originally in *Metrical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Phonology, as irrelevant to the definition of a metrical structure. E.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in Latin, the position of the accent depended on the quantity or weight

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the next to last syllable in a word. But that of the final syllable did

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not matter: therefore, in establishing the structure to which the rule

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of accentuation applied, the final syllable is 'extrametrical'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: extraposition. Construction of e.g. It's wonderful [to see you], It amazes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: me [that you have done it so fast], It was odd [meeting her in New York]. By

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: implication, the unit enclosed in brackets is ‘extraposed' from a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formally basic, though often in practice far less usual, position at the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: beginning: [To see you] is wonderful, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also of constructions in which an element is detached e.g. from a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: head noun. Thus the relative clause who wanted to see you would be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ‘extraposed', in some accounts, in The man is here who wanted to see you.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: extrinsic allophone. One which is not *intrinsic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: extrinsic ordering. See ordered rules.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: F

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Fo = fundamental frequency.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: F1 F2. See formant (1).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'face'. Developed as a technical term in explaining ways of being

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: polite. If one is ordered about by other people one will, in the ordinary

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sense, 'lose face': one's self-respect and freedom of action will be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diminished. Hence a tendency for people not to give direct orders;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: instead a request will be put in the form of a question ('Could you

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: come and hold this?'), making clear its slightness and that it is just a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: request (Could you perhaps come and hold this for a second?'), and so

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on. In an account by P. Brown and S. C. Levinson in the late 1970s, face

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is defined as a basic want' of individuals, and analysed into negative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: face (the want that one's freedom of action should not be impeded by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: others) and positive face (the want that one's own wants should be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: desirable to others also). The basic strategy of politeness is to minimize

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the threat to an addressee's ‘negative face' and enhance their positive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: face' as much as possible.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: factitive. (Verb) denoting an action or process that leads to a result.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. kill or make: to kill someone or something is to produce the result

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that they are dead; to make something or to make someone happy has

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the result that the thing exists or the person is happy.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: factive. (Verb, etc.) whose use commits a speaker to the truth of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subordinate proposition. E.g. know or realize: to say She doesn't know (or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: She hasn't realized) that it has stopped raining is to commit oneself to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: truth of 'It has stopped raining'. Think, by contrast, is non-factive: one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: makes no such commitment if one says She thinks it has stopped raining.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: facultative = optional.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'fading' (of meaning) = bleaching.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: north Atlantic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Faeroese. North *Germanic, spoken in the Faeroe Islands in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: low. Opp. rising in both senses.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: falling. 1. (Diphthong) of which the first part or element is the more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prominent: e.g. [5i] in boy as opposed to [jo:] or [1:] in your. 2. (*Tone,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: intonation) in which the pitch falls from relatively high to relatively

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fall-rise. Intonational contour in which there is a fall followed by a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rise on the same tonic or nucleus: e.g. in southern British English, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: questions such as When will dinner be "REady?

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'false friend'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'false friend'. A word in one language which sounds like one in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: another and may be taken by mistake as having the same meaning

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. English cold and German kalt mean 'cold'; therefore one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: misunderstands Italian or Spanish caldo 'hot' as also meaning 'cold'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: falsetto. *Voice quality in which voiced sounds are produced with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the vocal cords stretched and therefore thinner. Hence with a higher

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: range of *fundamental frequency, perceived as a higher pitch range.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between ‘T’ and 'V' forms.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: familiar form. Pronoun, form of verb, etc. used in addressing,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: among others, close friends: e.g. German du or French tu (familiar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: second-person singular) as opposed to Sie or vous. Cf. polite form; such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: oppositions are also described, from the forms in French, as holding

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: members.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: family. A group oflanguages that have developed from a single

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ancestor: e.g. *Indo-European, of which English is one of many

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. branch; phylum; stock. Some linguists have tried to apply

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: such terms to different levels in a hierarchy, on the analogy of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'genus', 'order', etc. in biology. E.g. Indo-European is a 'family'; any

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: groups above it would be variously or successively 'superfamilies',

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'macrofamilies', 'stocks', 'superstocks', or 'phyla'; those below it will

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be ‘subfamilies', in turn divided into 'branches', 'groups', etc. But such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinctions are not established consistently, and generally imply more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: than we do or can know. A safer alternative is to speak of a family

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whenever a common origin can be accepted as certain (thus Indo-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: European or e.g. *Austronesian), and of branches, larger or smaller,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: within it (e.g. *Indo-Iranian and, within that, *Iranian). When a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: common origin is speculative or less firmly supported, one may

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: simply talk of a 'conjectural family' (e.g. *'Nostratic'), a proposed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: family' (e.g. * Austro-Asiatic), or a probable family'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the others.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'family resemblance'. Wittgenstein's description of the links

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between different uses of a word. E.g. point may be used of the tip of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dagger or a needle, of a point of land sticking into the sea, of a mark

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on paper made by a point, of a point on a scale, and so on. There is no

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: single property that these and only these have in common, but there

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are similarities, as among people in a family, that link each of them to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Taken up by linguists especially in the 1980s; often associated, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: occasionally confused, with ideas in *prototype theory.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'family tree'. See genetic classification; Stammbaum model

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Fanagalo. See Zulu.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Farsi. See Persian.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: favourite sentence-forms. Bloomfield's term for the sentence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constructions predominant in a given language: e.g. in Erglish, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: feeding

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constructions of subject and predicate, or ofimperatives without

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subjects. Opposed at the other extreme to those of *minor sentences

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: such as Ouch! or Thank you.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: feature. Any property of or assigned to a unit. Originally in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonology, where often restricted to *distinctive features. Thus [i:] in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: beat is phonetically and phonologically a front vowel: that is, it has the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: feature 'front'. Thence to other types of unit: e.g. in a *componential

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: analysis of word meaning, woman has the features adult' and ‘female'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that is, it denotes people who are both adult and female.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Often formulated as a variable. Thus [front] or ± front] represents a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: variable feature with the values [+ front (front) and [– front] (not front;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: i.e. back). Units themselves are often described as bundles of features:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thus the vowel in beat would be constituted as a phonological unit

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: precisely by the bundle of features which distinguish it from others:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vocalic' (or [+ vocalic}), 'front' (or [+ front]), and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: feature matrix. A two-dimensional display of the phonetic features

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: characterizing each of a sequence of phonological segments. In the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: illustration, the features on the left are those proposed by *Jakobson in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the 1950s: each has two values, the positive (e.g. vocalic or [+ vocalic])

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: first, the negative second. In the table the value of each is shown, where

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: applicable, for each of the successive units of pin. Thus, in the first

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: column, [p] has a negative value for the feature ‘vocalic/non-vocalic'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and a positive value for ‘consonantal/non-consonantal'; these values

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are those of every consonant in English except [r] and [1]. In the third

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: row, [p] has the negative value 'diffuse' for the feature compact/diffuse',

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and so on. Where the distinction does not apply the space is blank.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A distinctive feature matrix (or DF-matrix) is strictly one, like this,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: displaying *distinctive features only.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: feature spreading. Term in *Autosegmental Phonology for the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: extension of a feature, e.g. of tone, to an adjacent element not already

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: associated with such a feature.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: feeding. The relation between rules which are *ordered in such a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: way that the application of the earlier rule enlarges the set of forms

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that the later will apply to. Especially in *Generative Phonology: e.g. a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: felicity conditions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rule by which a front vowel is inserted between two consonants might

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: feed a later rule by which velars are palatalized before a front vowel.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: Firth, John Rupert (1890-1960). From 1944 the first professor of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: general linguistics in Britain. Distinguished from other theorists of his

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generation by his insistence that language should be studied as part of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a social process. A linguist's data were for him events embedded in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: specific contexts, and linguistics in general was concerned with the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: techniques by which they are handled across a spectrum of varying

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: levels of abstraction. Hence, in particular, an emphasis on context at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: all points, and a profound disagreement with the prevailing view of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Saussure and his followers, in which the object of study was an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: integrated *language system seen as a reality underlying speech.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: in English is often defined as a stressed syllable plus any following

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: members, while a semantic or *notional definition might refer to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mathematical system. Thus a formal grammar is a set of rules that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: precisely specifies a set e.g. of *strings formed by an operation of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *concatenation; a formal language is a set so specified.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: extension from the second, the term has often been used to mean no

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more than 'explicit', 'cast in quasi-mathematical notation', etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
