layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: situations in which they are appropriate. E.g. in the formal style

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of a scholarly paper or legal document, words will be longer and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constructions will be more complex and without *ellipsis: in a casual

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conversation, the opposite. A broad distinction of degree: details are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: best referred to the descriptions of specific *registers (1).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sense.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Polite forms or *honorifics are described as ‘formal' in a similar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formalization. An account or formulation that is *formal (2):

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: especially, in linguistics, of a model of grammar or some part of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formal semantics. Branch of philosophy concerned with the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: assigning of precise interpretations to expressions in artificial systems

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of mathematics or logic. Thus especially, in the philosophy of science

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the mid-20th century, in accounts of scientific theories, conceived

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as calculi interpreted with respect to some empirical domain. Thence,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in linguistics, of a similar interpretation of languages, on the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: assumption, due originally to *Montague Grammar in particular, that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it is illuminating to represent them, at a sufficient level of abstraction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from the phenomena of speech, as systems of the same kind.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure rules.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formal universal. Chomsky's term in the mid-1960s for an abstract

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: condition on the form that, hypothetically, the *generative grammar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of any language may take. Thus it might be an abstract condition on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rules and representations in phonology that all features should be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: binary, or, in syntax, that, at a certain level, all rules are *phrase

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Opp. substantive universal. But as Chomsky's theory developed the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinction became increasingly artificial. E.g. if the format of rules

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in *X-bar syntax is universal, do 'Spec' or 'Comp' represent formal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conditions on them, or substantive categories or relations?

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formant (1). A peak of acoustic energy centred on one point in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: range of frequencies covered by the spectrum of a vowel. Vowels have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: several formants, but the distinctions as perceived between them lie,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in particular, in the three lowest. In e.g. [i), the lowest or first formant

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (F1) is centred on a frequency below 300 Hz, while the second (F2) and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: third are high, around 2,000 and 2,500 Hz. In [a], by contrast, they are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spaced more evenly over a marginally narrower range.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formant (2)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Changes in the frequencies of formants can be displayed by a sound

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *spectrogram. A formant chart is a plotting of one formant against

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: another (typically F, against F2). When a vowel is preceded or followed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by a consonant, changes in the shape of the vocal tract are reflected by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rapid shifts in formant frequencies: the direction of such formant

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transitions is the main acoustic feature distinguishing stops such as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [p}, [t], and [k].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formant (2) = formative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and point.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formation. Any specific process by which a unit is formed from one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or more other units. Thus an inflectional formation by which present

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: participles in English are formed by the addition of -ing: sing → singing.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also a compound formation by which e.g. ballpoint is formed from ball

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formative. An *affix or other element within a word which is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: introduced by a morphological process. E.g. in destroyers, er and -s are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formatives introduced by successive processes of suffixation: destroy →

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: destroy + er → destroyer + s. 2. Also used, e.g. by Chomsky in the mid-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1960s, of a minimal unit of syntax equivalent to the *morpheme.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: form class. Bloomfield's term for a *syntactic category

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Formosan. The indigenous languages of Taiwan, which form a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: branch of *Austronesian.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: forms of address. Any of the distinct forms that speakers must

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or will normally use to addressees who are e.g. of different social

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: standing or with whom their personal relationships are different.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thus addresseecontrolled *honorifics, *familiar forms vs. *polite

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: forms, forenames or surnames, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formula. A specific form of words used in a specific context: thus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: especially in ritual (e.g. recital of a Christian creed), or in other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ritualized activities (e.g. 'Return to Manchester, please' in buying

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a train ticket). Thence to other ready-made forms: e.g. those used

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by oral poets or story-tellers as building blocks in composition, or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *fixed expressions generally.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Formulaic discourse' or 'formulaic language' has a structure

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: built on formulae, especially in stricter senses.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: form word. A word which has *grammatical meaning. E.g. a is a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: form word (or grammatical word or function word) in a cow.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposed to voiced.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fortis. (Consonant) articulated, or claimed to be articulated, with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: higher muscular tension. Traditionally of voiceless consonants as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: From Latin fortis ‘strong'. Opp. lenis: cf. tense (2) vs. lax.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: free (4)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fortition. Any change or process by which a sound is, or is conceived

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as being, 'strengthened'; e.g. a sound change by which [t] > [tt], where a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: longer closure is seen as requiring greater effort of articulation. Opp.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and modelled on, lenition.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fossilized. (Form, construction) no longer used freely. Thus the hue of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hue and cry is a fossilized form used only in that phrase or, possibly, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: allusion to it; a sentence like The devil take the hindmost! has a fossilized

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: construction in which subjects, verbs, etc. cannot be freely combined.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'fourth person'. Usually = obviative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fragment. See sentence fragment.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the – people.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: frame. Any representation of a context, within a sentence, etc., in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which linguistic units can appear. E.g. adjectives, such as happy or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: helpful, are among the units that can fill the blank (—) in the frame

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Originally as a tool in the analysis of distributions: see substitution

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: frame. Subsequently as a representation in the lexicon of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constructions in which units can be used: see Case Grammar (for case

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: frames), subcategorization (for subcategorization frames).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Franco-Provencal. Philologists' term for the *Romance dialects

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spoken or once spoken in an area including the west of Switzerland,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the Val d'Aosta in north-west Italy, and in adjoining areas of France as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: far as a point west of Lyons.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: own, is a bound form.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: free (1). (*Morpheme) which can stand as a word on its own: thus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: kind in unkind is a free form, whereas un-, since it is not a word on its

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: he would come.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: free (2). (Pronoun, etc.) that is not linked syntactically to an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: antecedent: e.g. he is free in the domain formed by the sentence I knew

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Opp. bound (2). The sense is derived from use in logic, where a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: variable is free' if it must be assigned a value for the expression which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contains it to be meaningful.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: free (3). (Accent) which can fall in principle on any syllable. E.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Italian has a virtually free stress accent, falling in some words on the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: final syllable, in others on the penultimate, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: free (4). (Word order) which is not determined by a rule of syntax:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opp. fixed (2). A language with 'free word order' is accordingly one in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which the order of syntactic elements varies according to the context

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in which someone is speaking, for rhetorical effect, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Many languages have, to a greater or lesser degree, a free phrase

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: order. E.g. in Italian a subject and a verb might be in either order: Il

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mio amico (lit. 'the my friend') è arrivato (lit. 'is arrived’), or, with verb

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: free indirect style

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: first, È arrivato il mio amico 'My friend has arrived'. But within these

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phrases the order of words cannot vary. Other languages, such as Latin

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or Ancient Greek, have free word order' in a stricter sense: i.e. in many

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constructions words which stand in a close syntactic relation may be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: separated, e.g. in a specific context or for rhetorical effect, by others to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which neither, or only one, relates directly. Thus in Latin an adjective

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: could easily be separated from the noun it modifies, by a preposition

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (paucis post diebus ‘(a) few after days'), by a verb, or by a succession of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: words in various relationships.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: etc. are presented from the viewpoint of a character as well as that of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: present' time of the narration and the 'I' of the narrator: cf., in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speech, He thought 'She is going to ask me tomorrow'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: free indirect style. Style of e.g. literary narrative in which events,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the narrator. In Plainly she was going to ask him tomorrow', the past

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tense (was) and third person pronoun (him) are appropriate to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *indirect speech, He thought she was going to ask him the day after. But the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: adverb of time (tomorrow) refers to the future as seen by a character

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: who thinks the other character (‘she') will do this: cf., in *direct

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: From French ('style indirect libre’): see also empathy.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clause.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: free relative clause. A clause whose structure is or is like that of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a *relative clause but whose role in a larger construction is that of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: noun phrase; e.g. whatever she wants in Whatever she wants she gets, or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the archaic who dares in Who dares wins. Also called a nominal relative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'free ride'. The derivation of a form by means of a rule already

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: posited for some other purpose. Thus a rule was posited, in terms of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Generative Phonology, by which e.g. [dı'vΛin] (divine) was derived from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: underlying [divīn]: the purpose of this was to explain its alternation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with [divın] (in divinity). But then, by a 'free ride' on the same rule, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [aı] ofe.g. fine, which was involved in no alternation, could also be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: derived from underlying [ī].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: underlying forms.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The derivation was free' in the sense that the measure in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proposed *evaluation procedure was of rules alone. The perceived

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: advantage was that [aı] could then be eliminated as an element in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: free variation. The relation between sounds or forms which have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: similar or partly similar distributions but are not described as being

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in contrast. E.g. for some speakers of English. a flapped r {r} may be in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: free variation with a continuant [].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In a strict sense, free variation might be defined as variation which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: does not correlate with any other variable, e.g. context in a word or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence, or the style of speech or social background of a speaker.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: But its use will normally reflect the criteria for contrast in a given

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: investigation. E.g. [dri:md] and [drempt| (both written dreamed) might

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be treated as free variants in a study of morphology, but not in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stylistics or sociolinguistics.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: native language (notably Québecois in Canada) and as a second

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language, e.g. in Africa. The standard language is in origin the dialect

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thus, schematically, She telephone-FREQ 'She keeps on telephoning'.

layout_dets.text: Cf. iterative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fricative ['frikətiv]. Consonant in which the space between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *articulators is constricted to the point at which an air flow passes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *labiodental fricatives, with turbulence originating at the point

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: where air flows outwards through a channel constricted by the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: frictionless continuant. See continuant.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Frisian. *Germanic language most clearly related, within *West

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Germanic, to English; spoken mainly in the Dutch province of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Friesland, where it is losing speakers to Dutch, and, in different

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: forms, in parts of north-west Germany.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speakers still in six figures.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Friulan. *Rhaeto-Romance dialect spoken in the extreme north-east

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of Italy, in an area centred on Udine. Important regionally, with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: central.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: front. (Vowel) articulated with the highest point of the tongue

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: towards the front of the mouth: e.g. [i:] in seen. Opp. back; also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Hence [± front] as a *distinctive feature in phonology.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fronting. Any syntactic process by which elements are moved to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a *marked position at the beginning of a sentence. E.g. the object

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (that problem) is fronted in That problem I can't solve; a verb and its

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: principle be restricted e.g. to one which includes a *fossilized word

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that is normal in that combination only: e.g. spick and span, go berserk.

layout_dets.text: FSP = Functional Sentence Perspective.

layout_dets.text: f-structure. One of two levels of syntax in *Lexical-Functional

layout_dets.text: Fula. African language whose speakers are distributed over much of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Guinea to northern Cameroon. Major dialects are especially in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: full sentence. Bloomfield's term for a sentence that is not a *minor

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence: defined as an instance of a *favourite sentence-form.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: full word. One whose meaning is *lexical rather than *grammatical.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thus, in particular, a full verb, such as come in could have come, as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposed to the *auxiliaries could and have.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure. E.g. in I met my brother, the phrase my brother has the function

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or role' of *direct object: i.e. it plays the part of direct object in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: function. 1. Used very widely of the part that a unit plays in a larger

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: larger construction of which that is one element. Following the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: question ‘Can you come?', the utterance 'Yes' would function as an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: answer: i.e. it plays that part in a larger question-answer interchange.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The formula 'Let us pray' has a function, with other elements such as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: linguistics; functional syntax; functions of language; syntactic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: function. 2. Other uses reflect a mathematician's sense of functions as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: Functional Grammar. Model of *functional syntax developed since

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the late 1970s by S. C. Dik and his followers. Basically an account of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clause structure in which functions are distinguished separately on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: three levels: e.g., in Bill left yesterday, Bill has the syntactic function of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subject and the semantic function of *agent; it might also have the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pragmatic function of *theme. Semantic functions are associated with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *predicates (2) in the lexicon (e.g. agent with leave), and the *nucleus

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (1) of a clause (e.g. that represented by Bill left) may also be extended

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by *satellites (e.g. that represented by yesterday in Bill left yesterday);

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: syntactic functions are then assigned to its elements; then pragmatic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: functions. A clear distinction is drawn between the rules by which this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: functional structure is established, and the 'expression rules' which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: specify the ways in which it is realized, by order, intonation, cases or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prepositions, the voice of the verb, and so on. Of these, the order of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: elements in particular is determined, as far as the structure of a given

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language allows, by a universal principle.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: functional linguistics. Label adopted by various schools of linguists

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: who wish to emphasize the attention given in their theories to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: functions of language in general, or to those of specific features in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: functions of language

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: particular textual or other contexts. E.g. the 'functionalism' of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Prague School, of *Martinet, etc. seen in opposition to forms of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *structuralism in which the system of a language is explicitly studied

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in abstraction from its functions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Functional Sentence Perspective. A model of the *information

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure of sentences, developed in the early 1960s by J. Firbas and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: others in the tradition of the pre-war *Prague School. Parts of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence representing *given information are said to have the lowest

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: degree of communicative dynamism (or CD): i.e. the amount that,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in context, they communicate to addressees is the least. These form

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the theme: cf. theme (1). Parts representing new information have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the highest degree: these form the rheme. Parts which have an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: intermediate degree are sometimes said to form a transition between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: theme and rheme.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Suppose e.g. that A asks 'Who bought it?'. B might reply Joín

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bought it', with (in this context) bought it as theme and john as rheme.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: John. By a general principle this is taken to be, if all else is equal, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: functional syntax. 1. A treatment of syntax in which *syntactic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: functions, such as subject and object, are primitive or at least central.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2. A treatment of syntax in which aspects of the construction of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentences are explained by, or related to, the functions that they play

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: level, the senses are the same.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Some accounts are 'functional' primarily in sense 1, others primarily

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in sénse 2. But there is a widespread implication that, at some deeper

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: very high.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: functional yield. The number of *minimal pairs distinguished by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a given opposition between phonemes. E.g. there is a distinction for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: some speakers of English between voiceless [m] (in which, when, whin)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and voiced [w] (in witch, wen, win). But pairs such as these are few;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: therefore its functional yield is low. By contrast, that of {p] vs. [k] is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of [m] vs. [w].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also called 'functional load'. A low value has often been seen as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: factor in the loss of oppositions: e.g. the loss, for many other speakers,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: something, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: functions of language. Any of the kinds of things that can be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: done in, or through the use of, language. Thus an utterance may give

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: information, show that the speaker is angry, try to get someone to do

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: fundamental frequency. The frequency with which e.g. a vibrating

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: string vibrates as a whole. Thus, in speech, the fundamental frequency

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the production of a vowel is the frequency, as measured in hertz

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (Hz) = cycles per second, at which the vocal cords are so vibrating.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fusion. Any process by which units, etc. that are separate at one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *level of representation are realized by a form in which there is no

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corresponding boundary. Thus in morphology: e.g. flyer is made up of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fly [flaı] and -er [ə], but in some varieties of English [aı} and {ə] are fused

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to a single long vowel (roughly [fla:]). The morphological units fly and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: er may then be said to have fused exponents.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fusional. (Language) in which there is no clear boundary within the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: future perfect. Form of verb used of a future action or event, seen as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prior to some moment of time which is itself still later in the future:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thus, in Latin, venero 'I will have come' (will have come by e.g. the day

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: after tomorrow) as opposed to the ‘simple future' veniam 'I will come'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of truth, instead of an absolute distinction between true and false.

layout_dets.text: Generalized Phrase Structure Grammar. Formal model of syntax

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: developed by G. J. M. Gazdar, and subsequently by others, from the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: end of the 1970s. Basically a *phrase structure grammar, but with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: additional devices, in particular the use of *metarules and *slash

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: categories, that removed the need, assumed in most theories of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generative grammar at the time, for *transformations. A passive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence, for example, is characterized by phrase structure rules

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: derived in part, by a higher-level rule, from those that characterize an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: active; hence there is no need for a transformation that relates such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentences directly. In an interrogative like Who can you see?, who is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: related, by a phrase structure rule, to a phrase that must contain a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: null noun phrase: [can you see rl ]]. This removes the need for a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transformation (e.g. *move α) which would move who from the object

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The main applications are in computational linguistics, where

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parsing with phrase structure systems is simple and well understood.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Usually linked to a system of semantic interpretation, derived from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with those of syntax.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'generalized quantifier'. Logicians' term for an expression

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: interpreted as representing a set of subsets. Adapted, in *formal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantics, to represent the meaning of noun phrases: e.g. some people

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: denotes the set of all subsets of individuals whose members are a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subset of people; likewise, e.g. Matthews denotes the set of all subsets

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whose member is Matthews.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A sentence such as Some people like formal semantics is true if, in a given

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: situation, a property denoted by the predicate (that of liking formal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantics) holds of, in this case, some people. If noun phrases denote

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generalized quantifiers, a generalized quantifier can accordingly be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: represented as a function from a property (such as liking formal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantics) to a truth value (true or false in given circumstances).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generalized transformation. A *transformation which combines

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: two separate structures: e.g. one combining those of Mary asked

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (something) and Bill was happy to form that of Mary asked if Bill was happy.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generative capacity. The capacity of a given type of *generative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammar both to generate a specific range of *languages and to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: assign a specific range of structures. Thus the generative capacity of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *transformational grammars is greater on both counts than that of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generative capacity; the set of analyses that can be assigned to their

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentences the *strong generative capacity.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generative dialectology. The application of *Generative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Phonology, in the early 1970s, to the description of dialects. Variants

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the same form were assigned a common underlying representation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in all dialects, with different realizations derived by different

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonological rules, by the same rules ordered differently, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generative grammar. 1. A set of *rules (2) which indicate precisely

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: what can be and cannot be a sentence in a language. Formulated by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Chomsky in the 1950s as an abstract device interpreted as generating,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or producing, a set of *strings or sequences of units: a 'sentence' was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formally a string so generated, and a 'language' defined as a set of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentences. 2. Loosely, without the article, of schools or concepts of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: linguistics based at least historically on the construction of such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammars: thus especially the programme of Chomsky and his

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: followers, the 'generativist' schools of Chomskyan origin, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Phrase structure grammars and *transformational grammars were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: developed as specific types of generative grammar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Generative Phonology. Treatment of phonology and morphology

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: developed by *Halle and others from the end of the 1950s. In its classic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: form, the *surface structure of each sentence was a configuration of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'formatives' or *morphemes, each represented in the *lexicon by a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: single *feature matrix. Such representations were the input to a set

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of *ordered phonological rules, each conceived as an instruction to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: change, add, delete, or rearrange features in specific contexts. These

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Generative Semantics

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: resulted in *phonetic representations which were in turn feature

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: matrices.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The classic account is that of Chomsky and Halle, *SPE (1968). It

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was widely criticized from the early 1970s, especially for proposing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *underlying forms that were unjustifiably *abstract.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Generative Semantics. Theory of *transformational grammar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: developed from the late 1960s to the mid-1970s. The original proposal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was that a *base component of a grammar should directly generate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *semantic representations of sentences, which would be converted to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *surface structures with no intervening level of *deep structure. This

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was associated in particular with the view that lexical items were units

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: only at the surface level. But in the 1970s it became clear that the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proposed semantic representations could not be assigned by rules of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammar independent of the knowledge, beliefs, etc. of individual

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speakers. Therefore the break with what was later called the *Standard

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Theory of transformational grammar was in reality far more radical.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: generic reference. Reference to the entire class of individuals,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: specific members of it. Thus grass snakes or the grass snake have generic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reference in statements about the species: Grass snakes eat slugs, or The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grass snake is not poisonous. By the same token these are generic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: statements, or express generic propositions. In contrast, the grass

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: snake has non-generic or specific reference in, e.g. I just saw the grass

layout_dets.text: genetic classification. The classification oflanguages according to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: their presumed development from common ancestors. E.g. French and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Spanish are among those classed as *Romance languages, since both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: have developed from Latin. They are also *Indo-European languages,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with the same hypothetical ancestor as many others across Eurasia.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The method of genetic classification is the *comparative method

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. typological classification. Genetic relations are commonly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: represented by tree diagrams, called 'family trees'. But the connection

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with families in the ordinary sense is metaphorical.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: gesture. Any voluntary movement of the body which is significant

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: soft palate. In *Articulatory Phonology gestures are the basic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: Gilliéron, Jules (1854-1926). A pioneer in dialect geography, whose

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: first atlas, of the phonetics of the French-speaking Valais of his native

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Switzerland, appeared in 1881. Later associated with the phonetician

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: P. Rousselot in the programme that led eventually to the publication,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in 1902-10, of the Atlas linguistique de la France. The data for this had

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: been obtained on the spot by his co-author, E. Edmont, who had been

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: As a theorist Gilliéron denied that dialects themselves had any

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: objective reality. In monographs based on the atlas, he explored in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: particular changes in the lexicon, in response e.g. to *homonymic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clashes that result from sound change (word X, becoming

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: homonymous with Y, is replaced by Z), or to phonetic *erosion (word

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: X, having become too short for clear communication, is replaced by Y

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or extended by an affix). The findings of the atlas have often been cited

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: against the *Neogrammarian regularity principle in sound change.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: But Gilliéron's own etymological studies seem rather to presuppose it.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: given. Known to or recoverable by an addressee, etc. If parent A asks

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Where are the children?', parent B might answer Jane's gone to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hairdresser'. In the sentence uttered by B, the subject Jane corresponds

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to what is given: i.e. Jane is one of the children A has referred to. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: remainder, (ha)s gone to the hairdresser, corresponds to what is new: i.e.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: what A does not know already.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Usually, as in this account, of given vs. new ‘information'. But also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *information structure 'given Jane + new (ha)s gone to the hairdresser'.

layout_dets.text: glottochronology. Method proposed by M. Swadesh in the 1950s, by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which he hoped to determine the date at which genetically related

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages diverged. He assumed that every language had a basic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: but, in Mary saw John, the subject Mary is commanded by, and therefore

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'governed' by, *INFL, which labels it as 'nominative'. Likewise the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: gradable antonymy. Relation of *antonymy in which the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposition is one of degree. E.g. between large and small: although they

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are opposites, the same thing may be at once large by one standard

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and small by another, or larger than 'x' and yet smaller than ‘y'. In

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: gradation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: such a relation one term is often neutral. Thus if one wants to know

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the size of something one will normally ask 'how large' it is. One will

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not, except in a specific context or for some specific reason, ask 'how

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: small' it is. In that sense small is the *marked term in the opposition,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: large the unmarked.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for the category in which simple or positive' forms of adjectives and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: gradience. A series of instances intermediate between two

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: categories, constructions, etc. E.g. blackboard is, by all relevant criteria,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a *compound: it has stress on its first element (bláckboard), its precise

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaning does not follow from those of black and board individually,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and so on. Fine weather is equally, by all criteria, not a compound. But

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: many other cases are less clear. Bond Street is in meaning as regular as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Trafalgar Square, but stress is again on the first element. Able seaman has

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stress on its second element, but does not simply mean ‘seaman who is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: able'. White lie is likewise not in meaning 'lie which is white'; but it too

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: has stress on its second element and, in addition, white might be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: separately modified (a very white lie). So, by such criteria, these form

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: part of a gradience between compounds and non-compounds.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (close) and [a] (open), with intermediate [ε] (mid).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: such as and or some and the roles of corresponding operators in a

layout_dets.text: system of logic. They were not published fully until the end of his life

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (in Studies in the Way of Words, 1989), but ideas taken from them have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: been influential in linguistics since the early 1970s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Grimm, Jacob (1785-1863). Germanist, known to the world for the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Märchen collected and published by him and his brother Wilhelm, to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: linguistics for his Deutsche Grammatik (1819-37) and in particular for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the formulation of *Grimm's Law, based on the insight of *Rask, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the second edition (1822) of its first volume. At the end of their lives he

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and his brother worked together on the Deutsches Wörterbuch, published

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in parts from 1854 and finally completed over a century later.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Grimm's Law. *Sound law or series of sound laws by which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonants in *Germanic differ systematically in *manner of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: articulation from those of cognate forms in other Indo-European

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages. In a traditional account, 'voiced aspirated' stops (e.g. *dh)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: change in Germanic to voiced ([d)); voiced stops (*d) change in turn to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: voiceless ([t]); voiceless stops (*t) change to fricatives ([θ]).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Called by Germanists the 'First Sound Shift'. The 'Second Sound

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Shift', by which e.g. Germanic *t > ts, is peculiar to High *German.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: groove fricative = rill fricative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'group' = phrase, or specifically phrase (2) or word group.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Guaraní. Spoken throughout Paraguay, and the only language,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: though Spanish also has official status, of many of its people.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Paraguayan Guaraní is related to Classical Guaraní, now dead but

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: recorded by early Jesuit missionaries, within a branch of *Tupi-Guaraní

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that extends to neighbouring parts of Brazil, Bolivia, and Argentina.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Gujarati. *Indo-Aryan language, spoken mainly in the Indian states

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of Gujarat, where it has official status, and Maharashtra; also widely,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: through emigration, in South and East Africa and elsewhere. Written

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in a script derived from *Devanagari.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Gullah. English-based *creole spoken along the coast of Georgia and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: South Carolina in the USA. The African elements in it were the subject

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of a pioneering study by a native speaker, L. D. Turner, in 1949.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: guņa. Term in *Sanskrit for a unit analysed as the combination of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: simple vowel or resonant with a preceding a. Thus i is a simple vowel;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Gypsy

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e is the guņa form resulting e.g. from a fusion of a and i across a word

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: boundary. One of three degrees of 'strengthening': see vrddhi.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Gur. Family of languages in the Sahel region of West Africa, from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: south-eastern Mali and northern Ivory Coast across Burkina Faso and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the north of Ghana, Togo, and Benin, into north-west Nigeria. Moré,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spoken in an area which includes Ouagadougou, is the main

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indigenous language of Burkina Faso. The family is also called

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Voltaic'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Gurmukhi. *Indian script developed for *Punjabi.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'guttural'. Older term for *velar consonants and others produced in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the back part of the vocal tract; no longer used in any technical sense.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Gypsy. See Romany.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: H. See diglossia.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: habitual. (Verb, *aspect) indicating something done, etc. consistently

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or habitually. Thus the present tense has a habitual use in e.g. I exercise

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the dog on Sundays.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: half-close. (Vowel) that is auditorily one-third of the way from *close

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to *open: thus [e] and [o] in the system of primary *cardinal vowels.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also called close-mid.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: half-open. (Vowel) that is auditorily one-third of the way from *open

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to *close: thus [ε] and [ə] in the system of primary *cardinal vowels.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also called open-mid.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Halle, Morris (1923- ). American linguist, associated first with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Jakobson and, from the mid-1950s, with Chomsky. Responsible

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: especially for the development of *Generative Phonology.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Halliday, Michael Alexander Kirkwood (1925- ). British linguist

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: who retired in 1987 from a chair in Sydney. Originally a specialist in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Chinese, whose earliest general theory was the model of grammar

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: eventually called *Systemic Grammar. In the late 1960s he applied

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: this, in particular, in an analysis of English intonation and in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: general account of the dimensions on which sentences are organized.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The dimension of 'transitivity' concerns the relations of e.g. actor to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: action or action to goal; that of 'mood' their broadly *interpersonal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: function (e.g. as interrogative or declarative); that of 'theme' the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: theory, especially as it emerged in the 1970s, is centred on an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: all-embracing concept of *function, including both the functions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: these develop.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relations of *theme to *rheme or *given to new. Halliday's general

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of utterances and texts and those of individual units within their

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure, and on the thesis that the nature of language as a semiotic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: system, and its development in each individual, must be studied in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: context of the social roles that individuals play, and the ways in which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Originally a follower of *Firth. Hence his own theories and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: followers, especially in the 1960s, were often called 'Neo-Firthian'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Hamitic. See Afro-Asiatic.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hamza. Sign in Arabic writing used to represent a *glottal stop.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hanging participle. See dangling participle.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Han'gul. The Korean alphabet, traditionally ascribed to King Sejong

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (1419-50). The characters representing consonants and vowels are in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Harris, James

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: part composed of smaller elements, which represent phonetic features

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: such as, in particular, a *place of articulation. These basic characters

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are then in turn combined into larger units representing syllables.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Han'gul is the only native alphabet designed for a language in the Far

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: East, and is unique, among systems of writing in normal use, for the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonological insight that informed it.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shortened to hapax. Cf. nonce-word.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hapax legomenon ['hapaks lr'goməndn]. A lexical unit found only

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: once in the surviving records of a language. Greek ‘said once'; often

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (> English idolatry).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: haplology. *Sporadic change in which successive syllables, etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which are similar in form are reduced to one. E.g. Late Latin idololatria

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'worship (-latria) of idols' was reduced to forms such as French idôlatrie

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Harappan script. That of the Harappan civilization, flourishing in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the Indus valley in the 3rd-2nd millennia Bc. Undeciphered and not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: demonstrably connected to later Indian scripts.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: palatalized.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'hard'. Used conventionally of *velar plosives in Romance languages:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thus 'hard' [k], [g] (spelled c, g) as opposed e.g. in Italian to 'soft' [tf],

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: {d3} (also spelled c, g). Also more generally, in languages such as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Russian which have palatalized consonants, of those that are not

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hard palate. The roof of the mouth between the back of the ridge

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: behind the teeth and the fleshy part called the *soft palate. *Palatal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consonants are articulated in this area.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: harmonic. Any of a series of tones at higher intervals accompanying

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the fundamental tone produced by a vibrating body. The frequency

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the fundamental tone is the *fundamental frequency, the lowest

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: harmonic the 'first harmonic', and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: harmony. See vowel harmony; consonant harmony.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Harris, James (1709-80). Author of an important philosophical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grammar, Hermes: or, a Philosophical Inquiry Concerning Languuge and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Universal Grammar (London, 1751). His work is grounded in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: philosophy of Aristotle and includes an original analysis of word

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: classes, in which ‘substantives' and ‘attributives' are opposed as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: principal parts of speech to ‘definitives' and 'conjunctives' as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accessories. Substantives include nouns and pronouns; attributives

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: verbs and participles with adjectives and adverbs; definitives are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: articles with other determiners; conjunctives include both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: conjunctions and prepositions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Harris's grammar was widely read and published after his death in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: both German (1788) and French (1795).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Harris, Zellig Sabbatai

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Harris, Zellig Sabbatai (1909-92). The leading theorist of the *Post-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bloomfieldian school in the USA. In Methods in Structural Linguístics

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (1951) he set out a series of formal procedures by which, on the basis

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of a corpus or sample of actual or potential utterances, a description

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of a language, in abstraction from the meanings of its units, could in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: principle be obtained in a mechanical and therefore replicable way,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: without reference to anything outside the corpus. This was perceived

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at the time as a method by which descriptions could be justified

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: scientifically. In the course of the 1950s Harris developed, in concert

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with his pupil Chomsky, ideas which the latter was to make his own:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: popular level, Language and Information (1988).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in particular, those of a *generative grammar and of syntactic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *transformations. But by the end of the decade their paths had

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: separated, and Harris's later work, which deals especially with syntax,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: has had less influence. His thought is summed up in his last two

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: books, A Theory of Language and Information (1991) and, at a more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'hash mark' (#). See double cross.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Hausa. *Chadic language, native to northern Nigeria (roughly from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Kaduna northwards and some 200 km. east of Kano westwards) and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: neighbouring parts of Niger. Also widespread as a second language,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: there and elsewhere, and as a lingua franca across West Africa. Written

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in Arabic script before the 20th century, now largely in Roman.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: population of the Hawaiian islands.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Hawaiian. *Polynesian, now spoken by a tiny minority of the native

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: head (1). A single element in a construction which characterizes or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: may stand for the construction as a whole.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: There are two main definitions, one narrower and due largely to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Bloomfield, the other wider and now more usual, following work by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: R. S. Jackendoff in the 1970s. 1. In the narrower definition, a phrase p

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: has a head h if h alone can bear any syntactic function that p can bear.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E.g. very cold can be replaced by cold in any construction: very cold water

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or cold water, I feel very cold or I feel cold. Therefore the adjective is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: its head and, by that token, the whole is an adjective phrase'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2. In the wider definition, a phrase p has a head h if the presence of h

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: determines the range of syntactic functions that p can bear. E.g. the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constructions into which on the table can enter are determined by the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: presence of a preposition, on. Therefore the preposition is its head and,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by that token, it is a prepositional phrase'. Similarly, in I feel cold, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predicate feel cold is a ‘verb phrase' whose construction, as a whole,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with I is determined by its having as its head the verb feel. This second

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: definition is central e.g. to *X-bar syntax.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: See also dependency.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: head (2). The part of an intonation pattern that falls on syllables

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: preceding the nuclear or *tonic syllable: e.g. in I didn't see "HEr, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: head falls on I didn't see. Cf. tail.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: heavy syllable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Head-Driven Phrase Structure Grammar. Formal model of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: syntax developed by C. Pollard and I. Sag in the late 1980s. In essence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a variant of *Generalized Phrase Structure Grammar in which the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure of syntactic units is constrained directly or indirectly by the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: properties of lexical units as *heads (1). E.g. the head of Bill hates silence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is (in this treatment) hates. The lexical properties of hates are such that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it combines with a following noun phrase: [hates silence]. By a process

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of *unification this is in turn a verb phrase, and, since hates is a verb

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the third person singular, the phrase as a whole is one which, as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: non-lexical head, combines, again by a process of unification, with a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subject in the third person singular.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: As in other models which extend the role of the *lexicon, there

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are either no or few specific rules. As in Generalized Phrase Structure

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Grammar, there is no operation, as in earlier or contemporary versions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of *transformational grammar, by which units are moved.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'headline language'. The style of newspaper headlines, studied as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *restricted language. Cf. block language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: head marking. Marking of syntactic relations on the *head (1)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as opposed to a subordinate or dependent element. E.g. in Semitic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages such as Hebrew, a *possessive construction is marked by the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: form of the head noun (traditionally in the *construct state). Opp.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dependent marking: e.g. in Latin a possessive construction is marked

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: instead by the genitive case of the noun that depends on the head.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Head Parameter. A proposed *parameter in *Principles and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Parameters Theory distinguishing orders of syntactic units in which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *heads precede and those in which they follow. An unconscious

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: revival of L. Tesnière's distinction of *centrifugal vs. centripetal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hearer. Strictly, anyone who hears an *utterance, whether addressed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to them (as an *addressee) or not.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by mistake.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: heavy. (Noun phrase, etc.) whose length or complexity affects the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: positions it can occupy in a sentence. E.g. one can say I gave John advice

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or I gave advice to John; but if John is replaced by the man you will remember

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meeting last week the second construction is at the very least more likely.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: One says I posted a letter to John rather than I posted to John a letter; but the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: second order is possible e.g. in I posted to John a letter which was sent here

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Heavy noun phrase shift', or more generally 'heavy constituent

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shift', is a proposed syntactic process by which 'heavy' elements are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: moved to a position later in the sentence.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: heavy syllable. One which counts rhythmically as two units rather

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: than one. E.g. in Latin, one which ended in either a consonant or a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: long vowel: [lik] in [re'liktus} relictus left behind', [li:} in {re'li:kwi:}

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reliqui 'I left behind'. One which ended in a short vowel was light: e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Hebrew

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: [li} in ('relik"i:] reliqui 'the rest'. In the last two examples this difference

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: determines, in particular, the different positions of the stress accent.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Called, in the western tradition, 'long' (= heavy) as opposed to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from the ancient grammarians of Sanskrit.

layout_dets.text: Hebrew. West *Semitic, spoken in antiquity in the interior of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Palestine; the language of the Jewish Bible (Old Testament),

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and liturgical language, until revived in its modern form, especially

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from the 1920s, as a prospective official language of Jewish settlers in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: what is now Israel. Written in a *Semitic alphabet whose modern form

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (‘square Hebrew') can be traced back to the 3rd century AD.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hedge. Any linguistic device by which a speaker avoids being

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is not acceptable, and so on. Thus, instead of saying ‘This argument is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: convincing', one might use a hedge and say ‘As far as I can see this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: argument is convincing'; instead of simply giving an order Carry it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'Could you perhaps carry it into the kitchen?'

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: into the kitchen!' one might use an interrogative as a hedge and say

layout_dets.text: hendiadys [hen'daiədis]. Term in rhetoric for two words joined by a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: coordinator but seen as expressing a single complex idea: e.g. in These

layout_dets.text: an institution.

layout_dets.text: hermeneutics. Movement in the philosophy of science, according

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to which the task of the human sciences is to elucidate the structure

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the social institutions underlying behaviour. Thus the aim of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: linguistics, as one human (and therefore ‘hermeneutic') science, is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to elucidate the rules oflanguage, seen as rules that constitute such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of Chomsky.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: From a term that usually means 'interpretation' or 'exegesis'. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: movement developed in Germany in the 1960s; its ideas have been

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: applied in linguistics since the 1970s, in opposition especially to those

layout_dets.text: Hieroglyphic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hesitation form. Any sound used conventionally in a specific

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: community to indicate that one is about to start or to continue

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speaking: e.g. English [ə:] (er).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hesternal. (Tense, form of verb) used or basically used in referring

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to events, etc. that have taken place on the day before the day of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speaking. From Latin hesternus 'of yesterday': cf. hodiernal.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hetero-. From the Greek word for 'other'. E.g. a noun whose

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inflection follows something other than the regular pattern is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: traditionally 'heteroclite'; the head e.g. of a noun phrase is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: heterocategorial if it is itself something other than a noun;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: heteroglosses link speakers using different forms on either side of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an *isogloss. Often in implied or explicit opposition to *homo- 'same':

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. two successive consonants are heterorganic (as opposed to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *homorganic) if they have different *places of articulation; a word

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is heteromorphemic if it is formed from two (i.e. two different)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphemes; successive sounds are heterosyllabic (as opposed to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *tautosyllabic) if they belong to different syllables.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: same sense as *homograph.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: heteronym. Used by various scholars for varying cases of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *homonymy. E.g. of words with the same meaning, such as pail and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bucket, used by different speakers or in different dialects; also in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alternative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: heuristic. General term, e.g. in computing, for a procedure which is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: designed to solve a problem by exploring the most likely possibilities,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as opposed to an algorithm, which mechanically examines every

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of draw out as ['drə: 'aut].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hiatus [har'eitəs|. A division between vowels belonging to different

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: words or syllables. E.g. [:] and [au] are in hiatus' in a pronunciation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tertiary.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hierarchy. Any ordering of units or levels on a scale of size,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: abstraction, or subordination. E.g. a *phrase structure tree assigns a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hierarchical structure to sentences; *levels of representation are often

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: seen as forming a hierarchy from phonetics upwards; Jespersen's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: theory of *ranks (1) proposes a hierarchy of primary, secondary, and
